<page-num>II</page-num>
<header>PREFACE.</header>

## CONCERNING THIS SECOND EDITION.

For studies regarding the works of the Apostolic Fathers <note>Early Christian writers who were believed to have known the Apostles personally</note>, nothing more significant has happened in a long time than the discovery in the Sinai Bible manuscript <note>The *Codex Sinaiticus*, one of the most important ancient copies of the Bible, discovered by Constantine von Tischendorf in 1844 and 1859</note> of the complete Epistle of Barnabas along with the first part of the *Shepherd*. For that epistle, in the language in which it was originally written by the author <note>Greek</note>, was not available in its entirety until now, nor was there great confidence in the portions drawn from more recent manuscripts. Indeed, the Latin translation of the longer first part (chapters 1–17) <note>of the *Shepherd of Hermas*</note>, as it was found in a manuscript from roughly the eighth century—formerly held at Corbie <note>A significant monastery in France</note> and now in St. Petersburg—and in that manuscript alone, while it occasionally surpasses the common Greek versions, it often provides a very corrupted text, especially in those chapters which were previously missing in Greek.

The work known as the *Shepherd of Hermas* <note>A 2nd-century Christian literary work comprising visions and commandments</note> fared with almost no less difficulty, suffering from Latin manuscripts notable for their great variety of readings and a Greek text from the "Leipzig leaves" <note>Fragments of the text found previously</note> that was poorly regarded. Hence, it seemed that the extremely important resources of the Sinai manuscript for supplementing and correcting these books—which are closest in time to the apostles themselves—should not be reserved for an entirely new edition of the Apostolic Fathers, which we intend to produce ourselves in a few years, but should be applied immediately to expand and improve the Dressel edition <note>Referring to Albert Dressel’s 1857 edition of these texts</note>. 

This was carried out so that the first part of the Epistle of Barnabas was fully transcribed from both of our editions of the Sinai manuscript; furthermore, whatever in it differs from the Greek phrasing of that same epistle and the first part of the book of Hermas, as it was published in Dressel’s work, was accurately reviewed. Therefore, those copies of the 1857 Dressel edition which had not yet been released to the public have been enlarged by these supplements. For that reason, they now appear adorned with the title of a "second edition," offered moreover at a reduced price, so that the academic youth—

<summary>In this preface, the editor explains how the discovery of the Codex Sinaiticus necessitated an immediate update to the existing Dressel edition of the Apostolic Fathers to include newly found, complete Greek texts of Barnabas and Hermas.</summary>
<keywords>Codex Sinaiticus, Epistle of Barnabas, Shepherd of Hermas, Albert Dressel, patristics, manuscript recovery, 19th-century biblical scholarship</keywords>

so that this book might be recommended with confidence. At our request, Dr. Johann Heinrich Gerhardts, a Doctor of Philosophy, undertook the labor we mentioned; we can testify that he has handled this matter with great skill and diligence.

For those who wish to inquire more accurately into the age of the Sinai manuscript <note>The *Codex Sinaiticus*, the oldest complete copy of the New Testament</note>, unless one prefers to consult our magnificent Saint Petersburg edition—which is furnished with two plates showing the actual handwriting of the *Epistle of Barnabas* and the *Shepherd*—the Introductory Remarks <note>original: *Prolegomena*</note> of the Sinai New Testament will suffice. In those remarks, we believe we have demonstrated that the manuscript was written around the middle of the fourth century¹. Indeed, how great the excellence of the Sinai text is will be doubtful to no one who has compared and weighed the various readings for Barnabas and Hermas. Here are specific examples from Barnabas:

**Chapter IV.** <note>original Greek: λεγοντασ οτι η διαθηκη ημων μεν· αλλ εκινοι ουτωσ εισ τελοσ απωλεσαν αυτην, λαβοντοσ ηδη του μωϋσεωσ</note> **saying that the covenant is indeed ours; but they lost it in this way forever, though Moses had already received it** instead of those words which, being corrupt, have strangely troubled learned men: *and they say that the covenant is theirs, and not also ours. But it is ours, because they lost it forever, which Moses received.* <note>The Sinai manuscript clarifies a confusing passage about who possesses the divine covenant</note>

**Chapter VI.** <note>original: ωσ αν δη αναπλασσοντοσ αυτου ημασ</note> **as if he were refashioning us** instead of <note>original: ὡς ἂν δὲ ἀναπλασσομένους αὐτοὺς ἡμᾶς</note> *as though they were refashioning us.*

**Chapter VII.** <note>original: οι ιερεισ του ναου</note> **the priests of the temple** instead of <note>original: οἱ ἱερεῖς τοῦ λαοῦ</note> *the priests of the people* (Menard <note>Nicholas Hugh Menard, a 17th-century scholar</note>, against the evidence of the manuscripts available to him, correctly thought "of the temple" should be read).

**Chapter X.** <note>original: ου μη, φησιν, κολληθηση ουδε ομοιωθηση</note> **You shall not, he says, be joined to nor become like,** just as it appears in the works of Clement of Alexandria and in the ancient translator, though later Greek manuscripts incorrectly omit the words "nor become like." In the same passage: <note>original: περιπατουντεσ, και περιβλεπονται τινα εκδυσωσιν δια την πλεονεξιαν· ωσ και τα ορνεα ταυτα μονα εαυτοισ ου ποριζει την τροφην, αλλα αργα (αργα corrector reposuit pro και τα) καθημενα εκζητει</note> **walking about, and they look around for someone to strip bare because of greed; just as these birds alone do not provide food for themselves, but sitting idle, they seek it out** instead of *walking about; and sitting idle they seek these things out.* (*The Ancient Translator <note>The old Latin version</note> reads: walking about, whom they might despoil. So these birds, not acquiring food for themselves alone, but sitting lazy, they seek it.*) In the same place: <note>original: εχετε τελιωσ και περι τησ βρωσεωσ</note> **you have [this] perfectly also concerning food** instead of <note>original: ἔχετε τελείως καὶ περὶ τῆς γνώσεως</note> *you have it perfectly also concerning knowledge* (*The Ancient Translator: you have a complete [teaching] about foods*).

***

1) The corrector of the *Epistle of Barnabas*, whom we have designated with the symbol \*\*, seems to have lived in the seventh century; however, the one we marked with the same sign in the *Shepherd* is hardly younger than the original scribe; those who followed him (\*\* and \*\*\*\*) fall roughly into the seventh and ninth centuries.

**Chapter XI.** **bearing forgiveness** <note>original Greek: το φερον αφεσιν</note> instead of **bearing unto forgiveness**.

**Chapter XII.** **that the Father makes all things manifest concerning his Son Jesus. Therefore he says to Moses, [to] Joshua the son of Nun, having given him this name when he sent him as a spy of the land: "Take"** instead of **that the Father makes all things manifest concerning [his] Son to Joshua the son of Nun. And having given this name, when he sent a spy of the land, [he said]: "Take."** <note>This passage discusses the symbolic naming of Joshua/Jesus in the Old Testament as a precursor to Christ</note>

**Chapter XVI.** **how, being led astray, the wretched men hoped in the building, and not in their God who made them, as being the house of God** instead of **how, being led astray, the wretched [men] hoped in the way, and not in God himself who made them, but as being the house of God** (<note>original Latin: *Vet. interpr.* — The Old Latin translator reads: "how wandering they had hope in the temple, as if in the Lord who made them, as if it were the house of God"</note>).

**Chapter XVII.** **for salvation. For if I write to you concerning things present or future** instead of **for the salvation of things present. For if I write to you concerning things future.** (<note>The Old Latin translator reads: "if indeed I should write to you of things present and future"</note>).

**Chapter XIX.** **the workings that happen to you, you shall receive as good, knowing that without God nothing happens** instead of **the workings that happen to you, receive as good**, with the rest of the sentence omitted. In the same place, **to those who hope in the same God**, in which more recent manuscripts omit the word **God**. In the same place, the words **"give to everyone who asks of you,"** which clearly appear to have been brought in here from the Gospels, are not supported by the authority of the Sinai manuscript¹. In the same place, **you shall not turn toward prayer with an evil conscience** instead of **you shall not come to your prayer with an evil conscience.**

**Chapter XXI.** **you have among yourselves those to whom you may work that which is good; do not fail** instead of **you have [those] toward whom you have worked among yourselves; do not forsake.** These examples are joined by many others. They are of such a nature that, with few exceptions, they brilliantly restore the ancient text, and we now finally rejoice that the most precious book of Barnabas has been restored to Christian literature.

The same would have to be said of *The Shepherd* <note>The *Shepherd of Hermas*, a 2nd-century Christian literary work composed of visions, mandates, and similitudes</note>, if our codex provided it in its entirety. Nevertheless, even in the fragments it does provide, there is the greatest critical value. Regarding what I believed in the year 1856—that the Leipzig text <note>A version of the *Shepherd* previously published in Leipzig, which was suspected of being a modern forgery or a back-translation from Latin</note> was translated from Latin in the Middle Ages rather than derived from the ancient Greek source itself—

1) At the end of the fourth chapter, the very significant words **"as it is written"** <note>original Latin: *sicut scriptum est*</note> are claimed for the writer himself by the Sinai manuscript, rather than for a Latin translator as was previously suspected. <note>This is a crucial point for scholars, as it shows the author of Barnabas quoting the New Testament as authoritative Scripture</note>

<page-num>IV</page-num>

...that it had been preserved, a matter on which I had the agreement of the great Constantine Oeconomos <note>A prominent Greek scholar and theologian (1780–1857)</note> among others; yet that point, if you look at it as a whole and in its entirety, has not been confirmed. Indeed, there is a certain passage, famous in the Simonidean affair <note>Referring to Constantine Simonides, who claimed to have forged the Codex Sinaiticus</note>, which I had previously urged should be seen as proof of a Latin origin for the text—specifically Vision 3, chapter 3: **"you are cunning regarding the writings"** <note>original Greek: πανοῦργος εἶ περὶ τὰς γραφάς; based on Wilhelm Dindorf’s conjecture, this might read "regarding unwritten things," or *περὶ τὰ ἄγραφα*</note>. It has now become very clear, both from the Ethiopic translator and from the Codex Sinaiticus, that this passage did indeed flow from Latin sources. I am inclined to think other elements should be compared with this, which the Leipzig text has in common with most Latin versions, despite the opposition of the Sinaitic, Ethiopic, and Palatine manuscripts. Of such a kind are the words read in Vision 3, chapter 6, where the common Latin version is: *those who knew the truth and did not remain in it, nor were they joined to the saints; for this reason they are useless.* The Leipzig text corresponds perfectly to this, reading: **those who have known the truth, but not remaining in it nor clinging to the saints; because of this they are useless** <note>original Greek: οἱ ἐγνωκότες τὴν ἀλήθειαν, μὴ ἐπιμείναντες δὲ ἐν αὐτῇ μηδὲ κολλώμενοι τοῖς ἁγίοις· διὰ τοῦτο ἄχρηστοί εἰσιν</note>. However, the Sinaitic, Ethiopic, and Palatine codices agree in adding nothing after the phrase **"but not remaining in it."** Those readings which, in these and similar instances, are unsupported by the authority of the Sinaitic codex<sup>2</sup>, undoubtedly depend on another <term>recension</term> <note>A specific version of a text resulting from a deliberate revision</note>; whether someone first established this in the Latin or the Greek remains ambiguous. But others will see to these matters soon, and I hope that the opportunity will not be lacking for us ourselves, as already indicated, to investigate the details more accurately. For now, I am satisfied to have consulted the edition of Dressel—full of the long-standing labors of a learned friend—by adding the Sinaitic readings. Just as these readings sufficiently show how much the Leipzig text (though not to be despised) has turned away from the ancient truth, they also restore that entire portion of the *Shepherd* which they provide to its ancient splendor, with a few exceptions.

->I wrote this at Leipzig during the Easter festivities of the year 1863.<-

->Constantine **Tischendorf.**<-

1) See the *Leipzig Sinaitic New Testament*, 1863, page XLI.
2) In another notable place, Vision 3, chapter 5, the Ethiopic manuscript departs from its association with the Sinaitic and Palatine codices. For the Sinaitic, along with the Palatine, has: **because wickedness was found in them** <note>original Greek: διοτι ευρεθη εν αυτοισ πονηρια; original Latin: *quoniam inventa est in eis nequitia*</note>, which seems most correctly written; but the Leipzig text, along with the common Latin versions and the Ethiopic, has: **because wickedness was NOT found in them** <note>original Greek: διότι οὐχ εὑρέθη ἐν αὐτοῖσ πονηρία</note>.

He specifically highlights how certain variations in later texts likely originated from Latin translations or different editorial revisions.</summary>

<page-num>iv</page-num>

# ALBERTUS RUDOLF MAXIMILIAN DRESSEL

->Sands a Great Greeting to His Readers<-

The edition of the **Apostolic Fathers** <note>A group of early Christian writings from the 1st and 2nd centuries, traditionally considered to have been written by those who knew the Apostles personally.</note> by Cotelier <note>Jean-Baptiste Cotelier (1627–1686), a French scholar whose edition was the standard for over a century.</note> is considered by the common judgment of theologians to be among the most outstanding works of this literature. It has certainly earned that praise for a long time, both for its skill in interpretation and for the abundance and use of critical resources in which it excels. For this reason, it is not surprising that many were of the opinion that the text of the Apostolic Fathers had already been so well established in that single edition—especially as revised by Jean Le Clerc <note>A Genevan theologian who updated Cotelier's work in 1698.</note>—that we could rest satisfied with it. 

However, the present age no longer feels this to be entirely the case, even though no edition of the writings from the Apostolic age can afford to be without the labors of Cotelier and Le Clerc. Indeed, when the matter is considered more accurately, it easily appears that the edition does not everywhere provide what is now required in this field, not only in the <term>critical part</term> <note>Textual criticism: the process of comparing manuscripts to reconstruct the original text.</note> but also in the <term>exegetical part</term> <note>Exegesis: the interpretation and explanation of the meaning of the text.</note>. If those matters pertaining to various theological disciplines were to be judged more in accordance with the truth than was possible through Cotelier’s excessive partisan zeal, the text of the writers also had to be restored to more certain foundations by another standard and method. 

Those who, in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries and before, brought the assistance of manuscripts to emend this text, did not actually present every variation of the writing. Instead, they presented only what seemed useful and fit for the task according to their own understanding, while all the remaining variations—which were not infrequently the best—were buried once again in silence and oblivion. Yet how much light can be brought to the understanding of the text itself by a complete <term>critical apparatus</term> <note>A systematic list of variant readings from different manuscripts, usually found at the bottom of a page in scholarly editions.</note>, and how much darkness can and must be spread by a flawed critical method, is something that everyone with judgment in this matter is convinced of today. The judgment of a critic touches upon and reveals the correction of the text; good manuscripts complete it, perfect it, and make it true.

Since this is the case, twenty years ago I asked the late August Neander <note>Johann August Wilhelm Neander (1789–1850), a highly influential German church historian.</note> whether he thought it would be worth the effort if a new edition of the Apostolic Fathers were prepared after Cotelier and Le Clerc—one aided and supported by the critical helps that I had discovered hidden away in the libraries of Rome. That incomparable man urged me to do so, greatly desiring that a supply of these works, which had almost begun to go into exile from among us <note>A metaphor suggesting the texts were becoming rare or neglected in Germany.</note>, should be made available once again. 

But at the same time, William Jacobson in England and Karl J. Hefele in Germany had turned their minds to the same purpose and preceded me. However, although the former published a work filled with his own and others' learning, he looked only to a few writers of the Apostolic age; the latter, in his first edition, did not sufficiently answer our hopes. Therefore, we thought that our original plan should not be abandoned, not even when the more corrected books of those two men later appeared. For things which had been gathered from parchments <note>Manuscripts written on vellum or animal skin.</note> hitherto unknown for many years, where...

<page-num>VI</page-num>
<header>PREFACE.</header>

...as was permitted, supported by the funding of the most merciful King of the Prussians <note>Frederick William IV, who sponsored many scholarly expeditions to find ancient manuscripts.</note>, we were the first to bring these things to light. They were undoubtedly of such novelty and weight that it seemed they should be made public by any means possible. I will say no more of the rest, preferring that it be understood by others rather than spoken by me.

I have therefore worked out this edition with a text established everywhere according to the reliability of the best <term>Manuscripts</term> <note>original Latin: "Codicum." Hand-written ancient copies of texts.</note> with a critical conscience, and adorned it with the <term>variant readings</term> <note>Differences found when comparing one manuscript to another.</note> which I myself discovered. I was unwilling to repeat those readings found here and there in previously printed books because their reliability did not always seem certain. Anyone who realizes from the notes how often even the manuscript readings we owe to the most recent critics had to be corrected by my care will agree that I have not acted unadvisedly—indeed, that I had to do so. Often, in that area, there was a need for a reaper after the harvest, or an architect after the roof was finished. Perhaps someone will say that in the critical portion, we have "sown with the whole sack" <note>A classical idiom meaning to provide too much detail without sorting the important from the trivial.</note>, mixing the useful with the useless, and like a "white line" <note>original Latin: "alba linea." An ancient proverb referring to a rule that makes no distinctions.</note> as they say, we have swept everything together seeking only quantity without care for discernment. I feel otherwise: for even <note>original Greek: "ἐν ἀδιαφόροις"</note> *in matters of indifference*, it is right and lawful to religiously venerate the authority of the sources. Who, then, would call those things useless which are in any way suited to restoring the genuine text of those writers who drew what they recorded from the mouths of *the eye-witnesses of the Word*? <note>original Greek: "τῶν αὐτοπτῶν τοῦ Λόγου"; a reference to the Apostles and their immediate disciples who witnessed the life of Jesus.</note>

There was a time when I thought I would be granted sufficient opportunity to illustrate the text with an entirely new commentary. However, this hope was disappointed both by my failing health and, most significantly, by the adversities and obligations of my domestic life. Consequently, there were rarely moments of relief in which my mind—granted some break from business or the memory of misfortune—could be relaxed and allowed to devote itself to properly composing such a work. Therefore, we have placed the notes of learned men alongside our own, so that the matter would not be delayed any longer. If the inequality and uncertain proportion previously seen between the reliability of the text and the abundance of commentaries has vanished somewhat through our labor, we shall certainly not regret it.

Nor can I fail to give thanks to **Constantine Tischendorf** <note>One of the most famous biblical scholars of the 19th century, best known for discovering the Codex Sinaiticus.</note>, the glory of German theologians, who not only greatly assisted me with advice—enriching this work from the storehouse of his own learning with the greatest kindness and generosity—but also, despite being wonderfully occupied with his own duties, spared no effort in promoting the edition itself. To be brief: he learnedly inaugurated and consecrated our work.

->Written at Rome, July 31, 1856.<-

# PRELIMINARY REMARKS.

## I.

### BARNABAS.

However the author of the text is to be identified—to which a certain ancient tradition has prefixed the name of Barnabas—it is certainly held to be of no small importance among the remains of Christian antiquity. This is due to the way it judges the Holy Scripture of the Old Testament and the place it assigns to it in defining the <term>economy of salvation</term> <note>The divine plan for the management of the world and the redemption of humanity.</note>. Indeed, following the path of the Apostle Paul—sometimes moving further forward, sometimes stepping back—it provides a transition to the Alexandrian allegorical method of explaining the truth of Judaism, and simultaneously toward a more solid <term>Gnosticism</term> <note>A diverse movement in early Christianity that emphasized "gnosis" or secret spiritual knowledge as the key to salvation.</note>. The authority of this path would be of greater value if it were to be attributed to that renowned companion and tireless co-worker of the Apostle Paul, who appeared everywhere as a man of his own right, excelling in upright mind and character; this is a matter to be examined below. For now, let us investigate more accurately what is dealt with in the Epistle itself.

1. The author wishes to share with his "sons and daughters" that which he himself has received, so that they may have faith and <term>knowledge</term> <note>original Greek: "τῆς γνώσεως" (tēs gnōseōs).</note> brought to perfection, being abundantly gifted with spiritual graces (chapter 1). He says he will do this not endowed with the authority of a teacher, but as an equal among equals, as one of them: indeed, he well knows himself to be <term>offscouring</term> <note>original Greek: "περίψημα" (peripsēma). A term used to denote extreme humility, literally meaning "refuse" or "scum," as used by St. Paul in 1 Corinthians 4:13.</note>, for which he hopes the love of the brothers will be his reward (chapters 6, 1). Therefore, the heart of the matter turns on this: that along with perfect faith, they might also become masters of knowledge. For this reason, it must be understood how, by God's ordinance, only the hope of life was set before the ancients; the very beginning of life appeared with the first advent of Christ on earth, and the consummation of life is in heaven (chapter 2). Now, however, he is about to show the progress divinely given in Christianity and its perfection by the insufficiency of the Old Covenant, which has clearly been fulfilled and made true by the New. God surely revealed through the Prophets of the Old Testament that he does not need the sacrifices of goats and bulls, nor does he despise a contrite heart. By this "human offering," he indicates that the sacrifices of the Jews have been abolished. True fasting is mercy toward the needy. After God manifested this clearly, those called in simplicity through his Beloved should by no means approach their Law as if they were <term>proselytes</term> <note>Converts to Judaism who took on the obligations of the Mosaic Law.</note>.

And yet, we must cultivate purity of morals entirely, since the end—the advent of the Son of God—is already pressing near (chapters 2—4). Nevertheless, let us also flee the company of those who say the Law pertains to us not at all.

<page-num>VIII</page-num>

->### PRELIMINARY REMARKS.<-

The covenant that once belonged to the Jews has now become ours, because by transgressing they lost forever that which Moses received. The essence of the tablets broken by Moses has been sealed in our hearts through the love of Christ in these final times. Established in this new law, we must resist the Evil One and his temptations. Yet let those who are "spirit-bearers" not be puffed up as if they were already fully justified; rather, let them keep the commandments in the fear of God. For He judges not by outward appearance, but according to one's works. Our faith is aided by fear and endurance; patience and self-control fight alongside it (chapter 2), with faith and love joined together (chapter 11). Let us be vigilant and rightly understand what such great signs and wonders performed among the Jewish people—the destruction of Jerusalem and the rest—signify for us. Let us take care lest, falling asleep in foolishness, we are nonetheless lost, just like the people of the old covenant (chapter 4).

From this, it is understood that the author primarily warns against those "Judaizers" <note>Early Christians who insisted that followers of Jesus must still observe the Mosaic Law, such as circumcision and dietary restrictions.</note> among the Christians, while also explicitly stating that those who despise any law at all are risking their salvation no less. Indeed, the Mosaic law is of such value to him that <term>gnosis</term> <note>original: "gnosis." In this context, it refers to a deeper, spiritual insight into the hidden meanings of the scriptures.</note> perceives within it a "new law" <note>original Greek: "νέαν ἐντολὴν" (nean entolēn), meaning a new commandment.</note>. Since the "new people" are the true temple of God, they alone offer a true sacrifice within the heart (chapter 3). This people already enjoys true life here (chapter 1), and after many tribulations and hardships, they will rule over the entire world in the kingdom of the Messiah (chapters 15 and 8). Thus instructed regarding those things which have passed away, let no one fall into the nets, but instead, being reborn through the new covenant, let them be strong in understanding. To one who reflects and recalls what has been and what is, it will appear that the Jews were judged by the atoning death of Christ, while we were saved. The Prophets, who were the instruments of the divine voice, announced again and again that it had to happen this way. Attempting to persuade his readers, the author argues that the fasts of the Old Testament, the scapegoat, and the red heifer all point toward Christ (chapters 5–8); he teaches that circumcision is to be understood spiritually, as are the commandments regarding food; and that baptism and the cross were already <term>prefigured</term> <note>The practice of "typology," where Old Testament events or figures are seen as symbolic "types" or foreshadows of New Testament realities.</note> and announced in the Old Testament, with Joshua serving as a "type" of Christ (chapters 9–12). Since these things are so, Christians—not Jews—are proven to be the true heirs of God's covenant, now that the meaning of the Old Testament "types" has been unlocked. Thus the testament, which Moses received from the Lord and then shattered, has come down to us. That the Jews are not its heirs is also understood from the fact that they do not possess the true Sabbath, nor a temple acceptable to God, which exists only in a spiritual dwelling—that is, in the Christian church (chapters 13–17). To these examples of <term>gnosis</term> is added an exhortatory section (chapters 19–21) concerning the "Way of Light" and the "Way of Darkness." Those who walk the former must seek the goal through all kinds of good works, which are easily performed through spiritual insight; in the latter wander those who, alienated from God, have lost their souls to vice. God's commandments must be kept: the day of retribution or destruction looms for all.

He was refuted by Hefele³), and more subtly by Hilgenfeld...

Hilgenfeld. 4) <note>Referring to Adolf Hilgenfeld, a 19th-century German biblical scholar.</note> If neither its original integrity nor the continuous progression of its thoughts can be called into doubt, we must now ask to whom it was written. Indeed, the greeting formula is neither customary nor complete. As for the title "catholic" <note>original: καθολικὴ (*katholikē*); in this context, it means "universal" or "general," referring to an epistle intended for the whole church rather than a specific congregation.</note> given to it by Origen 5) (It is indeed written in the *catholic epistle of Barnabas* <note>original: Γέγραπται δὴ ἐν τῇ Βαρνάβα καθολικῇ ἐπιστολῇ</note>), this can hardly be maintained, unless perhaps the great Alexandrian master [Origen] is to be understood spiritually <note>original: πνευματικῶς (*pneumatikōs*)</note> even in this instance. By the same logic, any writing could be called "catholic" if it does not entirely lack the elements of Christian doctrine. To this we must add that in the subscription of the manuscripts, as many as we have seen, this title is sought in vain (cf. Epistle of Barnabas note 1). Nor would I believe this was said by Origen for any other reason than the general mode of speaking which the author uses in his greeting, signifying no distinct or certain group of readers. A passage that can be opportunely called upon to help solve this question is found in chapter 16: "Before we believed in God, the dwelling place of our heart was corrupt and weak, like a temple truly built by hands; for we were a house full of idolatry, and through idolatry we were a house of demons, because we did everything that was contrary to God." He speaks thus as one who was himself a **Gentile** <note>original: *Ethnicus*; meaning a non-Jew or pagan.</note>, and he addresses his words to Christians who have come from the Gentiles. **Similar things are said to Clement regarding similar matters** 6): "The will of God has become hidden in many ways: first, there was a bad introduction, a wicked upbringing, a terrible habit, poor company, and incorrect prejudice. Because of these things, there was error, then fearlessness, unbelief, immorality, greed, vanity, and a thousand other such evils. Like a great amount of smoke filling a single house—the world—these things clouded the vision of the men living within, and did not allow them to look up from the darkness to perceive the God who created them, or to know what is pleasing to Him. Therefore, those who love the truth must cry out from deep within their hearts for help, with a truth-loving mind, so that someone inside the smoke-filled house might approach and open the door, allowing the light of the sun from without to enter the house, and the smoke from the fire within to be cast out." (19) "I call the helper the true prophet, who alone is able to enlighten the souls of men, so that we may be able to see with our own eyes the way of eternal salvation." That frequent antithesis between "us" and "them" <note>original: ἡμεῖς (*hēmeis*) and ἐκεῖνοι (*ekeinoi*); used by the author to distinguish the Christian "us" from the Jewish "them."</note> points to this, nor can the words "...who was prepared for this, so that by appearing himself, he might redeem from darkness our hearts already consumed by death and surrendered to the lawlessness of error, and establish a covenant in us by his word" (chapter 14) be understood as referring to any others than those who formerly followed **Paganism**. Christ, the "light of the nations" 7) <note>original: φῶς ἐθνῶν (*phōs ethnōn*)</note>, illuminated those who were obscured by darkness (chapter 14). Who would assert the same regarding the Jews? <columns>2</columns>

It concerns Christians. Indeed, it is well known among everyone that many Gentiles <note>original: "Ethnicos"</note> outside Palestine observed several Mosaic ordinances, known as **eclectics** <note>original: *ἐκλεκτικοί* (*eklektikoi*); those who chose specific practices from various traditions</note>. The man who wrote in chapter 2, "we similarly wandering," had this group of people before his eyes. It is no wonder that the author loves, and commands above all others, that this kind of knowledge <note>original: "gnoseos"</note> be used to fill the Epistle with examples in **explaining allegories** <note>original: "allegoriis enucleandis"</note>, not without skill, delighting in the charms of words that seem to penetrate to the very origin of things. From this arose a disparity in his arguments and in the way he treats individual points. However, at that time, the most serious—not to say the only—question was what authority the Old Covenant held within the Gospel, after the Apostle Paul, leading the way with no small arguments, had been used by others to prove its immunity from the Law. Our author, however, shows how it is possible that the Law has already vanished, both by teaching through reasoning and by attempting to show it in his own specific way. Although he declares war on Judaism creeping into Christianity, he likewise notices others, but only gently encouraging, warning, persuading, and rebuking those who, puffed up by justification through faith alone, have little time for good works (chapter 4)—surely the precursors of later Gnosticism. Between these two parties, the author takes care to lay down the **right path of salvation**.

3. At what time the Epistle was written is not clear. Nevertheless, the following words (chapter 4) unambiguously signify that Jerusalem was overturned, the temple destroyed, and the Jewish people defeated by the Romans: "when you see such great signs and wonders among the people of the Jews, and thus the Lord has abandoned them." Nor are other things narrated in chapter 16: *For because they went to war, it [the temple] was pulled down by the enemies; and now even the servants of the enemies shall rebuild it. Again, it was made clear how the city and the temple and the people of Israel were about to be delivered up.* <note>original Greek: Διὰ γὰρ τὸ πολεμεῖν αὐτοὺς καθηρέθη ὑπὸ τῶν ἐχθρῶν· νῦν καὶ αὐτοὶ οἱ τῶν ἐχθρῶν ὑπηρέται ἀνοικοδομήσουσιν αὐτόν. Πάλιν ὡς ἤμελλεν ἡ πόλις καὶ ὁ ναὸς καὶ ὁ λαὸς Ἰσραὴλ παραδίδοσθαι, ἐφανερώθη.</note> From the manner of speaking in chapter 4, it is gathered that those to whom the Epistle was given were witnesses of that most heavy judgment by which the Lord judged the Jewish people and completed their destruction. Since no mention is made of persecutions, it is likely that it was written before Pliny was Proconsul in Bithynia <note>referring to Pliny the Younger's famous correspondence with Emperor Trajan regarding Christians around 112 AD</note>.

4. Those who, following the traces of old tradition⁸⁾, wish for Barnabas, the companion of the Apostle Paul, to be the author of the Epistle, use very weak, even futile arguments. For the entire method of treatment and the subjects handled themselves cry out against them. Barnabas, a Levite born in Cyprus⁹⁾, ought to have been more expert in the Mosaic law than appears from chapters 7 and 8. Nor would he have peddled the same claim about the Syrians, that they practice circumcision; this is something he should have known better from the time he himself stayed in Antioch with the Apostle Paul.¹⁰⁾ Certainly, it must be admitted that the author lacks the knowledge and learning of more things than is proper. For this reason, already H. Ménard <note>Hugues Ménard (1585–1644), a Benedictine scholar</note>, the first editor of the Epistle—

# XI

### BARNABAS.

<note>original: "authentiam eius impugnavit"</note> challenged its authenticity<sup>11)</sup>), and after him Daniel Papebrochius<sup>12)</sup>, Tentzelius<sup>13)</sup>, Natalis Alexander<sup>14)</sup>, Remi Ceillier<sup>15)</sup>, Ittigius<sup>16)</sup>, Moshemius<sup>17)</sup>, Lumperus<sup>18)</sup>, Hugius<sup>19)</sup>, Ullmannus<sup>20)</sup>, Neander<sup>21)</sup>, Mynster<sup>22)</sup>, and Winer.<sup>23)</sup> But you might say: "Look here! What about that tradition found in Clement of Alexandria's *Miscellanies* <note>original: "Stromata"</note> (Book II, VI, etc.), Origen's *Against Celsus* (I, 63), Eusebius's *Ecclesiastical History* (III, 25), Jerome's *On Illustrious Men* (Chapter 6), and Nicephorus in the *Stichometry* (from the 5th century)?" I would not doubt that this tradition existed even earlier in the Alexandrian church, and was not first introduced by Clement or Origen. They retained it, however, because the character of the entire Epistle was not unlike that of the man who, along with the Apostle Paul, had announced the gospel of salvation to the Gentiles. Therefore, piously respecting the tradition and not being compelled by any particular reason to perform a more subtle or critical examination of it, they handed it down to posterity exactly as they had found it. But if you wish to track the origin of the tradition itself, it must be said that the work could not have been attributed to any of the Apostles because of that very insult regarding <note>original: "τοὺς ἰδίους Ἀποστόλους, τοὺς μέλλοντας κηρύσσειν τὸ εὐαγγέλιον αὐτοῦ, ἐξελέξατο, ὄντας ὑπὲρ πᾶσαν ἁμαρτίαν ἀνομωτέρους"</note> **"the choice of His own Apostles, who were to preach His gospel, who were lawless beyond all sin"** (Chapter 5)—a statement perhaps consistent with the author's own opinion, but not with the truth, being a mere fiction <note>original: "commentum"</note>. If, nevertheless, a semi-apostolic authority seemed impressed upon the Epistle, those seeking an author could hardly have found anyone more suitable to suggest than Barnabas, who was himself a teacher of the Gentiles. Could this **falsely attributed work** <term>pseudepigraphon; a text written under a false name to gain authority</term> have also originated among the Alexandrians because the Gnostic *Clementine Homilies*<sup>24)</sup> depict Barnabas meeting Clement in Alexandria?

Indeed, it has always seemed to me to be of no small importance what is narrated in the Acts of the Apostles (15:37 and following). Barnabas, after a disagreement arose, departed from Paul and, taking John Mark with him, sailed to Cyprus. Did Barnabas set out elsewhere only for the sake of John Mark, or also to follow another path of teaching? Perhaps the very path we see him walking here in this letter? Yet it seems most highly noteworthy that the same John Mark, who is believed to have written quite extensively on the life and deeds of Barnabas, makes no mention of this Epistle. Neither the Vatican Codex 1667, from which Papebrochius<sup>25)</sup> published those accounts, nor the Paris Codex 1470 used by Tischendorf<sup>26)</sup>, nor the Vatican Codex 821 which I myself transcribed, vary on this point.

<page-num>XII</page-num>

# PRELIMINARY OBSERVATIONS

In the 17th century, Hugo Ménard, a monk of the Congregation of Saint Maur, discovered an ancient Latin version of the Epistle traditionally attributed to Barnabas. He found it following Tertullian's *Letter on Jewish Meats* in a manuscript from the monastery of Corbie. Jacques Sirmond—noticing that Ménard hesitated to publish it due to the countless errors in the text—offered him a Greek transcript found among the papers of Francesco Torres <note>original: "Turriani"</note>, which helped him establish a corrected text. However, death took Ménard before he could finish. His work was completed by Luc d’Achery, a member of the same congregation, who published Ménard’s edition in Paris in 1645. This edition featured the Greek transcript from Torres and the ancient Corbie Latin version, though from Chapter 18 onward—where the Latin version ends—Ménard’s own work was added.

After Sirmond, the same Epistle written in Greek was discovered by researchers in three other manuscripts: those of the Vatican Library, Cardinal Colonna, and Andreas Schott. In these, as in the Torres transcript, the text was joined to Polycarp’s *Letter to the Philippians* (which precedes it) and was <term>acephalous<note>Literally "headless"; a manuscript that is missing its beginning.</note></term>. Isaac Voss received a transcript of the Schott Greek manuscript and the ancient version from Claude Saumaise <note>original: "Salmasio"</note>, which he then shared with James Ussher <note>original: "Iac. Usserius"</note>. Ussher arranged for it to be printed in Oxford in 1643 along with the letters of Ignatius. However, nearly all copies of that edition perished in a massive fire that destroyed a significant part of the town. Consequently, because Ménard’s edition had been produced from only one manuscript and was poorly corrected, Isaac Voss published a more accurate version of the *Epistle of Barnabas* in Amsterdam in 1646. He made use of manuscripts from Florence, the Vatican, and the Roman Theatines, though he did so somewhat carelessly—at a glance, one might say—as I have personally observed many times. I have used this first edition of Voss in my own commentaries. It was reprinted in London in 1680. After Voss, those who contributed most to correcting the text include John Fell (Oxford, 1685), Jean-Baptiste Cotelier (Paris, 1672), Jean Le Clerc (Antwerp, 1698 and 1700; Amsterdam, 1724), Russell (London, 1746), and Gallandi (*Library of the Ancient Fathers*, Vol. I, Venice, 1765). Karl Joseph von Hefele and Reithmayr prepared their own editions based on these printed works, though neither had access to the original handwritten manuscripts. From Hefele’s *Apostolic Fathers*, we have primarily used the third edition, and occasionally the fourth; our own work was already in press before that one arrived here.

In our notes, we will cite: *Universal Letter of Saint Barnabas the Apostle. Translated from the Greek by Don Giovanni Battista Gallicciolli. Venice, 1797.*

There is no doubt as to who wrote the first Epistle that circulates under the name of Clement, nor to whom it was given—whether it was requested<sup>1)</sup> or, as is more likely, sent spontaneously after the discord among the Corinthians became known. Indeed, we gather from the beginning that the Romans wrote to the Corinthians, who—

<page-num>XIII</page-num>

### CLEMENT

The church was in turmoil over ecclesiastical office, and [the Romans] turned their attention to reconciling them—somewhat late, perhaps, because they themselves had been afflicted by the calamities of the times. For this reason, they sent three legates to deliver a letter <note>original: "c. 59"; Clement’s letter is often divided into 59 or 65 chapters depending on the edition.</note>.

The sedition that arose among the Corinthians seems all the more painful to the Romans because it foully tarnishes the glory of their faith and virtue, which had been celebrated everywhere, and makes the name of Christians a source of contempt among others <note>The original Latin uses "Ethnicos," referring to the Gentiles or non-Christian pagans.</note> (c. 1, 2, 47). Indeed, some people, swelling with that praise which they previously earned, and throwing everything into confusion through discord and envy, have brought the condition of the Corinthian church to a wretched state. Yet, it is proved by many examples, from both ancient and recent times, how much damage the unspeakable envy of the wicked has brought (c. 3–6). Now, however, having left behind vain contentions, one must turn toward repentance and toward God. The many warnings of Scripture look toward this goal; this is the meaning of Christ's blood, poured out for the salvation of all sinners (c. 7, 8).

Praise is heaped upon those from of old who were held worthy of eternal rewards because of their singular obedience and faith toward God (c. 9–12). Therefore, having laid aside the arrogance of pride, it is more profitable for us to obey God than to lend our ears to those who, led by rivalry, preside over disturbances and internal seditions. Christ left a noble example of humility to be imitated, for he endured the most grievous sufferings for our sins. The greatest men of the Old Testament, who excelled in piety toward God, as well as the Prophets, who were divinely inspired and held worthy to foretell the Messiah, conducted themselves with great humility. There are also outstanding records of David’s humility (c. 13–18). Let us imitate so many examples of a modest and submissive spirit, and let us seek peace while contemplating the splendid gifts and benefits of God, by which He has shown Himself merciful toward every creature. He Himself established the order of nature and stabilized it with eternal laws. Therefore, we, who have been gifted and adorned with the greatest benefits of God through Christ, should arrange our lives according to these same laws, abhorring disturbances and sedition. We must obey God alone, and not the leaders of riots. Let us venerate Christ, whose blood was given for us, not crying out against those in authority, but exhorting the younger to piety and the women to chastity and temperance. Scripture, in which we have faith in Christ, commands us to do this (c. 19–22).

To those who come to God with a simple mind, He has promised splendid rewards. Moreover, God is truthful and will stand by His promises. Let us not doubt the things that are not yet seen. Just as the omnipotence of God works tirelessly in the hidden recesses of nature to create what is later sent forth into the light, so we ourselves shall be: the fullness of our glory is the resurrection. Furthermore, there are many pledges of the resurrection and the future life: Christ raised from the dead, the alternation of day and night, the seed cast into the ground, and the Phoenix bird <note>Clement famously used the legend of the Phoenix as a biological proof for the possibility of the resurrection.</note>. The promise of the resurrection already exists in the Old Testament. Therefore, the truthfulness of God does not allow this hope of a future life to be rendered vain or void (c. 23–27). Since the power of God encompasses all things, let us attempt to do nothing that is contrary to Him. Turning to Him in simplicity of heart, let us do nothing except what pleases the benevolent Father, who chose us without merit (c. 28–30). How can we obtain the divine blessing? The Patriarchs were blessed because of their faith, as were the kings, prophets, and priests. But let no one think that by good works...

<header>INTRODUCTION.</header>

[it is] not necessary at all. Rather, imitating God, let us perform works of righteousness (chapters 31–33). Rewards will not be lacking for us, nor are they lacking now. No other way—namely, the path of faith and the work of righteousness—leads us to Christ (chapters 34–36). We are Christ’s militia. By the example of soldiers, it is proven that not only are those who command necessary, but also those who offer obedience. For this reason, so that the order established by internal law is not changed or confused at will, provision was made even in the Old Testament <note>The author uses "V.T." for *Vetus Testamentum* (Old Testament).</note> by defining the duties of priests, Levites, and laypeople with great accuracy. The Apostles, acting as instruments of the Holy Spirit, imitated this example and handed over the governance of the church in each city to overseers and deacons. Let us be subject to these divinely instituted roles. It is, therefore, a work of wickedness to remove them from their rightful place (chapters 37–46).

The goal and purpose of the entire Letter was an exhortation to establish peace and to obey. The intent of that proposal is now made clear throughout. An admonition is added so that the Corinthians do not forget what the Apostle Paul wrote to them regarding internal dissensions (chapter 47). Virtue must be considered as nothing if humility of mind is not joined to it. Love toward the brothers makes men like God and Christ. By practicing charity, we merit the forgiveness of sins (chapters 48–50). Those participating in the dispute, especially its authors, should seek pardon for their sins and contribute their part toward restoring peace. In this way, they will be pleasing and acceptable to God. Let them rather take the punishment upon themselves, or go into exile, provided that unity is restored. Prayers should be poured out for them, and mutual admonition should be given, so that no one falls away from the hope of Christ (chapters 51–57).

After a gap of about three pages in the *Codex Alexandrinus* <note>The *Codex Alexandrinus* is a 5th-century manuscript of the Greek Bible, one of the oldest and most complete, which contains the text of Clement's letter.</note>, there follow those things which pertain to the conclusion of the Letter.

2. The Letter to the Corinthians was written in the name of the Roman church. That the person who wrote it was one of its leaders, no one will doubt who has carefully read chapters 40–45; nor will they doubt that he faithfully expressed the mind of the Christians who were living as sojourners in Rome. He calls the Apostles Peter and Paul "the athletes [of faith] who were nearest to us" <note>original: "τοὺς ἔγγιστα γενομένους ἀθλητὰς"</note>, extolling the former with praise and following the path of the latter’s doctrine more closely. And there are those—such as Tillemont,<sup>2</sup> Constantius,<sup>3</sup> Venema, Schliemann, and others—who think he was of Israelite origin, relying on those things which they adapt for their own use from chapters 4, 31, and 55. Nevertheless, those things which are piously expressed there regarding the affairs and people of the Old Testament belong to Christians in a spiritual sense. Furthermore, the opinion of those who think the author was an Israelite only in part (perhaps from his mother) strives to rely on arguments too slight to be considered worthy of mention. He is certainly not ignorant of the Mosaic law, but he is also well-acquainted with the mythology of the Greeks, and with nature, astronomy, and other sciences worthy of a learned man's knowledge (chapters 6, 20, 25, 55). Indeed, [note] even the words: "we know many among us who have given themselves into bonds, etc." <note>original: "ἐπιστάμεθα πολλοὺς ἐν ἡμῖν παραδεδωκότας ἑαυτοὺς εἰς δέσμα κτλ."</note> (chapter 55) and "Let us consider those who serve as soldiers under our leaders, how orderly, how submissively, how obediently they carry out their orders. Not all are prefects, nor tribunes, nor centurions, nor commanders of fifty..." <note>original: "Κατανοήσωμεν τοὺς στρατευομένους τοῖς ἡγουμένοις ἡμῶν, πῶς εὐτάκτως, πῶς εὐείκτως, πῶς ὑποτεταγμένως ἐπιτελοῦσι τὰ διατασσόμενα. Οὐ πάντες εἰσὶν ἔπαρχοι, οὐδὲ χιλίαρχοι, οὐδὲ ἑκατόνταρχοι, οὐδὲ πεν-"</note>

<header>CLEMENT.</header>

[...not] commanders of fifty, nor the subsequent ranks; but each in his own order carries out the things commanded by the king and the leaders (chapter 37) <note>original Greek: τηκόνταρχοι, οὐδὲ τὸ καθεξῆς· ἀλλ’ ἕκαστος ἐν τῷ ἰδίῳ τάγματι τὰ ἐπιτασσόμενα ὑπὸ τοῦ βασιλέως καὶ τῶν ἡγουμένων ἐπιτελεῖ</note>—these words clearly indicate that the author is Roman.

These are the things generally gathered from the Letter itself regarding the author. Now let us listen to tradition.

The ancient Church Fathers claim that "Clement" is the author of the Letter. However, his name does not appear at the beginning <note>In ancient letters, the author’s name usually appeared in the opening greeting.</note>, as is usually the case, nor does he mention it elsewhere in the text. These words leave no doubt that Eusebius <note>A 4th-century bishop and the first great historian of the Christian Church.</note> had the Letter that still exists today before his eyes: "Of this Clement, then, one letter is acknowledged as genuine, great and wonderful, which he composed on behalf of the Church of the Romans to that of the Corinthians, when a sedition occurred at that time in Corinth." <note>original Greek: Τούτου δὴ οὖν τοῦ Κλήμεντος ὁμολογουμένη μία ἐπιστολὴ φέρεται, μεγάλη τε καὶ θαυμασία, ἣν ὡς ἀπὸ τῆς Ῥωμαίων ἐκκλησίας τῇ Κορινθίων διετυπώσατο, στάσεως τηνικάδε κατὰ τὴν Κόρινθον γενομένης. (Eusebius, Church History III, 16).</note> But indeed, Hegesippus, who is older than Eusebius, knew of it. For, having mentioned the dissensions of the Corinthians, he adds the following: "And that the affairs of the Corinthians were moved by sedition during the time of the aforementioned [Clement], Hegesippus is a reliable witness." <note>original Greek: Καὶ ὅτι γε κατὰ τὸν δηλούμενον (Κλήμεντα) τὰ τῶν Κορινθίων κεκίνητο στάσεως, ἀξιόχρεως μάρτυς ὁ Ἡγήσιππος.</note> You might add: "It is possible to hear what he (that is, Hegesippus) said after some remarks about Clement’s Letter to the Corinthians, adding the following, etc." <note>original Greek: Ἀκοῦσαί γέ τοι πάρεστι μετά τινα περὶ τῆς Κλήμεντος πρὸς Κορινθίους ἐπιστολῆς αὐτῷ εἰρημένα, ἐπιλέγοντος τάδε κτλ.</note> However, it is not clear from these whether Eusebius is presenting his own testimony or that of Hegesippus regarding the Letter’s author, even though Hegesippus clearly indicates that Clement was living in Rome at the time the Letter was sent.

Irenaeus, along with Hegesippus, is a witness that Clement lived in Rome at the time the Letter was sent to Corinth (during the reign of the Emperor Domitian). The way this is narrated leaves us no room to doubt that Clement himself flourished in authority among the Romans, acting as the interpreter of their mind in drafting the Letter.

Dionysius of Corinth wrote to the Romans in the name of the church of the Corinthians about eighty years after the Romans had sent the letter to them. His words, preserved in Eusebius, clearly attribute the work to Clement as the author.

Clement of Alexandria and Origen assert the same thing as Dionysius.

Those who have handed down the memory of the order of succession of the Roman bishops <term>successionis ordo: the chronological list of bishops tracing their authority back to the Apostles</term> state that Clement lived in Rome during the reign of Domitian. Irenaeus leads their choir <note>Meaning Irenaeus is the primary or most important witness in this group.</note>, whose account Eusebius explains more fully. Epiphanius, Jerome, and the *Martyrology of Clement* do not differ from them.

While these call Clement the fourth bishop of the Romans after Peter (assuming Linus was the second and Anacletus the third), another tradition differs greatly—the *Letter of Clement to James*, which is prefixed to the *Clementine Homilies*. For there, Peter himself appointed Clement as his successor. Tertullian agrees with this, and according to Jerome, most of the Latins <note>Referring to the Western/Latin-speaking branch of the early Church.</note> do as well.

<page-num>XVI</page-num>

# PROLEGOMENA.

<columns>2</columns>

Even the ancient writers worked to reconcile the two traditions of succession through the art of interpretation. Epiphanius 18) and Rufinus state that while the Apostles Peter and Paul were still alive, Linus and Anacletus held the governance of the Roman church, but that Clement was made bishop by Peter when the latter felt his own death approaching: "We have received this explanation for the matter: Linus and Cletus were indeed bishops in the city of Rome before Clement, but while Peter was still living; namely, so that they might handle the administrative duties of the bishopric, while he himself fulfilled the office of the apostleship. This is found to have been his practice even at Caesarea, where, though he was present himself, he nonetheless had Zacchaeus, whom he had ordained, as bishop. In this way, both accounts appear true: those others are numbered as bishops before Clement, yet Clement received the seat of teaching after Peter's death." 19) The Letter of Ignatius to Mary of Cassobola 20) and the author of the first catalog of Popes (from the year 354) arrange the order as follows: Peter, Linus, Clement, Anacletus. So too do Augustine, 21) Optatus of Milevis, 22) and the *Apostolic Constitutions*. 23) In that case, one would have to conclude that he presided over the Roman church around the year 67 AD. Others have entered upon different paths to settle this discrepancy. But only a few things can be conjectured that are actually probable; indeed, these are somewhat crude <note>original Greek: παχυμερέστερον (pachymeresteron)</note>, conceived without a scientific foundation—indeed, they are poured out, vague, and arbitrary, like the distant gaze of the mind's eye when things in the middle distance are clouded.

But since it can be demonstrated with solid arguments that the tradition of Clement succeeding Peter did not exist among the early Christians until after the *Homilies* or *Recognitions* were published, we must be careful not to lightly abandon that older tradition. <note>The *Homilies* and *Recognitions* are early Christian writings, often called the Pseudo-Clementines, which tell a fictionalized story of Clement following the Apostle Peter.</note> Certainly, the author of the *Homilies* or *Recognitions* seems to have invented Clement’s Caesarean ancestry 24) for no other reason than to make such a great man a companion of Peter. It is also credible that he adapted for his own use the name of the Consul Flavius Clemens, whom the Emperor Domitian executed, perhaps on account of too much zeal for the Christian cause. 25) Whether he discovered from tradition or from history that this Flavius Clemens was the hero of the *Recognitions*, it proves by no slight argument that Clement the bishop lived during the reign of Domitian. Furthermore, the character of the man who wrote the *Letter to the Corinthians* in the name of the Roman church is very similar to that Clement whom we know from the *Homilies* and *Recognitions* to have been educated in Greek literature—though that information is scattered and interrupted. It certainly seems so at first glance. And omitting other points, it may suffice to refer back to those matters which he investigated concerning the immortality of the soul in *Homilies* I, 1 and following, and those things read in the *Letter to the Corinthians*, chapters 24–27. Moreover, the doctrine proposed in both places was such that those who came to Christianity from both the Gentiles and the Jews could embrace it without anxiety of conscience. Clearly, what is called Paulinism and Petrinism <note>Refers to the two main "schools" of early Christianity: Paul's focus on Gentiles and grace versus Peter's focus on the Jewish law.</note> had become greatly softened toward the end of the first century, the harshness of both sides having been...

...from there already loosened and relaxed. An example of the hierarchy appears similarly in the *Letter to James* and the *Letter to the Corinthians*, though distinguished in both cases by the "color of the times" <note>This likely refers to the specific historical context and development of church offices in each period.</note>.

There is a passage in the *Shepherd of Hermas* conceived as follows:²⁶)
> "Write therefore two little books, and you shall send one to Clement, and one to Grapte. But Clement shall send it to the foreign cities; for to him that is permitted."

And these words clearly show that this Clement—who, considering the time, is scarcely removed from the author of the *Letter to the Corinthians*—was one of the presidents or **presbyters** <note>term: presbyter; an elder or early church official, from the Greek 'presbyteros'</note> of the church, not a **bishop** in the stricter sense of the word. Indeed, Hermas himself, one of the number of the faithful, appears endowed with no less dignity than Clement, having been chosen to be an interpreter of the divine will before the faithful.

Therefore, it seems that this Clement wrote the Letter, or saw to its writing under his own auspices: which changes nothing regarding the matter itself. Whether he was one of the disciples of the Apostles, as Irenaeus²⁷) recorded, or an Apostle himself, as Clement of Alexandria²⁸) wrote, or an "Apostolic man" according to Jerome²⁹)—that is certainly not clear. It is believable that those authors drew such titles from the nature of the Letter itself, since Clement himself nowhere says that he enjoyed the companionship of any Apostle. Eusebius³⁰) narrates that he succeeded Anacletus in the twelfth year of the Emperor Domitian, or the year 92 of the Christian era.

Regarding the end of his life, or his martyrdom,³¹) the final chapters of the *Epitome of the Deeds of Peter* peddle a mixture of truth and falsehood so intertwined that history can scarcely be distinguished from fables. It seems more faith should be placed in Eusebius³²) and Jerome,³³) who record that he departed this life in the third year of the Emperor Trajan, when Evarestus had succeeded him.

We shall only make mention of the opinion of those who say that Clement of Rome is the same man whom the Apostle Paul praises in the *Letter to the Philippians* 4:3. It has already been sufficiently demonstrated by learned men that this view, which was passed down by various of the ancient Fathers, arose from an inaccurate interpretation of the cited passage. Accordingly, we shall refrain from repeating here what has been said by others against it.³⁴)

**3.** However, there have been some [John Toland,³⁵) Salig,³⁶) Voetius,³⁷) Schwegler,³⁸) Baur³⁹)] who doubted the authenticity of the Letter, or did not think it was the same one we have praised by the ancients. But these men began their work poorly. For Polycarp already appears to have used it, transferring words into his *Letter to the Philippians* (chapters 4, 9, 7, 2, 2, 4) from the *Letter to the Corinthians* (chapters 1, 5, 7, 9, 13, 21). The same must be said of Irenaeus,

<page-num>XVIII</page-num>
<header>PRELIMINARY REMARKS.</header>

Clement of Alexandria, Origen, Eusebius, Cyril of Jerusalem, Epiphanius, and Jerome—whose passages are expressed more fully in Hefele’s *Prolegomena to the Apostolic Fathers* <note>original: "PP. App." referring to Patres Apostolici</note>, p. XXIV, 4th ed.—all attest to the work. Defenders of its authenticity <note>The quality of being genuine or truly written by Clement.</note> have also emerged more recently, including Bunsen⁴⁰), Ritschl⁴¹), and others. Some passages found among the ancient Fathers, such as in Basil’s *On the Holy Spirit* [ch. 29, no. 72, Vol. III, p. 61, Benedictine edition], are cited as being from Clement’s Letter but are missing from the text we have today. Consequently, other doubts against its authenticity have arisen. But anyone who remembers the significant **gap** <note>original: *lacunae*; a physical hole or missing section in a manuscript</note> that follows chapter 57 in the only surviving manuscript <note>This refers to the Codex Alexandrinus, which was the only known copy of this letter for centuries.</note> will think little of these doubts, especially since those known passages all seem to belong to the end of the Letter.

4. The doubts raised by Jerome Bignon in 1633 concerning the letter's integrity <note>Whether the text has been altered or remains in its original state.</note>—raised when the Letter was first published by Patrick Young <note>original: "Patr. Iunio"</note>—have already been refuted by Hugo Grotius⁴²). Edward Bernard and Jean Le Clerc, in both the 1698–1700 and 1724 editions of Cotelier’s *Apostolic Fathers*, were of the opinion that Clement of Alexandria was the actual author of all those passages that occur with the same or similar words in both our Letter and the fourth book of the *Stromata* <note>Clement of Alexandria's major work, "Miscellanies."</note>. Wotton⁴³) responded to them:
> "These efforts, however, are in vain. For anyone who argues in this way from Clement of Alexandria either does not know him well or acts in bad faith. By the same logic, the authenticity and reliability of every writer ever cited by Clement of Alexandria would be at an end. For none of the Fathers used greater liberty in citing authors, whether sacred or pagan; it was his habit not to always recite the full words of the authors, but at his own discretion to now shorten them, now insert his own words, omit others, or change them in various ways."

A certain appearance of truth is presented by the arguments of Lawrence Mosheim⁴⁴) toward the same end:
> "The first ten chapters have some traces of a deceptive hand, though not many; the author consistently follows his plan. But in chapters 11 and 12, in order to commend faith and hospitality, he approaches a point where no coherence at all appears with what precedes. Therefore, I am almost inclined to think these chapters were intruded <note>inserted later by someone other than the original author</note>. Clement returns to his purpose in chapter 13, and continues in it until chapter 22. In this chapter, however, suddenly and for no apparent reason, he hurries to a far different argument: the resurrection of dead bodies, which he discusses until chapter 28. In chapter 28, he seems to remember his purpose again; the beginning of this chapter fits well with the end of chapter 21, but can only be joined with the end of chapter 27 with great difficulty. For this reason, the six chapters concerning the return of corpses to life seem to have been attributed to Clement... Nor do I think better of chapters 40–45 and chapter 55, where you read things that could occur to no one except a man entirely forgetful of the matter he is handling." To which Hefele⁴⁵) replies:

$\alpha$) "Chapters 11 and 12 of our letter [connect] well with the preceding..."

$\theta$) “A diversity of style or speech is nowhere to be found in our letter.”

5. *Wotton*⁴⁶) explains at greater length those things in the first Letter of Clement which are found to be entirely worthy of an apostolic man, and *Grotius*⁴⁷) extols its traces of Christian antiquity.

6. In chapter 1, the letter declares that it was written after some persecution. **Cotelerius** was already convinced that it was sent during the reign of Domitian (in the year 96 or 97); however, **Grabe**, **Pagi**, **Orsi**, **Wotton**, **Galland**, and others believed it followed the Neronian persecution (in the year 68), based on the erroneous opinion that the author of the Letter was that *Clement* mentioned in Philippians 4:3. But in truth, those words in chapter 1, “Because of the sudden and repeated calamities and reverses happening to us,” <note>original: "Διὰ τὰς αἰφνιδίους καὶ ἐπαλλήλους γενομένας ἡμῖν συμφορὰς καὶ περιπτώσεις"</note> denote the character of a persecution which seems to have rushed in again after some interval: this does not fit the Neronian persecution, but could appropriately be said of the calamities that came upon the Christians during the reign of Domitian.

The internal structure of the entire Letter was learnedly explained by *Richard Lipsius* in the booklet titled, *An Inquiry into the First Letter of Clement of Rome to the Corinthians, Leipzig 1855.*

7. In the writings of **Eusebius**⁴⁸) we read: “In this very same letter [Dionysius’s letter to the Romans], he also mentions the letter of Clement to the Corinthians, showing that it had been a custom from the beginning, of old, to have it read in the church. He says, at any rate: ‘Today we have passed the Lord’s holy day, in which we have read your [letter]...’” <note>original: "’Ἐν αὐτῇ δὲ ταύτῃ... τὴν ἀνάγνωσιν αὐτῆς ποιεῖσθαι. <page-num>XX</page-num>
<header>PREFACE.</header>

"...the letter; which we have always been in the habit of reading for admonition, just as the former one written to you through Clement." <note>Original Greek: ἐπιστολήν· ἣν ἔχομεν ἀεί ποτε ἀναγινώσκοντες νουθετεῖσθαι, ὡς καὶ τὴν προτέραν ὑμῖν διὰ Κλήμεντος γραφεῖσαν.</note> Care must be taken that the "other second" one, which is called the Letter of Clement, is not understood here. For that word "former" <note>Greek: προτέραν (*proteran*)</note> is contrasted with what was said about our first Letter in relation to some other Letter (perhaps that of Soter, mentioned above?). Based on Apostolic Canon number 85, Gallandius (note 49) tried in vain to promote the authority of this "Second Letter of Clement," which he believed held authority in the third century. However, it is probable that this canon was actually composed at the end of the fifth century, as demonstrated by S. de Drey in *New Investigations into the Constitutions and Canons of the Apostles* (Tübingen 1832, pp. 370, 377, 445).

But even Eusebius (note 50) left these remarks concerning it: "It must be known that there is also said to be a certain second letter of Clement; yet we do not know this to be as well-known as the former one, since we do not know of the ancients having used it." <note>Original Greek: Ἰστέον δὲ, ὡς καὶ δευτέρα τις εἶναι λέγεται τοῦ Κλήμεντος ἐπιστολή· οὐ μὴν ἔθ᾽ ὁμοίως τῇ προτέρᾳ καὶ ταύτην γνώριμον ἐπιστάμεθα· ὅτι μηδὲ τοὺς ἀρχαίους αὐτῇ κεχρημένους ἴσμεν.</note> In later times, others followed the lead of Eusebius and named Clement as its author. This makes it all the more surprising that Jerome (note 51) stated, "A second letter in his name is also circulated, which is rejected by the ancients," <note>Original Latin: "Fertur et secunda eius nomine epistola, quae a veteribus reprobatur"</note> and in the 9th century, the Patriarch Photius (note 52) affirmed: "The so-called second [letter] to the same people [the Corinthians] is rejected as spurious." <note>Original Greek: Ἡ δὲ λεγομένη δευτέρα πρὸς τοὺς αὐτοὺς ὡς νόθος ἀποδοκιμάζεται.</note>

Because the earliest Fathers are silent about it, some have wrongly judged this silence to be of excessive weight; for one must argue from silence with caution. Nevertheless, the reports of Jerome and Photius are certainly of a kind that render the work suspect. You might add that it maintains neither a continuous flow of speech nor a logical connection of ideas. The complete disparity in the style of speaking, the repetition of chapter 23 of the first letter in chapter 11 of the second, and the lack of a formal greeting, make it "smell" more like a Homily <note>A sermon or religious discourse intended for spiritual edification rather than a formal letter.</note> than an Epistle (note 53). Those who, following the lead of Cotelerius (note 54), nonetheless attribute it to Clement as the author, have put forth their desires rather than solid arguments. As Hilgenfeld (note 55) notes, the text does not oppose the Ebionites <note>A group of early Jewish Christians who emphasized Jewish law.</note> but rather the Gnostics (ch. 9), the sort who sowed weeds among Christ's flock during the reign of Marcus Aurelius while Christians were being persecuted; this view rightly reveals the intention of the author's purpose.

8. Both Letters have come down to us preserved in a single manuscript book. This is the very ancient Codex <note>The Codex Alexandrinus, one of the most important surviving manuscripts of the Greek Bible.</note> which Cyril Lucaris—Patriarch first of Alexandria, then of Constantinople—sent as a gift to King Charles I of England in the year 1628 (note 56). At the end, after the Apocalypse of John, it displays the first letter and a fragment of the second (called the Letter of Clement), followed by the book of Psalms. However, the parchment, eaten by moths and torn by the injury of time, was full of holes in many places. Accordingly, "Patricius Iunius" <note>Patrick Young (1584–1652), the Royal Librarian.</note> filled the gaps in the first Letter by conjecture, marking his own additions with red ink; he translated it into Latin and was the first to publish it, along with the fragment of the second letter, at Oxford.

# III.

## IGNATIUS.

In the Vatican Library’s Royal Codex 81 (9th century) and Palatine Codex 150 (14th century), the Latin version of the Letters of Ignatius is followed by a speech inscribed as follows: "Here begins the praise of his disciple Hyron for him, who had succeeded him in the bishopric." These are the words: "Priest and advocate <note>original: *assertor*; the Royal Codex reads *assessor* (assistant)</note> of the most wise God, Ignatius, dressed in a spotless robe <note>original: *indute*; the Royal Codex reads *inducte* (brought in)</note>, filled by the perennial fountain, singing praise with the angels, certainly a friend of the Firstborn, liberated from sins, separated from the devil: established as a champion in the stadium of truth, you acquired precious salvation; you confounded Trajan and the Senate of Rome, which at that time <note>original: *tunc*; the Royal Codex reads *nunc* (now)</note> lacked wisdom; you were made a member of Christ's household in love, and <note>The word "and" is omitted in the Palatine Codex.</note> faith, and life. Be mindful of me, your son Hyron <note>The Royal Codex spells this "Hironis".</note>, so that I too, departing from this life, may be counted in holiness among the saints, and may deserve to obtain a worthy name, and may be found a stranger to the unjust and godless station <note>original: *a Deo aliena extraneus inveniar*; the Royal Codex reads *atque adeo alienus inveniar* (and thus may be found a stranger)</note>. Thrice and four times blessed are you who have attained such things, father Ignatius, the chariot of Israel and its driver <note>original: *auriga*; the Palatine Codex reads *equester* (knight/horseman)</note>: you escaped death by fleeing it, and flew from the earth to the heavens; you deserved the great and god-making crown, and...

"...you conquered in the lovely contest of God. Remember him whom you raised, blessed martyr, and grant me a conversation, just as you 8) used to do 9) before."

1. Of those three 10) who were called by the name of Ignatius in ancient times and were eminent for the holiness of their lives, we are here dealing with the Bishop of Antioch.

In the *Martyrdom* <note>A hagiographic account of a saint's death</note> found in Symeon Metaphrastes <note>A 10th-century Byzantine author famous for rewriting lives of saints</note>, chapter 1, and in the Greek *Menaia* <note>Eastern Orthodox liturgical books containing the lives of saints</note> found in Bollandus 11), it is recorded that Ignatius was that tiny child whom the Savior, having lifted him in His own hands, presented to the Apostles to commend simplicity and integrity 12). The origin and beginning of this narrative seems to have been an erroneous way of writing the epithet *Theophoros* <note>original: "Θεόφορος" (God-bearer) vs "Θεόφορος" (God-borne). The shift in accent changes the meaning from one who carries God to one who was carried by God</note>, which occurs frequently in his Letters. Where and from what place he originated is not established; for this reason, various authors have piled up different conjectures without much critical effort, though with much and profound confidence. Gregory Abulpharagius <note>Also known as Bar Hebraeus, a 13th-century Syrian scholar</note> calls him "Nuranian" 13), which some understand as referring to Nura in the island of Sardinia, or to Cappadocia. Tillemont <note>A 17th-century French ecclesiastical historian</note> thinks he was of Syrian origin rather than Greek. Another 14) derives the name from "fire," saying Ignatius is the same as "fiery" <note>A reference to the Latin "ignis"</note>.

The author of the *Acts of the Martyrdom of Ignatius*, chapters 1 and 3 (first edited by Ruinart) and Metaphrastes in chapter 2, along with several of the ancients 15), assert that he enjoyed the companionship of John the Apostle along with Polycarp. Gregory the Great 16) also writes that he was instructed by the Apostle Peter. Moreover, Ignatius was appointed as the prelate of the metropolis of Antioch, where the name "Christian" had recently originated; whether he was the first or the second is ambiguous; nor do we have it for certain whether Peter or Paul ordained him. The author of the *Apostolic Constitutions* (VII, 46) writes that Evodius was appointed head of the church of Antioch by Peter; Jerome says 17): "Ignatius, the third Bishop of the Church of Antioch after the Apostle Peter." The same order of succession is found in Nicephorus 18) and Metaphrastes in the *Acts of the Martyrdom*, chapter 1, and in our own edition from Vatican Codex 866. But the same author of the *Constitutions* in the place cited shows Ignatius as having been appointed prelate of that same church by Paul; Chrysostom 19) contends that it was done by Peter. According to the opinion of Theodoret 20), Ignatius succeeded Peter. To reconcile the discrepancy of the earlier tradition, some think that Evodius, appointed by Peter, died while Peter himself was still living, and thus Ignatius, who succeeded Evodius, was ordained by the Apostle. Another way of settling the dispute is indicated by Baronius 21) and also by Natalis Alexander 22), namely that because of—
