# XLVIII

### ON THE SOURCE OF THE GREEK HERMAS OF LEIPZIG.

While [Anger] has argued that an original archetype survives in the Leipzig fragments, it seems he did not act with enough caution. He assigned too much weight to the fact that certain passages read more correctly in the Greek than in the published Latin editions. Furthermore, his claim (on page XXI) that it is "of great importance to this case" that the new Greek text shares features with the Dresden manuscript alone—which had "not previously been collated" <term>collated: compared in detail to identify differences</term>—is not particularly convincing. When we are investigating a "custom" that was "not unusual during the Middle Ages" (page XI)—namely, the practice of translating old Latin texts back into Greek, even if those Latin versions had themselves originally come from the Greek—what does it matter whether a matching Latin manuscript has been compared by modern scholars or not? This point is self-evident. 

Indeed, this connects to the fact that the standard printed Latin text <note>original: "Latinus textus plerumque editus," often called the Vulgate version of Hermas</note>, which is clearly corrupted in many places, is given more weight than is appropriate when judging the quality of the Greek text. For even if it is proven beyond doubt that the Greek text in question could not have been derived from our standard Latin version (even if corrected against several good manuscripts), this says little about the older Latin manuscripts that would have been available to a medieval scholar. Anyone searching for texts much purer than the common versions would naturally be led to those very manuscripts that were better and more consistent with the Greek. Consequently, in this investigation into the sources, the claim that the Greek text is superior to the Latin is not only unsupported, but greatly weakened. 

I felt it necessary to say these things first because of the significance of the Palatine manuscript <note>Codex Palatinus</note>, which was only very recently examined by Albert Dressel. Indeed, that single manuscript renders many of the arguments brought forward by the illustrious Anger to prove the superiority of the Greek text over the Latin invalid. To provide some examples:

*   In **Visions II, 4**, the Palatine reads "through you" <note>Latin: "per te"; Greek: "διὰ σοῦ" (dia sou)</note>, whereas the common edition reads "openly" <note>Latin: "aperte"</note>.
*   In **Similitudes VIII, 10**, it reads "but any of them will die with difficulty" <note>Latin: "difficile autem aliquis eorum morietur"; Greek: "δυσκόλως δέ τις αὐτῶν ἀποθανεῖται" (dyskolos de tis autōn apothaneitai)</note>, whereas the common edition reads "but they will be moved with difficulty" <note>Latin: "difficile autem movebuntur"</note>.
*   In **Mandates VI, 2**, it reads "faithful" <note>Latin: "fidelis"; Greek: "πιστότατος" (pistotatos - most faithful)</note>, instead of "most happy" <note>Latin: "felicissimus"</note>; see the introduction to the first edition, page XXI.
*   Likewise, in **Mandates IV, 1**, where the common editions say: "But you, always be mindful of the Lord, at all hours, and you will never sin," the Palatine manuscript has: "but always being mindful of your wife, you will avoid <note>The translator suggests the Latin "carebis" (you will lack/be free from) might be a mistake for "cavebis" (you will avoid/shun)</note> this sin" <note>Greek: "τῆς δὲ σῆς μνημονεύων πάντοτε γυναικὸς οὐδέποτε διαμαρτήσεις" (tēs de sēs mnemoneuōn pantote gunaikos oudepote diamartēseis)</note>.
*   Similarly, in **Visions II, 1**, where the common editions say, "When I was setting out with these" (which Albert Dressel correctly edited to "at Cumae"), the Palatine has: "When I was traveling in the region of the Cumaeans" <note>Greek: "πορευομένου μου εἰς Κώμην" (poreuomenou mou eis Kōmēn). Formerly "εἰς Κώμας" (eis Kōmas)</note>.
*   Likewise, in **Visions IV, 2**, instead of "protections" <note>Latin: "praesidia"</note>, it has "whips" <note>Latin: "flagella"; Greek: "μάστιγας" (mastigas)</note>; see the introduction to the first edition, page XX.

The clear relationship between the Palatine manuscript and our Greek text carries great weight, especially since there are also passages where the common Latin is much closer to the Greek than the Palatine is. From this—and considering that the Palatine manuscript is not particularly ancient—it is easy to conclude that there was a Latin manuscript a few centuries older that contained all these readings found scattered in more recent ones. It was likely such a manuscript that a Greek translator of that same age used to create this Greek version.

<summary>The author argues that the Leipzig Greek version of *The Shepherd of Hermas* is likely a medieval back-translation from Latin, using evidence from the recently discovered Palatine manuscript to show that the Greek text's "superior" readings actually match specific Latin traditions.</summary>

# XLIX

### ON THE SOURCE OF THE LEIPZIG GREEK HERMAS.

These points have been made, then, against the probability of the argument proposed in the first edition, which relied on comparing the Latin and Greek versions. However, lest we seem to harsh critics to have said more than is just, we know well that one could imagine a Latin translation so faithful to its Greek original that any scholar who concluded the Greek was the work of the translator rather than the author would be talking nonsense. But our case is quite different.

Nor do I think we should be more satisfied with the fact that a significant agreement was found between the old excerpts <note>Ancient fragments of Hermas quoted by other early Christian authors.</note> and our Greek text. For what, I ask, prevents us from assuming that a medieval Greek translator knew the old excerpts well and had them collected? If it occurred to one of the learned men of those times to translate the book of Hermas—famous from earliest Christian antiquity—back into Greek to compensate for a lost original, would it be surprising if we found that he had first looked around for fragments of the Greek book? Regarding what I see written on this matter by the illustrious Anger (in the work cited, page XI): "the matter is settled by the fact that, since those fragments were written long before these small Greek portions of the book began to be collected from the works of the ancients, they nevertheless agree excellently with these excerpts," I do not quite follow his meaning. For what do recent collections of Greek fragments of Hermas have to do with a manuscript of the fourteenth or, as stated in the first edition, fifteenth century—even if we accept the age of the manuscript, which the translator himself must have far preceded? The question is: could someone in the Middle Ages have used such fragments preserved in the works of the ancients to translate Latin into Greek? In an age when we know nothing was more common than collecting the interpretations of the ancients and from them creating *catenae* <term>catenae: literally "chains," these were biblical commentaries made by stringing together quotes from earlier Church Fathers</term> and other similar books, who would find it surprising that someone eager to translate Hermas would have collected the aids for his work—that is, the Greek fragments of that same Hermas—from the books of the ancients?

But we must speak a little more accurately about what agreement is actually found between our text and the Greek excerpts of the ancients. It is of such a kind that here and there individual words, not even excepting small particles, agree perfectly, but here and there quite a lot of things differ. Regarding this, it seems to us that we should think of it this way: the translator, with his laudable diligence, did not necessarily prefer the Greek excerpts found in various places over the Latin text he was translating, unless perhaps they fit it exactly. Moreover, as in many other matters, Anger's argument has been severely undermined by the recovery of Simonides' <note>Constantine Simonides, a controversial 19th-century paleographer and dealer of manuscripts often accused of forgery.</note> transcript: indeed, that reckless license of Simonides invaded most of the passages already found in Greek among the ancients, upon which the first edition so heavily depended. Let a passage from Vision II serve as an example for all, already quoted by Origen in his book *On First Principles*, which survives only in fragments. There, the Leipzig Greek text, drawn from the true transcript, reads: "You shall therefore write two little books, and you shall send one to Clement and one to Grapte. Clement, then, shall send it to the cities abroad; for to him that task has been assigned <note>original Greek: ἐπιγέγραπται (*epigegraptai*); the author suggests this is a slight corruption of ἐπιτέτραπται (*epitetraptai*), meaning "entrusted to him"</note>; and Grapte shall admonish <note>roughly so: νουθετήσει</note> the widows and the orphans. But you shall read it in this city with the elders who preside—"

# L

### ON THE SOURCE OF THE LEIPZIG GREEK HERMAS.

...of the church. <note>The text begins mid-sentence, continuing a quotation from the Shepherd of Hermas, Vision 2, 4, 3.</note> In these Greek passages, there is a remarkable agreement with the Latin text—specifically the common "Vulgate" version—in which there is absolutely no difference except for that one word "however" <note>original: "autem"</note>, in place of which the Greek reads "therefore" <note>original: "οὖν"</note>; based on the authority of the Vatican manuscript, "therefore" <note>original: "ergo"</note> should be restored. Yet, the text found in the writings of Origen <note>An influential 3rd-century Christian scholar.</note> differs from these same Greek passages in a surprising way. For there it says: "You shall write two books, and you shall give one to Clement and one to Grapte. And Grapte shall admonish the widows and the orphans, but Clement shall send it to the cities abroad; and you shall announce it to the elders of the church." <note>original: "Γράψεις δύο βιβλία, καὶ δώσεις ἓν Κλήμεντι καὶ ἓν Γραπτῇ. καὶ Γραπτὴ μὲν νουθετήσει τὰς χήρας καὶ τοὺς ὀρφανούς, Κλήμης δὲ πέμψει εἰς τὰς ἔξω πόλεις· σὺ δὲ ἀναγγελεῖς τοῖς πρεσβυτέροις τῆς ἐκκλησίας."</note> Should we say, then, that Origen wrote this from memory? Certainly not: for after he had said several things about the *Shepherd of Hermas* (a book despised by some) and about the very passage he was about to cite from it, he continues in this manner: "and this is the wording," <note>original: "ἔστι δὲ ἡ λέξις αὕτη"</note> indicating that he intended to copy his source word-for-word. Nevertheless, for those who insist on selling our text as the original archetype, one escape remains: they might say—and as the Apostle Paul testifies, "all things are lawful, but not all things are helpful"—that there were already different Greek revisions of the *Shepherd of Hermas* by the third century. If anyone finds this plausible, I fear that Origen’s version would be judged immensely superior to the other, even if our text (which is not actually the case) perfectly matched everything written in that book of uncertain age titled *The Teaching for Antiochus Ducas*,<gloss>8)</gloss> as well as the homilies of Antiochus (who lived in the seventh century), and other places where excerpts from Hermas are read.

---

8) Let us add two examples of the Greek text taken from this very *Teaching* <note>The *Doctrina ad Antiochum Ducam*, a later Greek theological work.</note>, which makes it much more probable that the Leipzig fragments contain a translation of the Latin text (made, to be sure, using ancient excerpts) rather than the ancient Greek text of Hermas itself. In Mandate XII, 4, <note>The "Mandates" are the second major section of the Shepherd of Hermas.</note> our text reads as follows: "But those who have the Lord on their lips, but their heart hardened, and are far from God, to those people these commandments are hard and difficult to travel. Therefore, place the Lord in your heart, you who are empty and light in faith, and you will know etc." <note>original: "Οἱ δὲ ἐπὶ τοῖς χείλεσιν ἔχοντες τὸν κύριον, τὴν δὲ καρδίαν αὐτῶν πεπωρωμένην, καὶ μακρὰν ὄντες ἀπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ, ἐκείνοις αἱ ἐντολαὶ αὗται σκληραί εἰσι καὶ δύσβατοι. Θέσθε οὖν ὑμεῖς, οἱ κενοὶ καὶ ἐλαφροὶ ὄντες ἐν τῇ πίστει, τὸν κύριον ὑμῶν εἰς τὴν καρδίαν, καὶ γνώσεσθε ὅτι etc."</note> The *Teaching* provides the same as follows: "But those who have the Lord on the lips <gloss>1</gloss>, but the heart <gloss>2</gloss> hardened, and are far from the Lord <gloss>2b</gloss> through their own laziness <gloss>3</gloss>, to those people these commandments are hard and difficult to achieve <gloss>4</gloss>. Therefore, you who are faint-hearted <gloss>5</gloss> and light <gloss>6</gloss> in <gloss>7</gloss> faith, place the Lord <gloss>8</gloss> unceasingly <gloss>9</gloss> into your <gloss>11</gloss> hearts <gloss>10</gloss>, and you will know etc." <note>original: "Οἱ δὲ ἐπὶ τὰ χείλη[1] ἔχοντες τὸν κύριον, τὴν δὲ καρδίαν[2] πεπωρωμένην, καὶ μακρὰν ὄντες ἀπὸ τοῦ κυρίου[2b] διὰ τὴν ἑαυτῶν ῥαθυμίαν,[3] ἐκείνοις αἱ ἐντολαὶ αὗται σκληραὶ εἰσὶν καὶ δυσκατόρθωτοι.[4] Θέσθε οὖν ὑμεῖς, οἱ ὀλιγόψυχοι[5] καὶ ἐλαφροί[6] τῇ[7] πίστει, τὸν κύριον[8] ἀδιαλείπτως[9] εἰς τὰς καρδίας[10] ὑμῶν,[11] καὶ γνώσεσθε ὅτι etc."</note> There are twelve points of difference in this short passage, several of which are of no small importance. "Empty" <note>original: "κενοὶ"</note> instead of "faint-hearted" <note>original: "ὀλιγόψυχοι"</note> and "difficult to travel" <note>original: "δύσβατοι"</note> instead of "difficult to achieve" <note>original: "δυσκατόρθωτοι"</note> betray a translation from the Latin much more than a variation of the same Greek text. For who, after all, would think to write one for the other? Furthermore, "on the lips" <note>original: "ἐπὶ τοῖς χείλεσιν"</note> corresponds more accurately than "onto the lips" <note>original: "ἐπὶ τὰ χείλη"</note> to the Latin "in their lips" <note>original: "in labiis suis"</note>. The same logic applies to the words "into the heart" <note>original: "εἰς τὴν καρδίαν"</note> (Latin "in corde") instead of "into your hearts," "being light in the [faith]" <note>original: "ἐλαφροὶ ὄντες ἐν τῇ"</note> ("who are light in faith") instead of "light in faith," and "but their heart" <note>original: "τὴν δὲ καρδίαν αὐτῶν"</note> ("the heart of them") instead of "but the heart." Nor do those two additions—"through their own laziness" and "unceasingly"—seem to be attributed to the freedom of the excerpts, but they are absent in the Latin text as well as in the Leipzig Greek. Moreover, the Palatine manuscript <note>Another important manuscript of Hermas.</note> is missing here, and those few and trivial points that agree between both Greek texts against the common Latin can easily be derived from Latin variants.

A second example is found in Mandate V, throughout almost the entire second chapter. From the points where one text differs from the other, let us record only a few. Leipzig Text: "and from nothing the woman or the man becomes in bitterness because of worldly matters etc." <note>original: "καὶ ἐκ τοῦ μηδενὸς ἡ γυνὴ ἢ ὁ ἀνὴρ ἐν πικρίᾳ γίνεται ἕνεκεν βιωτικῶν πραγμάτων etc."</note> *Teaching*: "and thus a person is embittered because of worldly matters." <note>original: "καὶ οὕτως πικραίνεται ἄνθρωπος ἕνεκεν βι. πρ."</note> Leipzig Text: "but patience is great and having strong power and robust and prospering in great expansion, cheerful, exulting, un-..." <note>original: "ἡ δὲ μακροθυμία μεγάλη ἐστὶ καὶ ἰσχυρὰν δύναμιν ἔχουσα καὶ στιβαρὰ καὶ εὐθυνουμένη ἐν πλατυσμῷ μεγάλῳ, ἱλαρά, ἀγαλλιωμένη, ἀμέ-"</note>

# LI

### ON THE SOURCE OF THE LEIPZIG GREEK HERMAS.

But now we must proceed to the most weighty arguments for our opinion, which depend partly on the general character of the language used in the Greek text and partly on specific instances whose cause must inevitably be traced back to Latin sources.

Regarding the first point—the general character of the language of the Greek Hermas—the very learned men Robert Anger and Wilhelm Dindorf have already spoken in the introductions to the first edition. If we listen to them, "the language is <term>Hellenistic</term> <note>The common Greek (Koine) used in the Mediterranean after Alexander the Great, including the dialect of the New Testament.</note>, such as was used primarily in the first two centuries after the birth of Christ, with only a few forms of a later age mixed in; and these, because of their very rarity, should be attributed to the scribes rather than the author." It must not be forgotten, however, that this judgment depended in very large part on the forged <term>apograph</term> <note>A transcript or copy of a manuscript.</note> by Simonides. For in forging the booklet, Simonides’ primary goal—aided by the learning and advice of a man equally skilled in Latin and Greek, who died shortly before Simonides' fraud was discovered—was to restore to a better form whatever he found incorrectly or "barbarously" written. But we must speak of the uncorrupted "body of the offense"—that is, the "barbarism" of the <term>codex</term> <note>An ancient manuscript in book form.</note> itself; for I cannot help but use the term "barbarism." In this matter, our goal is not to attribute to the author of the book every error found in the transcript or in the three ancient leaves—and there are very many⁹)—while ignoring the carelessness and recklessness of the scribes. Nevertheless, there are quite a few faulty or "barbaric" forms which we must be careful not to dismiss as the author's work through excessive zeal or preconceived opinion. Among those forms whose origin you might doubt are these:

"daughter" <note>original: "θυγατέραν" (a non-standard accusative form)</note>, "woman" <note>original: "γυναῖκαν" (a non-standard accusative form)</note>, "four" <note>original: "τέσσερα" (a later spelling)</note>, "on the waters" <note>original: "ἐπ’ ὑδάτων"</note>, "old man" used for "old woman" <note>original: "πρεσβύτης" for "πρεσβῦτις"</note>, "they brought" <note>original: "ὑπένεγκαν" (used twice)</note>, "you condemned" <note>original: "ἐκατάκρινας"</note>, "I asked" <note>original: "ἐπερώτησα"</note>, "they have given back" <note>original: "ἀπεδώκασι"</note>, "they were throwing" <note>original: "ἐρρίπτουν"</note>, "being built" <note>original: "ᾠκοδομούμενον"</note>, "having been built" <note>original: "οἰκοδομημένον"</note>, "he had arrived" <note>original: "παραγεγόνει"</note>, "you took" <note>original: "ἐλάβατε"</note>, "they brought" <note>original: "ἔφεραν"</note>, "they seemed" <note>original: "ἐδοκοῦσαν"</note>, "do not doubt" <note>original: "μὴ διψυχήσεις" (found twice in Vision IV, chapter 1)</note>, "do not be lazy" <note>original: "μὴ ῥᾳθυμήσεις"</note>, "if he has" <note>original: "ἐὰν ἔχει"</note>, "if he went up" <note>original: "ἐὰν ἀνέβη"</note>, "if you will wish" <note>original: "ἐὰν θελήσετε"</note>, "even if he remains and does not repent" <note>original: "κἂν ἐπιμείνῃ καὶ μὴ μετανοήσει"</note>, "as many as shall work" <note>original: "ὅσοι ἂν ἐργάσονται"</note>, "as many as shall hear" <note>original: "ὅσα ἂν ἀκούσονται"</note>, "so that it is completed" <note>original: "ἵνα συντελεῖται"</note>, "so that they become and know" <note>original: "ἵνα γίνονται καὶ γινώσκουσι"</note>, "so that they might repent and be saved" <note>original: "ἵνα μετανοήσωσι καὶ ζήσωνται"</note>, "they might be set right" <note>original: "κατορθώσωνται"</note>, "stretching himself out and he put forward" <note>original: "ἐκτείνας ἑαυτὸν καὶ προέβαλλε"</note>, "if taking and you pour upon" <note>original: "ἐὰν λαβὼν καὶ ἐπιχέῃς"</note>, the beast...

LII

# ON THE SOURCE OF THE GREEK HERMAS OF LEIPZIG.

"roaring" <note>original: "ῥύζων"</note>, "the beast stretching himself out" <note>original: "τὸ κτῆνος ἐκτείνας ἑαυτὸν"</note>, and many other similar things. Some of these should be less offensive, since they are excellently attested in the books of the New Testament—those published according to the most ancient witnesses—the <term>Septuagint</term> <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> interpretation, and many books from the first two centuries of Christianity. This is especially true of those instances which, in the judgment of the famous Wilhelm Dindorf (see his introduction, page XXX), can hardly be doubted to be the fault of scribes in the current reading: "whenever he struck" <note>original: "ὅταν ἐπάτασσεν"</note>, "whenever they were placed" <note>original: "ὅταν ἐτέθησαν"</note>. But such forms, to pass over the New Testament, the Septuagint, and the <term>Apostolic Fathers</term> <note>Early Christian authors who lived in the 1st and 2nd centuries.</note>, are often read in Philo himself: compare Mangey's edition, volume I, page 109: "whenever he says" <note>original: "ὅταν φησίν"</note>; I, 120: "whenever he says" <note>original: "ὅταν φησίν"</note>; II, 112: "whenever it came into [his] mind" <note>original: "ὅταν εἰς ἔννοιαν ἦλθε"</note>; II, 252: "whenever you became" <note>original: "ὅταν ἐγίνεσθε"</note>; II, 584: "whenever he saw" <note>original: "ὅταν εἶδε"</note>. Therefore, a sensible critic can believe that Hermas might have written in such a way without compromising his 2nd-century authority.

Other things, however, are so foreign to the usage of those same times that the only choice given is whether a man of the Middle Ages wrote them, or if scribes introduced them into the text later; for they can in no way be attributed to Hermas. Such things are roughly: "from the house" <note>original: "ἀπὸ τὸν οἶκον"; note: This uses an incorrect grammatical case for 2nd-century Greek.</note>, "from a stadium" <note>original: "ἀπὸ στάδιον"</note>, "until the second hour" <note>original: "ἕως ὥραν δευτέραν"</note>, "be useful" <note>original: "εὔχρηστοι ἦσθε"; note: "utiles estote" in the Palatine Codex.</note>, "they leave behind" <note>original: "ἀφίνουσι"</note>, "the daughter" <note>original: "ἡ θυγατέρα"</note>, "your simplicity" <note>original: "ἡ ἁπλότητά σου"</note>, "I place [my] knees" <note>original: "τιθῶ τὰ γόνατα"</note>, "I place [my] knees upon" <note>original: "ἐπιθῶ τὰ γόνατα"</note>. Likewise, certain words seem to shrink away from the age of Hermas, such as "master" <note>original: "αὐθέντης"; Simonides, with his leader, had cautiously replaced this with "lord" (κύριος)</note> of the tower; "activity" <note>original: "ἐνεργεσία"; Simonides used "energy" (ἐνέργειαν)</note>; "take hold of" <note>original: "ἀντιλαμβάνετε"; Simonides used "take hold of for yourselves" (ἀντιλαμβάνεσθε)</note> one another; "they turned black" <note>original: "ἐμελάνωσαν"; Simonides used "they were becoming black" (ἐμελαίνοντο)</note>. Furthermore, there occur very often "small bench" <note>original: "συμψέλλιον"; Simonides everywhere used "seat" (ἐδώλιον)</note>, "cushion" <note>original: "κερβικάριον"; Simonides used "pillow" (προσκεφάλαιον)</note>, and "census-station" <note>original: "ἱστατων"</note>. Although it is well established that similar words (like "copy" <note>original: "ἐξεμπλάριον"</note> in the letters of Ignatius, even the shorter ones) were used here and there in apostolic times and afterward, it is nonetheless questioned whether Hermas would have favored such "barbarous" terms. The word "raw linen" <note>original: "ὠμόλινον"</note> in *Similitude* VIII, 4 presents the opposite case. There, in all the Latin manuscripts, it is "towel" <note>original: "sabanum"; "gird," "gird yourself," "gird yourself with a towel"</note>. It is hardly credible that this word would have passed to a Latin translator unless he had found "towel" <note>original: "σάβανον"</note> in the Greek. Now, however, the person who was turning the Latin back into Greek preferred to write "raw linen" <note>original: "ὠμόλινον"</note>.

What indeed shall we say of these expressions: *As I was going to Comae I was glorifying, As I was going to the village I remembered, While I was advising and debating these things in my heart I see, Why should I doubt, as I have been so firmly established?*^10) Likewise regarding these: *and I place my knees and I began to pray* <note>original: "καὶ ἐπιθῶ τὰ γόνατά μου καὶ ἠρξάμην προσεύχεσθαι"; Palatine Codex: "and I placed my knees and began to pray"</note>, *I place [my] knees and I began to pray* <note>original: "τιθῶ τὰ γόνατα καὶ ἠρξάμην προσεύχεσθαι"; Palatine Codex: "I placed [my] knees and began to pray"</note>, *and falling at her feet* <note>original: "πεσὼν δὲ αὐτῇ πρὸς τοὺς πόδας"; common version: "falling forward at her feet"</note>? Are these not spoken in a Latin rather than a Greek manner? Do they seem to have been written by Hermas or by some Greek translator of a Latin text?

Likewise, the translator, I believe, reveals himself by the fact that he usually avoids conjunctions, contrary to Greek usage, just as in *Vision* I, 1, these sentences follow one another: *After many years [I beheld] this woman* and *After many times I saw her*, likewise *After a certain time, as I was going* and *While walking I fell asleep*, likewise *Answering her I say* and...

---

10) These are more tolerable than the others: "as if a shuddering came upon me" <note>original: "ὡσεὶ φρίκη μοι προσῆλθε"</note>, "as I was alone" <note>original: "μόνου μου ὄντος"</note>, and "as I wished to sit on the right side she did not permit me" <note>original: "θέλοντός μου εἰς τὰ δεξιὰ μέρη καθίσαι οὐκ εἴασέ με"</note>.

<summary>The author analyzes linguistic "barbarisms" and oddities in the Leipzig Greek manuscript of The Shepherd of Hermas, arguing that many phrases reflect Latin syntax or later Greek dialects rather than the authentic 2nd-century original. He suggests the text may be a back-translation from Latin, pointing out where the forger Simonides attempted to "correct" these errors.</summary>

LIII

# ON THE SOURCE OF THE GREEK HERMAS OF LEIPZIG.

"Smiling, she says to me." <note>original Greek: "Γελάσασά μοι λέγει"</note> In the same Vision, chapter 3, these four phrases follow one another: *"After it ceased, she says to me; I also say; She says to me; I heard great things."* <note>original Greek: "Μετὰ τὸ παυθῆναι λέγει μοι, Λέγω κἀγὼ, Λέγει μοι, Ἤκουσα μεγάλας"</note> Likewise in Vision III, 10, these three follow: *"Answering, I say to him; Answering, she says to me; Answering him again, I said."* <note>original Greek: "Ἀποκριθεὶς αὐτῷ λέγω, Ἀποκριθείς μοι λέγει, Ἀποκριθεὶς αὐτῷ πάλιν εἶπον"</note> Similar patterns are found very frequently. Two other matters are connected to this usage: the very frequent use of the word <term>phēsin</term> <note>Greek: "he says," used to indicate a quotation</note> in exactly the same way the Romans use "inquit" <note>Latin: "he said," typically inserted in the middle of a quote</note>,¹¹) and the arrangement of individual words, which is more Latin in style than Greek.

Furthermore, the following seem to be spoken in a Latin rather than a Greek manner: *"of those not having food, their flesh is wasted."* <note>original Greek: "τῶν δὲ μὴ ἐχόντων ἐδέσματα, λυμαίνεται ἡ σὰρξ αὐτῶν." The scholar is noting a clunky grammatical structure.</note> (Indeed, one can hardly conclude these are Hebraisms <note>Influences of Hebrew grammar on Greek</note> of Hermas’s Greek style.) Likewise: *"For the Lord swore that those who denied their Lord have been rejected from their life; but to those who previously denied, through His great mercy, He became gracious to them."* <note>original Greek: "ὤμοσε γὰρ ὁ κύριος, τοὺς ἀρνησαμένους τὸν κύριον αὐτῶν ἀπεγνωρίσθαι ἀπὸ τῆς ζωῆς αὐτῶν· τοὺς δὲ πρότερον ἀρνησαμένους, διὰ τὴν πολλὴν αὐτοῦ εὐσπλαγχνίαν ἵλεως ἐγένετο αὐτοῖς."</note> Added to this are several passages that can hardly be understood unless one consults the Latin readings, which themselves seem to be faulty. For instance, in Vision I, 2, it reads: *"And she said: Why is the patient one gloomy... why so downcast in appearance and not cheerful? And I said to her: By a certain very good woman saying to me that..."* etc. The same passage in the Palatine Manuscript <note>A significant Latin manuscript of this text</note> reads as follows: "And she said to me: Why are you sad, O long-suffering one"... "why are you so sad in face and not cheerful?" "And I said to her: By a good woman saying to me that" etc. These are certainly understood in the Latin, but not so in the Greek. Since the common text <note>The "Vulgate" or standard version</note> shows the end like this: "Lady, an insult was thrown at me by a woman" etc., it becomes probable that the Palatine text suffers from an error, and that this error was even reproduced by the Greek translator. A similar situation occurs in Similitude IX, 14. There, the Greek reads: *"Now, I say, Lord, show me why the tower was not built on the ground... Still, he says, you are foolish and without understanding. I have a need, I say, Lord, to ask everything, because"* etc. The word *"Still"* <note>original Greek: "Ἔτι"</note>, which is in the transcript <note>The Simonides transcript</note>, clearly arose from an improper correction by one of the scribes, who wrote "still" instead of *"because"* <note>original Greek: "ὅτι"</note>: this becomes clear both from the Latin manuscripts and from the flow of the speech. From this it also follows that in the common Latin text, the phrase "therefore you ask" was correctly added. This addition is missing in the Palatine manuscript, and likewise in the Leipzig Greek fragments, which very probably depended on a similar Latin manuscript. To pass over Vision III, 1. *"You are grieved, Hermas,"* and other similar things, it is worth mentioning that since the transcript of Simonides has been recovered, even that [part] of the Greek text has perished—

---

11) It is worth noting that in several passages of Hermas inserted into the *Teaching to Antiochus the Governor* <note>original: "Doctrina ad Antioch. Duc."</note>, the words *"I say"* or *"he says"* <note>original Greek: "λέγω" or "λέγει"</note> are used, where the Leipzig Greek text uses <term>phēsin</term> <note>he says</note>. Compare Similitude VI, 3. *Teaching to Antiochus*: *"And he says to me: This is"* and the Leipzig Greek text: *"This, he says, is."* In the same place, *Teaching to Antiochus*: *"I say to him: I wished to know, Lord"* and the Leipzig Greek text: *"I wished, I say, Lord, to know."* Likewise compare Mandate VI, 1. where the *Teaching to Antiochus* has: *"I commanded you in the first commandment that you should keep faith and fear, and be self-controlled. I answered: Yes, Lord, it is so. He says: But now I want to show you also their powers, so that you may understand the power they have and their operation."* But the Leipzig Greek text: *"I commanded you, he says, in the first commandment that you should keep faith and fear and self-control. Yes, I say, Lord. But now I want, he says, to show you also their powers, so that you may understand which of them has what power and operation."*

<summary>The author argues that the Leipzig Greek manuscript of The Shepherd of Hermas displays "Latinisms"—grammatical structures and word choices that suggest it was translated from a Latin source rather than being the original Greek. He highlights specific phrases where the Greek text only makes sense if viewed as a flawed translation of known Latin manuscripts.</summary>
<keywords>The Shepherd of Hermas, philology, Latinisms, Leipzig manuscript, Codex Palatinus, Simonides, back-translation, textual criticism</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the philological argument regarding the Greek text of *The Shepherd of Hermas*. Having previously discussed sentence structure and Latinisms, the author now focuses on specific textual corruptions in the Leipzig manuscript (the Simonides fragments) that appear to be direct, and often mistaken, translations from Latin manuscripts.</meta>

LIV

# ON THE SOURCE OF THE GREEK HERMAS OF LEIPZIG.

...an ornament <note>original Latin: "tus ornamentum"</note> found in Vision IV, chapter 3: "in what way" <note>original Greek: "ποιῳ τροπῳ"</note>, which the Latin translators—confusing the words for "way" <note>τρόπου</note> and "place" <note>τόπου</note>—render as "in what place" or "into what place." It has perished, I say: for from his own codex on Mount Athos, Simonides drew with a faithful hand the phrase "in what way" <note>original Greek: "ποίω τρόπω"</note>. I have little doubt that the Greek codex, along with so many others, adopted this from the Latin—unless the origin of this Latin error is to be sought in even older Greek sources.

Finally, if our arguments seem to lack weight, it is all compensated by two passages where the errors that passed into the Greek text cannot but be derived from Latin. The first, mentioned above, is found in Vision III, 3: "you are clever regarding the scriptures" <note>original Greek: "πανούργος εἶ περὶ τὰς γραφάς"</note>. Since the discussion here is about a tower and its construction methods, this phrase is utterly absurd. This clearly flowed from the fact that several Latin codices—including Dressel’s Vatican codex, though not the Palatine—read "that you are clever regarding the scriptures" <note>original Latin: "versutum te esse circa scripturas"</note>, having confused the words for "structures" <note>Latin: *structuras*</note>—the topic is the specific methods of building the tower, for which the author likely wrote <term>oikodomaí</term> <note>Greek: "buildings" or "structures"</note> or something similar—with "scriptures" <note>Latin: *scripturas*</note>. Just as this confusion could happen very easily in Latin, it was entirely impossible in Greek, unless someone was translating Latin into Greek.

Even more significant, if possible, is the second passage. In Vision II, 3, it is written in Greek: "But you shall say to Maximus: Behold, tribulation is coming" <note>original Greek: "Ἐρεῖς δὲ Μαξίμῳ Ἰδοὺ θλῖψις ἔρχεται"</note>. But what on earth does this "Maximus" mean, when throughout the entire book there is no place for a character named Maximus? The nature of the matter seems not to have been hidden from Simonides, or rather from Simonides' learned Leipzig assistant; for by their labor it was restored and later published as: "But you shall say: behold, a very great tribulation is coming" <note>original Greek: "Ἐρεῖς δὲ· ἰδοὺ θλῖψις ἔρχεται μεγάλη σφόδρα"</note>. Once this is known, one does not need an <term>Oedipus</term> <note>A reference to the mythological hero who solved the riddle of the Sphinx; here meaning a master riddle-solver</note> to explain "Maximus." The common Latin text has: "But you shall say: Behold, a great tribulation comes" <note>original Latin: "Dices autem: Ecce magna... tribulatio venit"</note>. The light that shines from this onto the Greek reading will be enough for anyone investigating a little more carefully. Yet, lest we lack anything to explain the matter and persuade even the incredulous, the Palatine codex—which I shared with the most learned R. Anger nearly two months ago—not only provides "Behold, a greatest tribulation" <note>original Latin: "Maxima ecce"</note>, but it accurately precedes the very error of the Greek text, as Albert Dressel testifies, in this manner: "But you say to Maximus: Behold, tribulation approaches" <note>original Latin: "Dicis autem maximo. Ecce tribulatio supervenit."</note>.

Since these things are so, I have no doubt that in the Simonides fragments we have found a Greek text which someone in the Middle Ages, translating from the Latin, sought to use to replace the lost Greek original of the so-called Hermas. Let others look more closely at who this translator was. There will certainly be those who evade the force of so many combined arguments; truly, there are those who either by nature lack a sense of probability and certainty, or have lost it through their prejudices, and who prefer to conquer the truth as if it were an enemy rather than find it with an open mind. They might suggest that the text of the Leipzig fragments, though very ancient, was corrupted here and there by Latin influences—that is, by the most foolishly introduced errors of several Latin codices. Let us leave that conjecture, and all similar ones, to others. As for us, we are so thoroughly persuaded of the matter as we have set it out that we shall refrain from bringing forward more arguments. Those who examine the Palatine codex, which is of no small weight...

<summary>The author argues that the Leipzig Greek manuscript of The Shepherd of Hermas is a medieval back-translation from Latin. He proves this by highlighting "Maximus" and "scriptures," which originated as Latin scribal errors (maxima/maximo and structuras/scripturas) that make no sense in the Greek context.</summary>

LV

# ON THE SOURCE OF THE GREEK HERMAS OF LEIPZIG.

...the ornament <note>original Latin: "ornamentum"</note> of the edition of the Apostolic Fathers by Dressel, having also not neglected those things which have been and will be brought forward from the Latin codices, once they have compared them with the Leipzig Greek text. <note>original Latin: "editionis PP. AA. Dresselianae... cum Graeco textu Lipsiensi contulerint." This refers to Albert Dressel's 1857 edition of the Apostolic Fathers.</note>$^{12}$) If anyone grieves that this text has been stripped of the great honor and importance it seemed to hold—even though it must still be placed in no low position among the critical aids for the book of Hermas—I would wish him to remember that in no matter, however learned or serious, is anything nobler or greater than the truth. That we should seek truth most zealously in all our labor is not hindered by the fact that—as we ourselves have learned well enough from experience, as the old proverb says—truth begets hatred. <note>original Latin: "veritas odium parit," a famous Roman aphorism from Terence.</note>

->Written at Leipzig, July 20, 1856.<-

->**Constantin Tischendorf.**<-

---

12) It is not surprising that this very text can be corrected in places using our Greek text. For the Greek translator, since he relied on the Simonides codex—as is shown by the very frequency of the errors with which the three 14th-century leaves are burdened—is older than the Palatine codex. An example of such a correction is in Vision III, 9: “When therefore you have kept the works of their mother, you will be able to see all.” <note>original Latin: "Quando ergo operas matris earum servaveris, omnes poteris videre."</note> Consulting the Greek, it should be written: “...if you keep [the commandments] all, you will be able to live.” <note>original Latin: "servaveris omnes, poteris vivere." This highlights a confusion between "see" and "live" and "works of their mother" versus "all the commandments."</note>

In the same vein, I am not sure whether those things can also be applied which are read at the beginning of the book of the *Shepherd of Hermas* in the codex, and from there also in Simonides' copy. Those words are read in a remarkably corrupt state: a state which certainly flowed for the most part from the ignorance of Simonides, who very often slipped while reading especially the first leaves of his codex. Furthermore, the true copy differs greatly from that text which the first editor drew from Simonides' falsified copy and attempted to restore in the preface on page IX. Nevertheless, as the first editor already saw, it is clear that the note in the codex, or rather the prologue, depends very much on that passage in the *Ecclesiastical History* of Eusebius (Book III, chapter 3), where the *Shepherd of Hermas* is mentioned. Indeed, the translator of the Latin text could very aptly place those words at the beginning of his work to signify the antiquity and weight of the book he was translating into Greek.

The points we made above regarding the Greek style of the Leipzig Hermas do not lose their force simply because one or two of the things we identified as “Latin rather than Greek” are not unheard of among Greek writers. For if that were the case, where else would a Greek translator of the Latin Hermas, being familiar with his native tongue, have gotten them? Thus, while we may stay silent on the word *sympséllion* <note>original Greek: "συμψέλλιον", meaning a bench or stool</note> discussed in Stephanus’s *Treasury of the Greek Language*, the grammarian Herodian already mentioned the word *kerbikárion* <note>original Greek: "κερβικάριον", meaning a pillow or bolster, derived from the Latin "cervical"</note> among "barbarisms" in his work on grammatical errors. So too there are examples of genitive absolutes of almost the same kind—not to say more than is just—as the type we criticized; for instance, one is found in the New Testament, though it is hardly comparable to ours, in Matthew 1:18: "For when his mother Mary was betrothed to Joseph, before they came together, she was found to be with child." <note>original Greek: "μνηστευθείσης γὰρ τῆς μητρὸς αὐτοῦ Μαρίας τῷ Ἰωσήφ, πρὶν ἢ συνελθεῖν αὐτοὺς εὑρέθη ἐν γαστρὶ ἔχουσα."</note> On this matter, see Winer’s *Grammar of New Testament Greek Idioms*, page 187. Nevertheless, we must stand by the opinion that such locutions, when so many are joined together, reveal a Greek translator of Latin texts—and one from the Middle Ages when ancient Greek was significantly decaying—rather than Hermas, a not inglorious writer of the early second century. If something is added to these locutions that cannot be explained except by the translation of Latin—such as errors clearly specific to Latin codices translated into Greek—I believe it is the mark of sound judgment to no longer hesitate in doubt or fluctuate between probabilities, but to confidently and firmly follow what is certain.

---

**N. B.** From the first edition, several items passed incorrectly into our own against the evidence of the manuscript copy. Therefore, delete: 574, 15: *tauta* <note>"these things"</note>; 585, 11: *en* <note>"in"</note>; 592. II. 1: *kai* <note>"and"</note>; 593. II. 2: *meta* <note>"with"</note>; 594, 18: *de* <note>"but/and"</note>. Likewise, 572, 6: the manuscript has *hōs* <note>"as/how"</note> instead of *hoti* <note>"that"</note>; 576, 25: *gnōsthēsetai* <note>"it will be known"</note>; 578, 33 and following: *moi legei* <note>"he says to me"</note>; 581, 25: preferably *mneian* <note>"mention"</note> instead of *mnēmēn* <note>"memory"</note> and 27: *de ep’* <note>"but upon"</note>; 586, 22: *douleusetai* (correct to *-te*) <note>"he/you will serve"</note>; 595, 12: *kai* <note>"and"</note> instead of *apo* <note>"from/by"</note> for the third time; 598. XI. 2: *kathedran* <note>"seat/chair"</note>; 621, 14: *to de deut.* <note>"and the second"</note> and 40: *lampidoni* (correct to *-pē-*) <note>"with a torch/brightness"</note>. Furthermore, 578, 6: the manuscript has *autēs* <note>"of her"</note> rather than *autē* <note>"to her"</note>; 588, 7: *apollousan* <note>"perishing/destroying"</note>; 590. III. 4: *tōn proterōn* <note>"of the former things"</note>.

He emphasizes the pursuit of truth over the prestige of the manuscript and provides a list of errata for his edition.</summary>

<meta>This page transitions from the discussion of the "Shepherd of Hermas" text found in Leipzig to a detailed catalog of manuscripts (codices) containing the writings of the Apostolic Fathers found in Roman libraries, specifically the Vatican. # ACCOUNT OF THE MANUSCRIPTS.

Since almost nothing has been known until now about the handwritten **Roman books of the Apostolic Fathers**, I will briefly describe not only the number and outward appearance of those I have seen and examined, but also their scholarly importance.

->a. *Manuscripts of the Vatican Library.*<-

1. Vatican Manuscript (Codex Vaticanus) 859, made of vellum, consisting of 288 large quarto leaves, written in the 11th century by a learned Greek hand. It contains, among other works by various authors: *A Commentary on the Holy Apostle Philip*; *Methodius of Patara, the most wise, on the End Times*; *Dionysius the Areopagite on the Celestial Hierarchy, on Mystical Theology, on Divine Names*, *by the same author from the Erotic Hymns, on the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, and *various letters*; *Discourses of James, the brother of the Lord and Archbishop of Jerusalem*; *Gregory of Nazianzus's discourse on the birth of the Lord Jesus Christ*. <note>The original Greek titles are: Ὑπόμνημα εἰς ἅγιον ἀπόστολον Φίλιππον; Μεθωδίου πάτρων τοῦ σοφωτάτου εἰς τὸν ἔσχατον καιρὸν; Διονυσίου Ἀρεοπαγίτου περὶ τῆς οὐρανίας ἱεραρχίας, κτλ.</note> There follow sermons by Basil and Chrysostom, and on leaf 255, *the faith and teaching of the 318 holy fathers at Nicaea*, <note>original Greek: πίστις τῶν ἁγίων τη' τῶν ἐν Νικαίᾳ καὶ διδασκαλία</note> which is followed by other sermons by Eusebius, Epiphanius, and Chrysostom. On leaves 151–195, the longer versions of the Letters of Ignatius are read in this order: to the Trallians (the beginning is missing), Magnesians, Tarsians, Philippians, Philadelphians, Smyrnaeans, Polycarp, Antiochians, Hero, Ephesians, and Romans. There follow the "Letter of Polycarp to the Philippians" (leaves 195–198), joined with which (leaves 198–211) is the work that circulates under the name of "Barnabas." The manuscript is of the highest quality; the style of writing is typical of Greek scribes, and therefore, due to "itacism," <term>itacism: a common scribal error where different Greek vowels or diphthongs that sounded alike (like 'i', 'ee', and 'ey') were swapped</term> it frequently confuses vowels and diphthongs. The headings are in red. That Nerses of Ghelat, who once owned the book, added a short note in the Armenian language at the end of the Letter of Barnabas. <note>Nerses of Ghelat, also known as Nerses of Lambron (1153–1198), was a famous Armenian archbishop and scholar.</note>

Since he died in the year 1173, it is clearly apparent that Angelo Mai, along with Jacobson (in the first edition of the *Apostolic Fathers*, page 5), erred in assigning the manuscript to "perhaps the 13th century." I have designated this manuscript with the letter *V*.

2. Ottobonian Manuscript (Codex Ottobonianus) 348, made of paper, in small quarto leaves, from the beginning of the 14th century. On the second leaf: "Greek Letters of the blessed martyrs Ignatius and Polycarp." <note>original Latin: 'Ignatii et Polycarpi martyrum beatorum Epistolae graecae.'</note>

->“From the Manuscripts of Giovanni Angelo, Duke of Altemps.”<-

It contains (leaves 2–63) eleven letters of Ignatius in the longer version, the first being the letter to the Trallians, which is "headless" <term>headless: "acephalous," meaning the beginning of the text is missing</term> just as in the Vatican manuscript, and in the same order as found there. This is followed (leaves 63–84) by the "Letter of Polycarp to the Philippians," which is followed immediately by a fragment of the "Letter of Barnabas" without any separation between them. It is written with frequent abbreviations that are often ambiguous. In the margins, there are scholia <term>scholia: ancient or medieval marginal comments explaining a text</term>, notes, corrections, and conjectures that are not to be disregarded. The titles are in red. It seems to have flowed from the same source as the Vatican manuscript. I have designated this with the letter *O*.

<summary>This page catalogs and describes two significant Greek manuscripts in the Vatican collections, Cod. Vat. 859 and Cod. Ottob. 348, which contain the writings of Ignatius, Polycarp, and Barnabas.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the catalog of manuscripts (codices) containing the writings of the Apostolic Fathers, specifically moving from the Vatican collections into various "Royal" and "Palatine" collections. It maintains the descriptive numbering started on the previous page.</meta>

# ACCOUNT OF THE MANUSCRIPTS.

3. Royal Manuscript (Codex Regius) 30, made of vellum, in eight-leaf sections <note>Tischendorf refers to "foliis octonariis," meaning the parchment was folded into quires of eight leaves.</note>, from the beginning of the 11th century. It contains the works of "Dionysius the Areopagite" with notes that are not unlearned, as well as materials regarding "John the Apostle" (leaves 1–160). After these, a fragment of "Ignatius’s Letter to the Ephesians" is presented on six and a half leaves. The various readings it provides should be held in high regard. This manuscript is our *R*.

4. Vatican Manuscript 813, made of paper, consisting of 321 four-leaf sections, completed by a scribe on November 23rd in the year 1378. It is a Menologium <note>A collection of lives of the saints organized by their feast days in the calendar.</note> ("Metaphrastes for the month of December from the 4th to the 20th"), preceded by an "excellent index of the present book" <note>original Greek: πίναξ ἄριστος τοῦ παρόντος βιβλίου</note>. On leaves 304–312, you find the "Martyrdom of Ignatius." The manuscript is quite accurate, and at its end is written: "This book reached its end in the month of November, the 23rd, in the year 6887 <note>This year in the Byzantine calendar corresponds to 1378 AD.</note>, of the current eighth indiction. [In the name of] Jesus Christ the Almighty: remember my father Ignatius." <note>original Greek: Εἴληφε τέλος ἡ βίβλος αὕτη... μέμνησθε πατρός μου τοῦ Ἰγνατίου</note> I have designated it with the letter *E*.

5. Vatican Manuscript 815, made of vellum, from the beginning of the 14th century, consisting of 194 large four-leaf sections; on the first page one reads "Metaphrastes for the month of December," and "Companion index of this book" <note>original Greek: Πίναξ σύνθωκος ταύτης τῆς βίβλου</note>. Among the lives of the Saints, you find the "Martyrdom of Ignatius" on leaves 41–51, by the author Simeon Metaphrastes <note>A famous 10th-century Byzantine author known for rewriting and standardizing the lives of the saints.</note>, written with great care. This manuscript will be *N*.

6. Vatican Manuscript 866, made of vellum, with 395 half-leaves, from the 10th century. From this (leaves 185–188), I extracted the unpublished "Acts of Ignatius the Martyr." Other martyrdoms are included, as well as Letters of the Saints and similar works that are still little known. I have marked it *Vat*.

7. Royal Manuscript 81, made of parchment, with 97 eight-leaf sections, notable for its character and age, as it dates back to the 9th century. It contains (leaves 13–88) the "Old Latin version of the twelve Letters of Ignatius," which are inscribed with red numbers but without the names of the sender or recipient. There follows "Hero’s Praise of Ignatius," the "Old Latin version of Polycarp’s Letter to the Philippians" (leaves 89–95), and the "Life of Polycarp" (leaves 95–97). Once this was finished, the scribe added these verses in red:

> This work of writing finally ends here.
> This book shines with the teaching of Saint Ignatius.

This Codex is to be highly valued, as it provides a Latin version of *The Shepherd* <note>original Greek: "ποιμένος" (Poimenos)</note> that has hitherto not been known anywhere else. Since this version differs considerably in the "Visions" from the one we see published in edited books, it is possible that in the "Mandates" and "Similitudes" it represents a different Greek text than that translation. Due to the translator's anxiety, the author of this version often uses Latin prepositions in the Greek manner; in other respects, he renders the Greek more than is proper—not without damage to the Latinity—even neglecting grammatical gender. Thus, he becomes unfaithful to the sense because of an excessive worry and literal faithfulness in the translation. It confirms many conjectures made by learned men and skillfully illuminates quite a few passages obstructed by difficulties through an elegant arrangement of thoughts. I have added the words enclosed in brackets. 15. **Casanatensis Manuscript G. V. 14**, <note>The Biblioteca Casanatense is a public library in Rome, founded by Cardinal Girolamo Casanate in 1701.</note> written on paper in octavo format <note>original: "foliorum octonariorum," referring to quires of eight leaves</note>. > ->Didymus against the Manichaeans.<-
>
> This Didymus was Alexandrian by birth and is to be distinguished from the other Didymus the Alexandrian, the elder Grammarian; nor should he be confused with Didymus the Egyptian Monk. <note>The author is likely referring to Didymus the Blind (c. 313–398), a famous theologian of Alexandria.</note>

>

> **Saint Dorotheus**, Bishop of Tyre and Martyr: On the names of the Apostles and the place of their preaching, death, and burial.
>
> **Saint Polycarp**, Bishop of Smyrna and Martyr: Letter to the Philippians.”

These works follow one another in the Codex itself in a different order. For following that 'Chain of the Greek Fathers on the Gospel of Luke' are the 'nine (or rather eight) Letters of Ignatius,' written neatly on forty-eight and a half leaves. These are the same letters that Isaac Vossius <note>A 17th-century Dutch scholar who published the first edition of the "shorter recension" of Ignatius’s letters.</note> first published from that precious *Medicean Manuscript 7, Shelf LVII*. Indeed, as I surveyed the Casanatensis book, it long seemed to me that the Medicean was its source and model. I was moved to this opinion by the character of both manuscripts, as well as the external appearance of the final Letter (To those in Tarsus <note>original: "πρὸς τοὺς ἐν Ταρσῷ"</note>) in both places.

The Casanatensis ends in the same way as the Medicean, with this difference: in the former, four and a half blank leaves follow. But this seems to be explained by other factors. For, to omit the titles of all nine (or eight) Letters and many other things of this kind, a more careful comparison between the two manuscripts reveals a notable discrepancy in the readings. It is more credible, however, that both codices originated—though through winding paths—from the same very ancient original source <note>original: "archetypo"</note>. That source undoubtedly contained the Letter to the Tarsians in its entirety. It seems, however, to have happened by some chance that the scribe of the Casanatensis Manuscript was unable to transcribe it from there, even though he had previously observed and measured it; he therefore left a space to describe it in full. For this reason, he only transcribed a fragment from the Medicean. Hence, the Casanatensis and the Medicean, as far as the text of the Letter—

16. **Medicean Manuscript** (Shelf LVII, no. 7), <note>The "Medicean" manuscripts are held in the Laurentian Library in Florence, founded by the Medici family. "Plut." or "Pluteus" refers to the specific reading desk or shelf where the volume was chained.</note> written on vellum <note>original: "membraneus," referring to animal skin parchment</note>, in large quarto format. It was described by Salvini for the use of Aldrich and by Holstenius, and has been collated <note>Collation is the process of comparing different manuscripts of the same text to identify variations.</note> several times since the era of Isaac Voss until Jacobson. Heyse, or P. del Furia on my behalf; indeed, even after the proven care and diligence of others, we have again religiously collated the most important passages. I have designated this as **L**.

17. **Medicean Manuscript** (Shelf VII, no. 21), written on paper, 15th century, in small quarto format. It contains (cf. Bandini in the place cited above, vol. I, p. 269) "eleven interpolated <note>Interpolated letters are those that have had later additions or changes made to the original text.</note> Letters of Saint Ignatius, one by Polycarp, and an oration by Hippolytus on the end of the World, the Antichrist, and the second coming of our Lord Jesus Christ." Joined with the Letter of Polycarp is the "Letter of Barnabas," which escaped Bandini's notice. My friends and I have also inspected this manuscript again and again in all places that seemed of any importance, following in the footsteps of previous scholars. I have designated this as **F**.

The other manuscripts that will be named here and there in the Commentaries have long since been made public knowledge through other editors of the Apostolic Fathers. Therefore, they did not seem to require our own explanation. However, refer to what was said by us above regarding this matter when reviewing the editions of the individual Fathers.

### CODEX SINAITICUS.

## THE EPISTLE OF BARNABAS

### I.

Greetings, sons and daughters, in the name of the Lord who loved us in peace.

Since the ordinances <note>original: "dikaiomata" — refers to the righteous requirements or decrees of God</note> of God toward you are great and rich, I rejoice beyond measure and exceedingly over your blessed and glorious spirits; so innate is the grace of the spiritual gift you have received. For this reason, I also congratulate myself all the more, hoping to be saved, because I truly see that a spirit has been poured out upon you from the riches of the Lord's love. I was so amazed by you when I saw your long-desired faces. I am persuaded of this, and conscious <note>original: "sunidon"; a variant note suggests "sunidos"</note> within myself that, having spoken much among you, I know that the Lord has traveled with me on the way of righteousness. I am altogether compelled to love you more than my own soul, because great faith and love dwell within you in the hope of His life. Therefore, I have considered this: if I take care to share with you some portion of what I have received, it will be a reward for me to have served such spirits. I have made haste to send you a little something from time to time, so that along with your faith, your knowledge <note>term: "gnosis" — a deeper, spiritual understanding often emphasized in early Christian writings</note> may also be complete.

There are, then, three doctrines <note>term: "dogmata" — used here as fundamental principles or decrees</note> of the Lord: life, faith, and hope—which are our beginning <note>A punctuation mark after "beginning" was erased in the original manuscript here and in the following sentence.</note> and end; and righteousness—the beginning <note>Punctuation erased here as well.</note> and end of judgment; and love—joy and the testimony of works of righteousness. For the Master has made known to us through the prophets things past and present, and He has given us the first fruits of the taste of things to come. Seeing these things being carried out one by one as He spoke, we ought to offer a richer and more sublime worship in fear of Him. But I, not as a teacher but as one of you, will show a few things through which you will be gladdened in the present circumstances.

### II.

Since the days are evil and the worker of evil <note>original: "energountos" — likely referring to the adversary or Satan, who is active in the world</note> himself has authority, we ought to take heed to ourselves <note>The manuscript adds "and" (kai) here in a later correction.</note> and seek out the ordinances of the Lord. The helpers of our faith are fear and endurance; and our allies are patience and self-control. While these qualities remain pure in matters relating to the Lord, there rejoice with them wisdom, understanding, science, and knowledge.

# THE EPISTLE OF BARNABAS. II. III.

For he has made it clear to us through all the prophets that he needs neither sacrifices nor burnt offerings nor oblations, saying at one time: "What is the multitude of your sacrifices to me? says the Lord. I am full of burnt offerings, and I do not desire the fat of lambs or the blood of bulls and goats, not even when you come to appear before me. For who has required these things from your hands? Trample my court no more. Even if you bring fine flour, it is vain; incense is an abomination to me. Your new moons and sabbaths I cannot endure." <note>This is a quotation from Isaiah 1:11–13, where the prophet expresses God’s rejection of empty ritualism.</note> These things, therefore, he has abolished so that the <term>new law</term> <note>original: "kainos nomos" — a central concept in this text, suggesting that the teachings of Jesus replaced the old Mosaic regulations</note> of our Lord Jesus Christ, which is without the yoke of necessity, might have an offering that is not man-made.

And again he says to them: "Did I command your fathers when they came out of the land of Egypt to offer me burnt offerings and sacrifices? Rather, I commanded them this: Let none of you treasure up evil against his neighbor in his heart, and do not love a false oath." <note>Citing Jeremiah 7:22–23 and Zechariah 8:17.</note> We ought, therefore, not to be without understanding, but to perceive the intent of the goodness of our Father; for he speaks to us, desiring that we should not wander into error like those people, but should seek how we may approach him. To us, then, he speaks thus: "A sacrifice to God is a broken heart; a heart that glorifies its Maker is a fragrance of sweet odor to the Lord." <note>A variation of Psalm 51:17.</note> We ought, therefore, brothers, to be very careful concerning our salvation, so that the Evil One does not sneak in <note>original: "pareisdusin" — literally to "slip in alongside"</note> among us and, by creating an error, hurl us away from our life.

### III.

He speaks again to them concerning these things: "Why do you fast for me, says the Lord, so that your voice is heard today with a cry? This is not the fast I have chosen, says the Lord, not a man humbling his soul; not even if you bend your neck like a ring <note>original: "krikon" — refers to a circular hook or ring, describing the posture of someone bowed low in performative mourning</note> and spread sackcloth and ashes under you, not even then shall you call it an acceptable fast." <note>Quoting Isaiah 58:4–5.</note> But to us he says: "Behold, this is the fast I have chosen, says the Lord: not a man humbling his soul, but loose every bond of injustice, untie the knots of forced contracts, send the oppressed away in forgiveness, and tear up every unjust agreement. Break your bread for the hungry; and if you see the naked, clothe him. Bring the homeless into your house; and if you see a humble man, you shall not despise him, nor shall you turn away from those of your own household. Then your light shall break forth early, and your healing shall quickly rise; and righteousness shall go before you, and the glory of God shall surround you. Then you shall cry out, and God will hear you; while you are still speaking, he will say, 'Behold, I am here,' if you remove from yourself the bond, and the pointing of the finger, and the word of murmuring, and if you give your bread to the hungry from your soul, and—"

1) and 2) The letters *iota* and *kappa* were deleted by the first hand. — 3) The letter *epsilon* was supplied by the first hand. — 4) The letter *iota* was deleted by the first hand. To the word "having made" [poiesas] a later corrector added "in" [en]. — 5) A later corrector added "but" [de]. — 6) The letter *alpha* written above the line is more elegant than what usually belongs to the later corrector, yet it is not clearly from the first hand either. Nevertheless, it is likely that the scribe himself, before finishing "garments" [imatia], which he clearly intended to write, replaced it with "healings" [iamata], and later the *alpha* was restored with dots above the *iota*. — 7) The letters *kappa-alpha* [and] were noted by the first hand.

<summary>This page contains a polemic against Jewish ritual sacrifices and fasting, using Old Testament prophets to argue that God desires ethical behavior and a "broken heart" over external ceremonies. It emphasizes a "New Law" of Christ that prioritizes social justice and sincere devotion.</summary>
<keywords>New Law, sacrifice, fasting, Isaiah, social justice, manuscript corrections, ritualism vs spirituality, early Christian polemic</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the Epistle of Barnabas, concluding the discussion on spiritual fasting and transitioning into a stern warning about the "final stumbling block" or the end times. The author argues that the Jewish people lost their covenant at Mount Sinai due to idolatry, and that this covenant now belongs exclusively to followers of Jesus.</meta>

-># THE EPISTLE OF BARNABAS. III. IV.<-

...and you will show mercy to a humbled soul. <note>original: "psychēn tetapinōmenēn" — This concludes a section where the author quotes a version of Isaiah 58, arguing that God desires a humble spirit rather than physical fasting.</note> Concerning this, then, brothers, the Patient One <note>A title for God, emphasizing His long-suffering nature.</note> foresaw how the people whom he prepared in his **Beloved** <note>A common early Christian title for Jesus.</note> would believe in innocence, and he revealed these things to us beforehand so that we might not be shattered <note>original: "prosrēssōmetha" — literally "dashed against," like a ship on rocks.</note> as if we were converts <note>original: "epilytoi" — This is a difficult term; it likely refers to "proselytes" or those following the Jewish law. The scribe indicates this word was not corrected in the manuscript.</note> to their laws.

## IV.

It is necessary, therefore, for us to search deeply into current events and seek out the things that have the power <note>The scribe corrected the Greek text here from "things that happened" to "things that have power."</note> to save us. Let us flee completely from all the works of lawlessness, lest the works of lawlessness take hold of us; and let us hate the error of the present time, so that we may be loved in the future. Let us not give our soul relaxation, so that it has the liberty to run with sinners and the wicked, lest we become like them. The final **stumbling block** <note>original: "skandalon" — a trap or something that causes one to fall from faith.</note> has approached, concerning which it is written, as **Enoch** says: "For to this end the Master has shortened the times and the days, so that his Beloved might hurry and come into his inheritance." <note>This quote is not found in the surviving books of Enoch, suggesting the author had access to lost apocryphal traditions.</note>

And the prophet also says this: "Ten kingdoms shall reign upon the earth, and after them shall rise a little king, who shall humble three of the kings under one." <note>A reference to the prophecy of the "Little Horn" in the Book of Daniel.</note> Similarly, concerning the same thing, **Daniel** says: "And I saw the fourth beast, wicked and strong and more dangerous than all the beasts of the earth, and how ten horns sprang from it, and from them a little horn as an offshoot, and how it humbled three of the large horns under one." You ought, therefore, to understand.

Moreover, I ask this of you, as one of your own—loving you all specifically more than my own soul—to take heed now to yourselves and not be like certain people who heap up your sins, saying that "our covenant" <note>Referring to the biblical agreement between God and humanity.</note> remains ours. But they <note>The author refers here to the Jewish community.</note> lost it forever at the very end, even as **Moses** was receiving it. For the Scripture says: "And Moses was on the mountain fasting forty days and forty nights, and he received the covenant from the Lord, stone tablets written by the finger of the hand of the Lord." But when they turned toward idols, they lost it. For the Lord says: "Moses, Moses, go down quickly, for your people whom you brought out of the land of Egypt have acted lawlessly." And Moses understood and threw the two tablets from his hands, and their covenant was broken, so that the covenant of the **Beloved Jesus** might be sealed into our hearts in the hope of his faith.

Though I wish to write many things—not as a teacher, but as becomes one who loves—I have hastened not to leave out anything of what we have. Therefore, I am your **offscouring** <note>original: "peripsēma" — a term of extreme humility, meaning "scrapings" or "refuse," used by early Christians to show they were the servants of all.</note>. We take heed in the last days; for the whole time of your faith will profit you nothing unless now, in this lawless time and among the coming stumbling blocks, we resist as becomes sons of God. Thus, the **Black One** <note>A name for the Devil or Antichrist.</note> will have no secret entrance. Let us flee from all vanity, let us hate...

2. Not corrected.
3. The letters "dy" [δυσ] appear to have been corrected from "ge" [γε] by the first hand. The letter "a" [α] was written above by the same hand. Therefore, the scribe himself replaced "things that happened" with "things that have power."
4. Variant reading: "that we may be loved."
5. Noted by the first hand.
6. The letter "l" [λ] noted by the first hand.
7. The first "s" [σ] was lightly erased and marked with signs.
8. and 9. "-tes" and "-tas" endings: nothing was changed.
9. 10. Variant reading: "his" instead of "their."
10. 11. Variant reading: "to write."
11. 12. Nothing was corrected in these words.

<meta>This page continues the Epistle of Barnabas, following the warning about the 'final stumbling block.' The author is currently urging the community to remain vigilant and communal rather than isolating themselves, leading into an explanation of why Christ had to suffer.</meta>

->## THE EPISTLE OF BARNABAS. IV. V.<-

...completely the works of lawlessness. Do not withdraw into yourselves and live like hermits <note>original: "monazetai" — referring to those who isolate themselves from the community.</note> as if you were already justified. Instead, come together in the same place and seek out what is for the common good. For the Scripture says: *Woe to those who are wise in their own eyes and clever in their own sight.* <note>A reference to Isaiah 5:21.</note> Let us become spiritual; let us become a perfect temple for God. As much as it is in us, let us practice the fear of God and strive to keep <gloss>1</gloss> his commandments, so that we may rejoice in his <gloss>2</gloss> ordinances. The Lord will judge the world without partiality. Each person will receive according to what they have done: if they are good, their righteousness will go before them; if they are wicked, the reward of wickedness is before them. Let us never rest as if we were merely "called" and fall asleep in our sins, lest the Evil Ruler <note>original: "ponēros archōn" — a common early Christian term for the Devil or Antichrist.</note> gain authority over us and thrust us out from the Kingdom of the Lord. And furthermore, my brothers, consider this: when you see <gloss>3</gloss> that after such great signs and wonders <gloss>4</gloss> were performed in Israel, they were still forsaken, let us take heed lest we be found as it is written: *Many are called, but few are chosen.*

# V.

For this reason, the Lord endured giving up his flesh to corruption, so that we might be purified by the forgiveness of sins, which is through the blood of his sprinkling. <note>A reference to the ritual sprinkling of blood in the Old Testament, now applied to Jesus' death.</note> For it is written concerning him, partly with reference to Israel and partly to us. It speaks thus: *He was wounded for our transgressions and bruised for our sins; by his stripes we are healed. He was led as a sheep to the slaughter, and as a lamb is silent before its shearer.* <note>Quoting Isaiah 53:5-7, the "Suffering Servant" passage.</note> Therefore, we ought to be exceedingly thankful to the Lord, because he has made known to us the things of the past, he has given us wisdom in the things of the present, and concerning the things of the future, we are not without understanding.

Now the Scripture says: *Not unjustly are nets spread for the birds.* <note>Proverbs 1:17.</note> This means that a person deserves to perish if, while having knowledge of the way of righteousness, they pin themselves into the way of darkness. Furthermore, my brothers: if the Lord endured suffering for our souls—even though he is the Lord of the whole world, to whom God said at the foundation of the world, *Let us make man according to our image and likeness* <note>Genesis 1:26. Barnabas argues that Jesus was present and active at Creation.</note>—how then did he endure suffering at the hand of men? Learn! The prophets, receiving grace from him, prophesied concerning him. But he himself endured so that he might destroy death and show forth the resurrection from the dead, because it was necessary for him to be manifested in the flesh. He suffered so that he might fulfill the promise made to the fathers and, while preparing <gloss>5</gloss> the new people for himself, he might demonstrate while on <gloss>6</gloss> earth that he himself will judge after bringing about the resurrection.

# THE EPISTLE OF BARNABAS THE APOSTLE.

I. After the salutation, the writer announces that he will share something with the brothers from what he himself has received.

Greetings,<sup>2</sup> sons<sup>3</sup> and daughters, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, who loved us, in peace. Knowing that an abundance of the great and honorable righteous ordinances<sup>4</sup> of God exists within you, I rejoice beyond measure<sup>5</sup> in your blessed and illustrious spirits, because you have thus received a natural<sup>6</sup> grace. Because of this, I congratulate myself greatly, hoping<sup>7</sup> to be set free, because I truly see in you the spirit poured out from the honorable<sup>8</sup> fountain of God, since<sup>9</sup> I am persuaded of this, and

1) That Greek inscription <note>original: "Ἡ ΦΕΡΟΜΕΝΗ ΤΟΥ ΑΓΙΟΥ ΒΑΡΝΑΒΑ ΑΠΟΣΤΟΛΟΥ ΕΠΙΣΤΟΛΗ ΚΑΘΟΛΙΚΗ"</note> "The General Epistle of the Holy Apostle Barnabas as it is handed down," which appeared in the first edition by Hugo Menard, has been varied by those who published the work of Barnabas after him. In Eusebius (Church History III, 25), it is "the epistle attributed to Barnabas." Origen indeed left it as: "It is written in the general epistle of Barnabas" (Against Celsus I, 63). Even if someone wished only to briefly "read the character" <note>original: "φυσιογνωμεῖν" - to judge by outward appearance</note> of the traits and genius of this Epistle, he will easily persuade himself that it was given to a specific and defined group of readers, and not to a universal one. Nevertheless, no one will surely deny that it can be called "general" <term>catholic</term> <note>In this context, "catholic" refers to a "general" or "universal" letter intended for the whole church rather than a specific city.</note> according to Origen's understanding, by the same right as the writing of any other Alexandrian author. The manuscripts of the Barberini, Vacanate, Florentine, Ottobonian, and Vatican libraries, which I have compared, do not recognize that epithet in the signature. We have expressed the title following the lead of the Vatican Manuscript. See below, chapter 21, note 12.
</margin>

2) An ancient Latin translation of the Epistle, though indeed full of errors and incomplete, exists in the Corbie Manuscript, which is said to have been written before the 9th century. From there we have borrowed the first four chapters and half of the fifth, since they are missing in the Greek. The chapter headings, however, are our own.
</margin>

To the ancient translator of this Epistle, the Greek word <note>original: "δικαίωμα"</note> means a right action or rectitude, but also a statute or a precept of justice. The former meaning applies here; the latter is found in the following chapters. Compare below chapters 10, 16, 21; Romans 5:18 and Luke 1:6; Romans 1:32, 2:36.

In the same sense, in the opening of the Epistle of Ignatius to the Ephesians: "Having welcomed in God your much-loved name, which you have acquired by a righteous nature."

II. The new law of Christ is without the yoke of necessity; therefore the sacrifices of the Jews have now been rendered void.

Since, therefore, the days are most evil,¹ and the adversary <note>original: "contrarius" - referring to Satan</note> holds the power of this world, we ought to be attentive and seek out the righteous ordinances of the Lord.

The helpers of our faith <note>original Greek: Τῆς μὲν οὖν πίστεως ἡμῶν; Latin: Fidei ergo nostrae</note> are fear and endurance; those things which fight on our side are patience and self-control. When these remain pure before the Lord, wisdom, understanding, science, and knowledge rejoice along with them.

For He has revealed to us through all the Prophets that He does not make use of our sacrifices, nor victims, nor offerings, saying these things: "To what purpose⁴ is the multitude of your sacrifices to me? says the Lord. I am full of the burnt offerings of rams and the fat of lambs; and the blood of goats and bulls I do not desire; not even if you come to appear⁵ before me. For who has required these things from your hands? You shall no longer trample my court. If you bring me fine flour, it is in vain; your incense is an abomination to me. Your New Moons⁶ and great day I cannot bear; your fasting and holidays and feast days my soul hates."⁷ These things, therefore, He has made void, so that the new law of our Lord Jesus Christ, which is without the yoke⁷ of necessity, might have a human⁸ offering. The Lord says again to them: "Did⁹ I command your fathers when they came out of the land of Egypt to offer me sacrifices and victims? # THE EPISTLE OF BARNABAS. III. IV.

...and if you give bread to the hungry from your soul.⁵ In this matter, therefore, brothers, God is farsighted and merciful, because the people whom he prepared for his Beloved were destined to believe in simplicity; and he showed this to all of us beforehand, so that we should not run, like <term>proselytes</term> <note>converts to Judaism</note>, toward their law.

## IV. The error of the present time must be avoided, and those already called must take care lest, by contempt for the law, they grow proud as if they were already justified.

It is necessary, therefore, regarding imminent matters,¹ to write much while searching out the things that can heal us.² Let us flee from every work of iniquity, and let us hold in hatred the error³ of this present time, so that we may be loved in the future.⁴ Let us not give our soul⁵ any room to have the power of running about with the wicked and sinners, lest we ever become like them. For the final temptation,⁶ as it is written [and] as Daniel⁷ says, has drawn near. For this reason, the Lord cuts short⁸ the times and the days, so that his Beloved may hasten to his inheritance. The prophet says thus: "Ten kingdoms⁹ shall reign upon the earth; and there shall rise up after them a little one,¹⁰ who shall lay low three [kings] into one." Likewise concerning the kingdoms.¹¹ Concerning this very thing,¹² Daniel says again: "And¹³ I saw the fourth beast, wicked and strong, and more savage than the other beasts of the sea, and ten horns appeared on it; and another short horn ascended in the midst of them, and it cast down three of the larger horns." We ought, therefore, to understand.¹⁴ Furthermore,¹⁵ I ask you as one of your own, loving you all...
