# THE EPISTLE OF BARNABAS. IV. V.

...perfect to God. Insofar as it is in us, let us meditate <note>original: "meditemur"; see Isaiah 33:18</note> on the fear of God, and let us strive to keep His commandments (so that we may rejoice in His righteous ordinances).

The Lord <note>See 1 Peter 1:17 and Galatians 2:6</note> judges the world without partiality; each person will receive according to what they have done. If one is good, their goodness goes before them; if one is wicked, the penalty of wickedness follows them. <note>See Isaiah 58:8</note> Take heed, lest at any time, resting <note>See Matthew 25:5</note> as those already called, we should fall asleep in our sins, and the wicked one, gaining power over us, <margin>over us</margin> should be stirred up and exclude us from the kingdom of the Lord. Understand this as well: when you have seen <note>The city of Jerusalem was already destroyed by this time; therefore "seen" refers to a completed past event rather than the future.</note> such great signs and wonders among the people of the Jews, and yet the Lord has thus abandoned them. Let us therefore take care lest we be found as it is written: *Many are called, but few are chosen.* <note>Matthew 20:16; 22:14</note>

### V. We are saved by the death of Christ; the Jews are judged.

For this reason, the Lord endured the surrender of His body to destruction, so that we might be sanctified through the forgiveness of sins, which is by the sprinkling of His blood. <note>1 Peter 1:2</note> For it is written concerning Him, partly for the people of the Jews and partly for us. He speaks <note>Specifically to us; see Isaiah 53:5, 7</note> thus: "He was wounded for our transgressions, and bruised for our sins; by His stripes we are healed. He was led as a sheep to the slaughter; and as a lamb before its shearer is silent, so He opened not His mouth." We ought therefore to be exceedingly grateful to the Lord, because He has both shown us the past and made us wise, and regarding the future we are not without understanding. <note>The sense is: We are not ignorant of the things that are to come.</note> But He says: "Not unjustly are nets spread for birds." <note>Proverbs 1:17. The sense: Although we are made wise by the Lord's mercy, we must beware lest we fall into nets like birds, perishing in the way of darkness.</note> This He says because a man deserves to perish <note>The translator notes that "periit" (perished) is a common later Latin form for "periet" (will perish).</note> who, having the way of righteousness and knowledge, does not restrain himself from the dark path. And furthermore, <margin>And besides, the Lord endured suffering.</margin> the Lord endured suffering for our souls, though He is the Lord of the whole world, to whom God said <note>Referring to the Father</note> on the day before the foundation of the world: "Let us make man according to our image and likeness." <note>Genesis 1:26</note> Learn, then, how He endured it when He suffered this at the hands of men. The prophets, having received the gift from Him, prophesied concerning Him; but He, in order that He might abolish death and show the resurrection from the dead...

# THE EPISTLE OF BARNABAS. V. VI.

...to your [fathers] he might show the resurrection, because it was necessary for him to appear in the flesh, he endured it, so that he might deliver the promise to the fathers, and he himself <note>original Latin: "ipse sibi"</note> preparing the new people <note>original Greek: "τὸν λαὸν τὸν καινὸν"</note> for himself, he showed while being upon the earth that, having himself brought about the resurrection, he will judge. Finally, while teaching Israel and performing such great wonders and signs, he preached to them and loved them exceedingly. But when he chose his own Apostles, who were about to preach his gospel—men who were lawless beyond all sin—in order to show that "he came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance" <note>A reference to Matthew 9:13</note>—then he revealed himself to be the Son of God. For if he had not come in the flesh, how could men have been saved by beholding him? For when they look upon the sun, which is the work of his hands and is destined to cease to be, they are not able to gaze directly against its rays. Therefore the Son of God came in the flesh for this purpose, that he might bring to a head the total sum of sins for those who persecuted his prophets unto death. Therefore he endured for this purpose. For God says of the wound of his flesh, that it is from them: [and another prophesies], "When I shall smite the shepherd, then the sheep of the flock shall be scattered." <note>A reference to Zechariah 13:7</note> He himself willed to suffer thus; for it was necessary that he should suffer upon the wood <note>The "wood" refers to the Cross</note>. For the one prophesying of him says: "Spare my soul from the sword," and "Pierce my flesh with nails, for the assemblies of evildoers have risen up against me." <note>References to Psalm 22:20 and 119:120</note> And again he says: "Behold, I have given my back to scourges, and my cheeks to blows; and I have set my face as a solid rock." <note>A reference to Isaiah 50:6-7</note>

# EPISTLE OF BARNABAS. VI.

...but that he has created us anew. For the Scripture says concerning us, as he says to the Son: *Let us make man according to our image and according to our likeness, and let them rule over the beasts of the earth, and the birds of heaven, and the fish of the sea.* <note>original: Gen. 1:26</note> And the Lord said, seeing the beauty of the human creature: *Increase, and multiply, and fill the earth.* <note>original: Gen. 1:28</note> These things were spoken to the Son. Again, I will show you how he made a second creation for us in the last times. The Lord says: *Behold, I will make the last things as the first.* <note>original: "ἰδοὺ ποιήσω τὰ ἔσχατα ὡς τὰ πρῶτα" - a reference to the new creation in Christ.</note> To this end, therefore, the prophet proclaimed: *Enter into a land flowing with milk and honey, and rule over it.* <note>original: Exod. 33:3</note> Behold, therefore, we have been created anew, just as he says again in another prophet: *Behold, says the Lord, I will take away from them*—that is, from those whom the Spirit of the Lord foresaw—*their hearts of stone, and I will put hearts of flesh in them;* <note>original: Ezek. 11:19</note> because he himself was about to be manifested in the flesh and to dwell in us. For, my brothers, the dwelling-place of our heart is a holy temple to the Lord. For the Lord says again: *And in what shall I appear before the Lord my God, and be glorified?* He says: *I will confess to you in the assembly in the midst of my brothers, and I will sing to you in the midst of the assembly of the saints.* <note>original: Ps. 22:23</note> Therefore, we are the ones whom he brought into the good land. What then is the "milk and honey"? It is because a child is first nourished with honey, and then with milk; so also we, being nourished by faith in the promise and by the Word, shall live and rule over the earth. But he said above: *Let them increase and rule over the fish.* Who then is able now to rule over beasts, or fish, or birds of heaven? For we ought to perceive that to rule implies authority, so that one may give commands and exercise lordship. If, therefore, this does not happen now, he has told us when it will: when we ourselves are perfected so as to become heirs of the Lord’s covenant.

# VII. Fasting as a type, and the scapegoat as a figure of the suffering Jesus.

Understand then, children of gladness, that the good Lord has manifested all things to us beforehand, so that we might know whom we ought to thank for all things...

...we have been created anew. For the Scripture says concerning us, where the Father speaks to the Son: "Let us make man according to our image and our likeness; and let them rule over the beasts of the earth, and the birds of the sky, and the fish of the sea." <note>Genesis 1:26</note> Then the Lord, seeing man, his beautiful handiwork, said: "Increase and multiply, and fill the earth." These things were addressed to the Son. But again, I will show you how, in these last times, He has performed a second creation for us. For the Lord says: "Behold, I make the last things as the first." <note>A reference to the "new creation" in Christ, often linked by early Christians to Isaiah 43:18-19</note> Looking toward this, the prophet proclaimed: "Enter into a land flowing with milk and honey, and rule over it." Behold, therefore, we have been formed anew; just as He says again in another prophet: "Behold," says the Lord, "I will take away from them"—that is, from those whom the Spirit of the Lord foresaw—"their hearts of stone, and I will bestow upon them hearts of flesh;" <note>Ezekiel 11:19</note> because He willed to appear in the flesh and to dwell in us. For the habitation of our heart, my brothers, is a holy temple to the Lord. For again the Lord says: "Wherewith shall I appear before the Lord my God, and be glorified?" He says: "I will confess to You in the assembly, in the midst of my brothers, and I will sing to You in the midst of the assembly of the saints." <note>Psalm 22:22</note> Therefore, it is we whom He has brought into the good land. But why milk and honey? Because an infant is kept alive first with honey, then with milk; so also we, being nourished by faith in the promises of God and by the word of preaching, shall live possessing the earth. But He said above: "Let them increase and rule over the fish." Who is able now to rule over beasts, or fish, or the birds of the sky? For we ought to understand that "to rule" signifies power, so that one may give orders and dominate. Even if this does not happen now, He has certainly promised it to us. When will it happen? When we ourselves have become so perfect that we are made heirs of the Lord’s covenant.

# THE EPISTLE OF BARNABAS. VII.

...we ought to praise. If, therefore, the Son of God, being Lord and being destined to judge the living and the dead, suffered, 2 so that his wound might bring us life, let us believe that 3 the Son of God could not have suffered except for 4 our sake. But even when he was crucified, he was given vinegar and gall to drink. 5 Hear how 6 the priests of the people have revealed concerning this. 7 Since there was a written commandment that whoever 8 does not keep the fast shall be utterly destroyed by death, the Lord commanded this because he himself was destined to offer 9 the vessel of the spirit <note>original: "τὸ σκεῦος τοῦ πνεύματος" — referring to his physical body</note> as a sacrifice for our sins; so that the type <note>A "type" is a person or event in the Old Testament seen as a symbolic foreshadowing of Christ.</note> that occurred in Isaac, who was offered upon the altar, might be fulfilled. 10 What, then, does he say in the prophet? "And let them eat 11 from the goat that is offered during the fast for all sins." Pay close attention: "and let 12 all the priests alone eat the entrails unwashed with vinegar." Why? Because, he said, 13 since you are going to give me 14 gall with vinegar to drink when I am about to offer my flesh for the new people, you alone must eat, while the people fast and mourn in sackcloth 15 and ashes. 16 This was to show that he must suffer for them. How then did he command? Pay attention. "Take 17 two goats, fine and similar, 18 and offer them; and let the priest take 19 one as a burnt offering for sins." But what shall they do with the other one? "The one," 20 he says, "is accursed." Pay attention to how the type of Jesus is revealed. "And 21 you shall all spit 22 upon it, and pierce it, and put 23 the scarlet wool around its head; and so let it be cast into the desert." And when this is done, the one who carries the goat leads it into the 24 desert, and removes the wool, and places it upon a bramble bush called 25 *rache* <note>original: "ῥαχήν" — likely a species of blackberry or briar</note>, the shoots of which we are accustomed to eat in the countryside...

<column-break/>

<margin>2) The Son of God suffered. <note>original Latin: "haec per (τὸ σκεῦος) passum esse docuerit"</note> Although these things are spoken through the "communication of properties" <term>communication of properties: a theological term (communicatio idiomatum) expressing that the attributes of both Christ's divine and human natures can be attributed to his single person</term>, and Barnabas said above in this very chapter that the Son of God suffered, it clearly appears that his doctrine agrees with the orthodox faith. For the human nature of Christ suffered on the cross while being most closely, but without confusion, joined with the divine; thus it happens that through the communication of properties both can be said: a) the Son of God suffered, and b) Christ offered his body as a sacrifice.</margin>

...and we ought to offer praises. If, therefore, the Son of God, who is Lord and is to be the judge of the living and the dead, suffered so that his wound might make us alive, let us believe that the Son of God could not have suffered except for our sake. But when he was fixed to the cross, he was given vinegar and gall to drink. Hear how the priests of the Jewish people gave signs concerning this matter. When the commandment was written that whoever did not keep the fast should be destroyed by death, the Lord commanded it because he himself was going to offer the vessel of the spirit as a sacrifice for our sins; so that the type <note>original: "figura" — a prophetic symbol or foreshadowing</note> made in Isaac, who was offered upon the altar, might be fulfilled. What, therefore, does he say through the prophet? "And let them eat of the goat which is offered during the fast for all sins." Attend diligently: "and let all the priests alone eat the unwashed entrails with vinegar." For what purpose? "Because," he says, "you are going to give me gall with vinegar to drink when I am about to offer my flesh for the sins of the new people; therefore you alone shall eat, while the people fast and mourn in sackcloth and ashes." This was to show that it was necessary for him to suffer for them. How then did he command? Attend. "Take," he says, "two goats, good and similar, and offer them; and let the priest take one as a whole burnt offering <term>holocaustum: a sacrifice consumed entirely by fire</term> for sins." But what shall they do with the other? "Accursed," he says, "is the one." Attend to how the type of Jesus is revealed. "And spit upon it, all of you, and pierce it; and place scarlet wool around its head; and so let it be cast out into the desert." And when it has been done in this way, he who carries the goat leads it into the wilderness, and takes the wool from it, and places it upon a bush which is called the bramble, the shoots of which we are accustomed to eat when found in the fields; and the fruit of this thorn-bush alone is sweet.

"So," he says, "those who wish to see me and to lay hold of my kingdom must receive me through affliction and suffering."

<header>VIII. The sacrifice of the red heifer as a type of Christ and of his kingdom.</header>

Then they are no longer men [sinners], no longer is there the glory of sinners. But the children who sprinkle are those who preach to us the forgiveness

# THE EPISTLE OF BARNABAS. VII. VIII.
->17<-

But why is this done? Pay attention: one [goat] is placed upon the altar, but the other is cursed. And why is the one who is cursed crowned? Because they will see him on that day wearing the scarlet robe reaching to the feet <note>original: "talarem coccineam"</note> about his body, and they will say: is this not he, whom we once despised, pierced, and mocked, and then crucified? Truly it is he, who then said he was the Son of God. Why is it likewise, and why are these goats similar, beautiful, and equal? So that, when they see him coming then, they may be struck with awe at the similarity to the goat. See therefore the figure of Jesus who was to suffer. But why do they place the wool in the midst of thorns? That is a figure of Jesus, set before the church. For they place the wool among the thorns so that whoever wishes to take away the scarlet wool—because the thorn is formidable—must suffer many things, and having been afflicted, gain possession of it. So, he says, those who wish to see me and reach my kingdom must possess me through afflictions and torments.

## VIII. The sacrifice of the red heifer as a type of Christ and his kingdom.

What figure do you think it is, that it is commanded to Israel that men of perfected wickedness should bring a heifer, and burn it after it has been slaughtered; and that then boys should take the ash and put it into vessels; and afterwards they should bind scarlet wool with hyssop to a stick; and thus the boys should sprinkle the people one by one, so that they may be cleansed from their sins? Behold, how the Lord speaks to us in simplicity. That calf is Jesus; the wicked men who bring it are those who offered the Lord to be put to death. But now they are no longer wicked men, nor are they any longer held to be for sinners. The boys who sprinkle are those who announced to us the remission of sins,

Why is the wool <note>original: τὸ ξύλον, literally "the wood," but here referring to the wool on the wood/stick used for sprinkling</note> put upon the wood? # IX. The circumcision of the Old Testament is to be understood spiritually.

For He speaks again concerning the ears, how He circumcised our heart as well. The Lord says in the prophet: "At the hearing of the ear they obeyed me." And again He says: "By hearing they shall hear, those who are far off; what I have done they shall know." And "Be circumcised," says the Lord, "in your hearts." And again He says: "Hear, O Israel, for thus says the Lord your God." And again the Spirit of the Lord prophesies: "Who is he that wishes to live forever? Let him hear the voice of my servant." And again He says: "Hear, O heaven, and give ear, O earth, for the Lord has spoken." These things are for a testimony. And again He says: "Hear the word of the Lord, you rulers of this people." And again He says: "Hear, children, the voice of one crying in the wilderness." Therefore, He circumcised our hearing, so that by hearing the word we might believe; for the circumcision in which they trusted has been abolished. For He spoke of a circumcision not of the flesh—

No one has learned a more reliable word from me, but I know that you are worthy.

Learn therefore, children, abundantly concerning all things, that Abraham, who first instituted circumcision, circumcised while looking forward in spirit toward Jesus, <term>employing a doctrine</term> <note>original: "doctrinam adhibens"</note> of three secret letters. For the scripture says: "And Abraham circumcised 318 men of his household." What knowledge was then given to him in this? Learn first the eighteen, then the three hundred. Now, eighteen is expressed by I (ten) and H (eight). <note>In Greek numerals, Iota (I) = 10 and Eta (H) = 8</note> You have the beginning of the name of Jesus. Furthermore, the cross in the shape of the letter T was to be the sign of the <term>grace of our redemption</term> <note>original: "redemptionis nostrae"</note>; wherefore he says "three hundred." <note>In Greek numerals, Tau (T) = 300</note> Thus he shows Jesus in two letters, and the cross in the third. He knows this, who has placed the deeper gift of his doctrine within us. No one has received a more authentic word from me; but I know that you are worthy.

# THE EPISTLE OF BARNABAS. X.

He comprehends three doctrines in his understanding. Furthermore, the Lord says to them in Deuteronomy: "And I will ordain my precepts for this people." <note>original: "et disponam ad populum hunc praecepta mea." Referring to Deuteronomy 4:1 or similar passages regarding the Law.</note> Is it not therefore a command of God that they should not eat? It is; but Moses spoke in the spirit. For this reason, he spoke of the "swine" as if to say: you shall not associate with such men who are like pigs. For when they live in luxury, they forget their Lord; but when they are deprived of necessities, they acknowledge the Lord. Indeed, the pig does not know its master when it eats; but when it is hungry, it cries out; and having received food again, it is silent. "Nor shall you eat," he says, "the eagle, nor the hawk, nor the kite, nor the raven." You shall not associate, he says, with those men who do not know how to provide food for themselves by labor and sweat, but wickedly seize the property of others; and though they seem to walk in simplicity, they nevertheless lie in wait for others. And these birds, while they sit idle, seek how they may devour the flesh of others, and are pestilential in their malice. "Nor shall you eat," he says, "the lamprey, nor the polyp <note>an octopus or similar cephalopod</note>, nor the cuttlefish." You shall not, he says, associate with, nor be like such men, who are impious forever and are already condemned to death; just as these little fish, alone cursed, wallow in the deep, and do not emerge like other fish, but dwell in the earth which is at the bottom of the sea. But also "the hare," he says, "you shall not eat." By which he means, you shall not be a corrupter of youth, nor shall you make yourself like such people; because the hare multiplies its filthy lair every year. For as many years as it lives, so many holes it has. <note>A medieval folk belief regarding the hare's anatomy and habits.</note> "But neither shall you eat the hyena." You shall certainly not be, he says, an adulterer, nor a corrupter of youth, nor shall you be likened to such. Why? Because that animal changes its sex annually, and becomes now male, now female. But he also pursued the weasel with a just hatred. You shall show yourself, he says, unlike those men whom we hear commit wickedness with an impure mouth; nor—

# XI. Baptism and the cross prefigured in the Old Testament.

Let us inquire, then, whether the Lord took care to forewarn about the water and the cross. And indeed, concerning the water, it is written regarding the Israelites how they would not receive the baptism which brings the remission of sins, but would prepare another for themselves. Thus says the prophet: "Be astonished, O heaven, and let the earth shudder at this, because this people has done two great and evil things: they have forsaken me, the living fountain, and have dug for themselves broken cisterns. <header>XII. Elsewhere also in the Old Testament there is typical mention of the cross and of Christ.</header>

Likewise, he signifies the cross in another prophet who says: "And when shall these things be accomplished? The Lord says: when a tree is bent [cut down] and stands erect again, and when blood shall flow from the tree." <note>original: "cum lignum inclinatum [succisum] denuo erectum constiterit, et cum de ligno sanguis stillaverit." This apocryphal quotation is not found in the canonical Bible but was common in early Christian literature.</note> You have here again a prophecy concerning the cross, and of him who was to be fastened to the cross. Furthermore, he speaks of this matter in Moses, when Israel was being attacked by foreigners. And so that he might remind them that they were being delivered unto death because of their sins, the Spirit says to the heart of Moses that he should make a figure of the cross and of him who was to suffer; because, if they do not hope in him, they shall be defeated forever. Moses therefore placed armor upon armor in the midst of the mound, and standing above them all, he stretched out his hands, and thus the Israelites were victorious again. But whenever he let down his hands, they were again being killed. Why this? So that they might know that they could not be saved unless they placed their hope in him. And in another prophet he says: "All day long I have stretched out my hands to an unbelieving people who contradict my righteous way." <note>Isaiah 65:2</note> And again, Moses makes a figure of Jesus (showing that he was to suffer, and that he himself, whom they thought they had destroyed by the sign of the cross, would provide life) while Israel was falling. For since sin occurred through the serpent in Eve, God brought it about that all sorts of serpents bit them; and they died, so that he might prove to them that they were to be delivered into the straits of death because of their sins. Finally, Moses, who had commanded: "You shall have neither a carved nor a molten image for your God," <note>Deuteronomy 27:15</note> himself does this very thing to show a figure of Jesus. Moses therefore makes a bronze serpent, and places it on a beam, and through a herald calls the people together. When they were gathered, they prayed to Moses that he might offer a sacrifice for them, entreating for their healing. But Moses said to them: "Whenever," he said, "someone of—

# THE EPISTLE OF BARNABAS. XII. XIII.
<page-num>31</page-num>

...if any of you should be bitten, let him come to the serpent placed upon the wood <note>original: "ligno"; referring to the cross</note>, and let him believe and hope that, although it is dead, it is able to provide life; and immediately he shall be saved. And so they did. In this you also have the glory of Jesus: that all things are in him and for him. What does Moses say again to Joshua, the son of Nun <note>original: "Navae"</note>, when he, as a prophet, gave him that name [Joshua=Jesus]? Therefore, having given him that name when he sent him as a scout into the land [of Canaan], he said: "Take a book into your hands, and write what the Lord says: that the Son of God will, in the last days, cut off the entire house of Amalek by the roots." Behold again: he is not the son of man, but the Son of God, Jesus, who appeared in figure and in the flesh. Behold how David calls him Lord and the Son of God.

# XIII. Concerning the people who are the heirs.

But let us see whether this people <note>the Christians</note> is the heir, or the former people <note>the Jews</note>; and whether the covenant belongs to us or to them. Hear now what the scripture says concerning the people. Isaac prayed for the sake of his wife Rebecca, because she was barren; and after this she conceived. But Rebecca went out to inquire of the Lord, and the Lord said to her: "Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples in your belly, and one people shall overcome the other, and the elder" [by birth] "shall serve the younger." You ought to understand who Isaac is, who Rebecca is, and concerning whom he declared that this people is greater than that one. And in another prophecy, Jacob speaks more clearly to his son Joseph, saying: "Behold, the Lord has not deprived me of your face; bring your sons to me, so that I may bless them." And he brought Ephraim and Manasseh, desiring that [Manasseh] be blessed, because he was the elder. And so—

XIV. The Testament <note>original: "Testamentum" - the Covenant</note>, which Moses received and afterwards broke, the Lord has now renewed through Jesus Christ.

Yes. But we must seek to know if He has actually given the covenant which He swore to the fathers to give to the people. He did give it; but they were not worthy to receive it because of their sins. For the prophet says: "And Moses was fasting on Mount Sinai for forty days and forty nights, to receive the covenant of the Lord for the people." And he received from the Lord the two tablets written by the finger of the hand of the Lord in the spirit; and having received them, Moses brought them down to give to the people. And the Lord said to Moses: "Moses, Moses, go down quickly, for your people, whom you brought out of the land of Egypt, have committed lawlessness." And Moses understood that they had again made molten images <note>original: "χωνεύματα" - specifically the Golden Calf</note>, and he flung the tablets from his hands, and the tablets of the covenant of the Lord were shattered. Moses indeed received it, but they were not worthy. But learn how *we* received it. Moses received it as a servant, but the Lord Himself gave it to us to be a people of inheritance, having endured suffering for our sakes. He was made manifest so that they might fill up the measure of their sins, and that we, through Him who inherited it, might receive the covenant of the Lord Jesus; He was prepared for this purpose, so that by appearing, He might redeem from darkness our hearts, which were already consumed by death and delivered over to the lawlessness of error...

# XV. Concerning the false and the true Sabbath.

Furthermore, it is also written concerning the Sabbath in the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments</note> or the "ten words," which the Lord spoke to Moses on Mount Sinai, face to face: "And sanctify the Sabbath of the Lord with clean hands and a pure heart." Finally he says: "You shall sanctify it with clean hands and a pure heart." # THE EPISTLE OF BARNABAS. XV.

<note>original Greek: καταπαυόμενος ἁγιάζει αὐτήν...</note> ...resting, He will make it holy, when we ourselves are able to do what is right <note>original: δίκαια</note>, having received the promise, when lawlessness is no more, but all things have been made new by the Lord. # XVI. A spiritual temple is now being built for the Lord.

I will also speak to you concerning the temple, how those wretched men, being led astray, set their hope on the building <note>original: τὴν ὁδὸν; the translator notes suggest this refers to the physical path or way of the Mosaic law leading to the temple</note>, and not on their God who made them, but as if it were the house of God. For they consecrated Him in the temple almost like the Gentiles do. But learn how the Lord speaks, in setting it aside: *Who has measured the heaven with a span, or the earth with his fist? Was it not I?* says the Lord. *The heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool; what kind of house will you build for me, or what is the place of my rest?* Know that their hope is in vain. Furthermore, He says again: *Behold, those who tore down this temple, they themselves shall build it.* It is happening. For because of their warring, it was torn down by the enemies; now even the servants of the enemies shall rebuild it. Again, it was revealed how the city and the temple and the people of Israel were to be delivered up. For the Scripture says: *And it shall come to pass in the last days, the Lord will deliver up the sheep of the pasture and the sheepfold and their tower to destruction.* And it happened according to what the Lord had spoken. Let us seek, therefore, if there is a temple of God. There is, where He Himself says He is making and perfecting it. For it is written: *And it shall be, when the week is finished, the temple of God shall be built gloriously upon...*

**Chapter XVI.** 1) I retain "the way" <note>τὴν ὁδὸν</note> according to B, C, F, O, V and the common reading, and I think it refers to the "way" (Compare Acts 19:23 and 22:4) of the Mosaic law leading to the temple of the Lord. The ancient interpreter read "the house" <note>τὸν οἶκον</note>.

# THE EPISTLE OF BARNABAS. XV. XVI.
<page-num>37</page-num>

someone sanctifies it <note>referring to the Sabbath</note> only when we ourselves are able to do what is right, having received the promise, with lawlessness destroyed and all things made new by the Lord. Then we shall be able to sanctify it, if we ourselves have first been sanctified. Finally, He says to them: *'Your new moons and your Sabbaths I cannot bear.'* <note>Isaiah 1:13</note> See how He speaks: the present Sabbaths are not acceptable to me, but rather that which I have made; namely, when I have brought all things to an end, I will make a beginning of the eighth day, which is the beginning of another world. Therefore, we also celebrate the eighth day with joy, on which Jesus rose from the dead. And after He had appeared, He ascended into the heavens.

## XVI. A spiritual temple already built for the Lord.

I will also speak to you concerning the temple, how those miserable men, wandering in error, did not set their hope on God Himself, their creator, but on the building, as if it were the house of God. For they worshipped Him in the temple almost like the heathens do. But observe how the Lord speaks, rendering the temple void: *'Who has measured the heaven with a span, or the earth with his palm? Was it not I? Says the Lord: Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool. What kind of house will you build for me, or what is the place of my rest?'* <note>Isaiah 40:12; 66:1</note> Recognize that their hope is vain. And finally He says again: *'Behold, those who destroyed this temple shall themselves build it up.'* And so it happened. For because they went to war, the temple was destroyed by their enemies; and now even the servants of those enemies are rebuilding it. Again, it was made clear that the city, along with the temple and the people of Israel, was to be delivered up. For the Scripture says: *'And it shall come to pass in the last days, the Lord will deliver up the sheep of the pasture and the sheepfold and their tower to destruction.'* <note>original: "et erit in novissimis diebus, tradet Dominus oves pascui et ovile et turrim eorum in exitium."</note> And it happened just as the Lord spoke. Let us inquire, therefore, if a temple of God still exists. It does exist, where He Himself testifies that He is making and perfecting it. For it is written: *'And it shall be, when the week is completed, it shall be built...'*

## XVII. Conclusion of the first part of the Epistle.

This is the spiritual temple built for the Lord.

<header>XVII. Conclusion of the first part of the Epistle.</header>

As far as it was possible to show you these things with clarity, it is my hope that, according to my zeal, I have omitted nothing of those things which concern your salvation <note>original: "salutem"</note> and which are present. For over the one are stationed the angels of God who bring light, but over the other are the angels of Satan. And the former is Lord from eternity to eternity; but the latter is the prince of the present time of iniquity.

This, then, is the way of light. If anyone desires <note>original: θέλων</note> to travel the way to the appointed place, he will be zealous in his works. Therefore, the knowledge <term>gnosis; here meaning practical spiritual insight</term> given to us for walking in it is as follows: You shall love Him who redeemed you from death. You shall be simple in heart and rich in spirit. You shall not join yourself with those who walk in the way of death. You shall hate everything that is not pleasing to God; you shall hate all hypocrisy. You shall not forsake the commandments of the Lord. You shall not exalt yourself, but shall be humble-minded. You shall not take glory upon yourself. You shall not take evil counsel against your neighbor. You shall not give boldness to your soul. You shall not practice fornication, you shall not commit adultery, you shall not corrupt boys <note>original: παιδοφθορεύσεις; a reference to pederasty, common in early Christian prohibitions</note>. The word of God shall not go out from you among any who are impure. You shall not show partiality <note>literally: "accept the face"</note> in reproving anyone for a transgression. You shall be meek, you shall be quiet. You shall be one who trembles at the words which you have heard. You shall not bear a grudge against your brother. You shall not be of a divided mind <note>original: διψυχήσῃς; "double-souled" or wavering in faith</note> as to whether a thing shall be or not. You shall not take the name of the Lord in vain. You shall love your neighbor more than your own soul. You shall not murder a child by abortion, nor again shall you kill it when it is born. You shall not withhold your hand from your son or from your daughter, but from their youth you shall teach them the fear of the Lord. You shall not covet the things of your neighbor, nor shall you be greedy. You shall not be joined in your soul with the lofty, but you shall associate with the righteous and the humble. Accept the trials that happen to you as good. You shall not be double-minded <note>original: δίγνωμος</note> nor double-tongued, for the double tongue is a snare of death. You shall be subject to the Lord, and to [other] masters as a type of God, in reverence and fear. You shall not command your maidservant or slave in bitterness, for they hope in the same God, lest you should not fear the God who is over both; for He came not to call according to appearance, but to those whom the Spirit has prepared. ## XIX. Concerning the Way of Light.

This, then, is the way of light. If anyone desires to reach the designated place by this path, let him strive to achieve it through his works. The knowledge given to us for walking in this way is as follows: You shall love your Creator; you shall glorify Him who redeemed you from death. You shall be simple in heart and rich in spirit. You shall not cling to those who walk in the way of death. You shall hate whatever is displeasing to God; you shall hate all hypocrisy. Do not forsake the commandments of the Lord. You shall not exalt yourself, but shall be humble. You shall not take glory for yourself. You shall not hatch an evil plot against your neighbor. You shall not allow insolence in your soul. You shall not commit fornication, you shall not commit adultery, you shall not corrupt boys <note>original: "pueros non corrumpes" — a reference to pederasty, common in early Christian moral codes</note>. The word of God shall not go forth from you in the impurity of certain people. You shall not show partiality when reproving someone for a transgression. You shall be gentle; you shall be quiet. You shall tremble at the words you have heard. You shall forgive your brother. You shall not doubt whether a thing shall be or not. Do not take the name of the Lord in vain. You shall love your neighbor more than your own soul. You shall not kill a fetus by abortion, nor shall you kill it after it is born. Do not withdraw your hand from your son or your daughter, but from their youth you shall teach them the fear of the Lord. You shall not covet your neighbor’s goods, nor shall you be greedy. You shall not cling in your soul to the proud, but you shall walk with the righteous and the humble. Accept the trials that happen to you as good things. You shall not be wavering or double-tongued, for a double tongue is a snare of death. You shall be subject to the Lord God, and to [other] masters as to an image of God, with modesty and fear. ## XX. Concerning the Way of Darkness.

But the **Way of Darkness** is crooked and full of cursing. For it is the way of eternal death with punishment, in which are the things that destroy the souls of men: idolatry, recklessness, arrogance of power, hypocrisy, duplicity of heart, adultery, murder, robbery, pride, transgression, deceit, malice, haughtiness, <term>sorcery</term> <note>original: "veneficium"; literally poisoning or magic potions</note>, magic, avarice, and no fear of God. [The one who walks in the way of light] shall be glorified; but he who chooses the other things <note>original: "ἐκεῖνα" (those things), referring to the Way of Darkness described in the previous chapter</note> shall perish together with his works. # CLEMENT
# FIRST EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS¹

-> 1. Greeting. Praise of the Corinthians before the rise of the schism. <-

The Church of God which sojourns² at [Rome] to the Church of God which sojourns at Corinth, to those who are called and sanctified by the will of God through [our Lord Jesus Christ. Grace] to you and peace from God [Almighty] through Jesus Christ be multiplied.

[Because of the] sudden and repeated misfortunes and [calamities]³ which have befallen us, brothers, we [consider]⁴ that we have been somewhat slow in turning our attention to the matters in dispute [among] you,⁵ beloved; and especially to that detestable and unholy sedition, so alien and strange⁶ to the elect of God, which a few headstrong and self-willed persons have kindled to such a pitch of madness that your venerable and celebrated⁷ name, worthy of all men’s love, has been greatly reviled. For who⁸ that has stayed among you did not approve your virtuous and steadfast faith? Who did not admire your sober and gentle piety in Christ? Who did not proclaim the magnificent character of your hospitality? And who did not beatify your perfect and sound knowledge?⁹ For you did all things without partiality, and you walked in the laws¹⁰ of God, submitting yourselves to your leaders¹¹ and rendering the honor...

<margin>
1) This title is from the first printed edition (Patrick Young, 1633). In the Codex Alexandrinus—the only manuscript containing the first Epistle of Clement with a fragment of the second—nothing appears at the top except <note>original: "ΚΟΡΙΝΘΙΟΥΣ Α."</note> "To the Corinthians I"; however, the same title is placed at the end of the Epistle itself. Regarding the conjectures proposed by editors from the first to the last to fill the gaps in the Codex, we have also included them in brackets. In indicating these gaps, a strange discrepancy is found among those who have inspected the Codex, so that this part of the critique seems to need a harvester even after a repeated harvest. The Latin version is by Cotelier, amended here and there by Hefele and ourselves; the series of headings is as arranged by Gallandi in Hefele.

2) <note>original: "παροικεῖν"</note> "To sojourn" = to live as a pilgrim or foreigner, as in the beginning of the Epistle of Polycarp to the Philippians, and elsewhere.

3) I am persuaded, along with others, that the Epistle of Clement was written during the raging persecution of Domitian <note>Roman Emperor, r. 81–96 AD</note>, and not at the time when the storm first broke out against the Christians under Emperor Nero. For those sudden and successive calamities fit the reign of Domitian better than that of Nero. The testimonies of Eusebius (Ecclesiastical History III, 15–17), when carefully compared, support this. Chapter 5 of this Epistle, where the author looks back to the times of Nero, is of no weight for interpreting our passage differently.

4) To fill this gap, Young first substituted <note>original: "νομίζομεν"</note> "we consider"; however, having inspected the place again, he thought it should be replaced...
</margin>

-># CLEMENT’S<-

->## FIRST EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS##<-

1. Greeting. Praise of the Corinthians before the outbreak of the schism <note>A formal division or split within a church.</note>.

The Church of God which sojourns <note>original: "peregrinatur"; implies living as a resident alien or temporary pilgrim</note> at Rome, to the Church of God which sojourns at Corinth, to those who are called and sanctified by the divine will through our Lord Jesus Christ. May grace and peace from Almighty God through Jesus Christ be multiplied unto you. Because of the sudden and successive calamities and adverse misfortunes which have befallen us, we consider that we have turned our attention somewhat slowly, brothers, to those matters which were requested by you, beloved, and to that impious and detestable sedition <note>A rebellion against authority</note>, foreign and strange to the elect of God, which a few reckless and audacious men have kindled to such a pitch of insolence, that your honorable and illustrious name, worthy to be loved by all men, is greatly blasphemed. For who, having stayed among you, did not approve your virtuous and steadfast faith? Who did not admire your sober and moderate piety in Christ? Who did not proclaim the magnificent and noble character of your hospitality? And who did not count as blessed your perfect and certain knowledge? For you did all things without respect of persons, and you walked in the laws of God, being subject to those set over you, and [giving due honor to] the elders <term>presbyters: from the Greek 'presbyteros', referring to church leaders or elders</term>,

<column-break/>

<margin>The reading appeared to be <note>original Greek: "δυσζολμεν"</note>. This was repeated by the margin of Cotelerius (1672), Colomesius (1634), and Wotton. Others propose <note>original Greek: "γνωρίζομεν" (we recognize)</note> without just cause.</margin>

<margin>From this manner of speaking, some conclude that the Christians living in Corinth sought by letter from the Roman church that it should intercede by its authority to settle their disputes regarding ecclesiastical office. It seems more likely that the report of the Corinthian sedition was carried to Rome. Compare below, chapter 47, and Hilgenfeld, *The Apostolic Fathers*, page 54, note 2.</margin>

<margin>The Alexandrian Codex <note>A 5th-century manuscript of the Greek Bible and Clement's epistles</note> reads <note>original Greek: "ξένοις" (to strangers)</margin>, which was undoubtedly placed there by a scribe who, due to itacism <note>A shift in pronunciation where different vowels/diphthongs came to sound like 'ee'</note>, exchanged the diphthongs *oi*, *ei*, and *e* at will, instead of the adjective <note>original Greek: "ξένης" (strange/foreign)</note> which sounds the same. Therefore, one should not think of "strangers in the land" here.</margin>

<margin>In a similar way below in chapter 47: "the dignity of your world-renowned brotherly love [in your] epistle."</margin>

<margin>The passage "For who... walked in [the laws] of God" is cited by Clement of Alexandria in *Stromata*, Book IV, chapter 17, page 610, Potter edition.</margin>

<margin>Compare the Epistle of Barnabas, chapter 6.</margin>

<margin>Colomesius gathered that this is the genuine reading from sections 3 and 40 and Clement of Alexandria (cited above), although the Manuscript shows "laws" <note>original Greek: "νόμοις"</note>.</margin>

<margin>The Leaders <note>original Greek: "ἡγούμενοι"</note> are not the same as the elders (presbyters). Indeed, all those who were appointed to rule and govern the church are numbered among the former, whereas the name of "presbyters" was used by the primitive Christians to call their brothers not only because of their office, but also out of honor. Compare Lipsius, *Inquiry into the First Epistle of Clement of Rome to the Corinthians*, page 28.</margin>

-> # I. CLEMENT TO THE CORINTHIANS. I. II. <-

...assigning due honor to the **elders** <note>original: "presbyteroi," the leaders of the local church</note> among you. You instructed the young to think with moderation and dignity; you charged the women to perform all their duties with a blameless, dignified, and pure conscience, loving <note>original: "stergousas"</note> their own husbands as is fitting. You taught them to remain within the rule of subjection <note>original: "kanoni tēs hypotagēs"</note> and to manage their households with dignity and great discretion.

-> ## II. Continuation of the former praise of the Corinthians. <-

And you were all humble in mind, not boasting at all, being subject rather than subjecting others, giving rather than receiving. Content with the provisions <note>original: "ephodiois," literally travel supplies or rations for a journey</note> of God, and diligently attending to His words, you had laid them up in your hearts <note>original: "ensternismenoi," literally "en-breasted" or deeply embraced</note>, and His sufferings were before your eyes. Thus, a deep and rich peace was given to all, along with an insatiable desire for doing good, and a full outpouring of the Holy Spirit came upon everyone. Being filled with a glorious counsel, with good enthusiasm and pious confidence, you stretched out your hands to the Almighty God, beseeching Him to be merciful if you had committed any sin unwillingly. You struggled day and night for the whole brotherhood, so that the number of His elect might be saved with mercy and a good conscience. You were sincere and innocent, and bore no malice toward one another. Every faction and every schism was abominable to you; you mourned over the transgressions of your neighbors; you judged their deficiencies as your own. You were without regret in every act of kindness, ready for every good work. Adorned with a most virtuous and venerable way of life, you performed all things in His fear; the commandments and ordinances of the Lord were written upon the tablets of your heart.

To the young men, you gave instructions that they should pursue moderate and honorable things; the women you commanded to perform all things with a blameless, honorable, and chaste conscience, loving their own husbands as duty demands; and you taught them to remain within the rule of obedience <note>original: "canone," referring to a standard or rule of conduct</note> and to manage their domestic affairs with gravity, behaving themselves honorably in all things.

<header>II. Continuation of the previous praise of the Corinthians.</header>

You were all humble in mind, in no way given to vain boasting, subject to others rather than subjecting others to yourselves, more willing to give than to receive. Content with the provisions of God <note>original: "viatico," literally travel-provisions, here meaning spiritual nourishment</note>, and attending diligently to His words, you kept His words intimately hidden in your hearts, and His sufferings were before your eyes. Thus, a deep and abundant peace with an insatiable desire for doing good was given to all; there was also a full outpouring of the Holy Spirit upon everyone. Being filled with a holy will, with sincere alacrity of mind and pious confidence, you stretched forth your hands to Almighty God, imploring Him to be merciful toward you if you had sinned in any way against your will. Day and night you were anxious for the entire brotherhood, so that the number of God's elect might be saved through mercy and a good conscience. You were sincere and simple, and mindful of no injuries against one another. Every sedition and every schism was an abomination to you; you mourned over the transgressions of your neighbors; you judged their defects as your own. You never repented of any good deed, being ready for every good work. Adorned with a full and venerable way of life in all virtues, you performed everything in His fear; the commandments and precepts of the Lord were written upon the breadth of your heart.

<page-num>50</page-num>
->I. CLEMENT TO THE CORINTHIANS III. IV. V.<-

The dishonored rose up against the honored <note>original: "ἄτιμοι... ἐντίμους"</note>, those of no reputation against the renowned, the foolish against the wise, and the young against the elders. For this reason, righteousness and peace are far removed, while each one abandons the fear of God and becomes dim-sighted in his faith, neither walking in the laws of His commandments nor living in a manner worthy of Christ <note>original: "Χριστῷ"</note>. Instead, each follows his own evil lusts, having taken up an unrighteous and impious jealousy, through which also death entered into the world.

IV. Many evils have flowed from this source even since ancient times.

For it is written thus: And it came to pass after some days, that Cain brought of the fruits of the earth a sacrifice to God, and Abel also brought of the firstlings of the sheep and of their fat. And God looked upon Abel and his gifts, but He paid no heed to Cain and his sacrifices. And Cain was deeply grieved, and his countenance fell. And God said to Cain: "Why have you become so sorrowful? And why has your countenance fallen? If you offer rightly, but do not divide rightly, have you not sinned? Be calm; his recourse is to you, and you shall rule over him." And Cain said to Abel his brother: "Let us go out into the field." And it happened while they were in the field, Cain rose up against Abel his brother and killed him. You see, brothers, how jealousy and envy brought about the murder of a brother. Because of jealousy, our father Jacob fled from the face of Esau his brother. Jealousy caused Joseph to be persecuted even unto death, and to enter into slavery. Jealousy compelled Moses to flee from the face of Pharaoh, king of Egypt, when he heard from his fellow countryman: "Who appointed you a judge or a ruler over us? Do you wish to kill me, in the same way you killed the Egyptian yesterday?" Because of jealousy, Aaron and Miriam were lodged outside the camp. Jealousy brought Dathan and Abiram down alive into Hades, because they rebelled against the servant of God, Moses. Because of jealousy, David suffered envy not only from foreigners, but was also persecuted by Saul, king of Israel.

V. No less evils have arisen from this in the most recent times. The martyrdom of Peter and Paul.

But to leave behind the ancient examples, let us come to the athletes <note>A common early Christian metaphor for martyrs who "competed" for the faith.</note> who lived nearest to our time. Let us take the noble examples of our own generation. Through jealousy and envy, [the greatest] and most righteous—

<header>I. CLEMENT TO THE CORINTHIANS V. VI.</header>

The pillars <note>original: στύλοι; referring to the leaders of the Church</note> were persecuted, and [went] even unto death. Let us set before [our] eyes the good Apostles. Peter, through unrighteous jealousy, endured not one, nor two, but many labors, and having thus borne witness <note>original: μαρτυρήσας; the root of the word "martyr," meaning to give testimony through death</note>, he went to the merited place of glory. Through jealousy [and] strife, Paul showed the prize of endurance; seven times he was in bonds, driven into exile, and stoned. Having become a herald both in the East and in the West, he received the noble renown of his faith, having taught righteousness to the whole world, and having come to the limit of the West, and borne witness before the rulers. Thus he was set free from the world and went to the holy place, having become the greatest example of endurance.

VI. Continuation. More other martyrs.

To these men who lived holy lives was gathered a great multitude of the elect, who, having suffered many outrages and tortures through jealousy, became a most beautiful example among us. Through jealousy, women were persecuted—as Danaids and Dirces <note>A difficult reference; likely comparing Christian women's tortures to the violent myths of the daughters of Danaus and Dirce, who were tied to bulls</note>—suffering terrible and unholy outrages, they reached the goal in the steady course of faith, and they, though weak in body, received a noble reward. Jealousy has estranged wives from husbands, and altered that which was said by our father Adam: "This is now bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh." Jealousy and strife have overthrown great cities and uprooted great nations.

<page-num>54</page-num>
<header>I. CLEMENT TO THE CORINTHIANS VII. VIII.</header>

<header>VII. Exhortation to Repentance.</header>

These things, beloved, we write not only to admonish you, but also to remind ourselves; for we are in the same arena <note>original: σκάμματι - literally the "dug-out" area of a wrestling pit or stadium</note>, and the same struggle lies before us. Therefore, let us leave behind empty and vain cares, and let us come to the glorious and venerable rule <note>original: κανόνα - "canon" or standard</note> of our holy calling. Let us see what is good, and what is pleasant, and what is acceptable in the sight of Him who made us. Let us fix our gaze upon the blood of Christ, and see how precious it is to God His Father; because, having been poured out for our salvation, it brought the grace of repentance to the whole world. Let us review all the generations, and learn that in generation after generation the Master <note>original: δεσπότης - "Despot," used here as a title for God implying absolute sovereignty</note> has given a place for repentance to those who desire to turn to Him. Noah preached repentance, and those who obeyed were saved. Jonah preached destruction to the Ninevites; but they, repenting of their sins, appeased God through their supplications and received salvation, even though they were aliens to God.

<header>VIII. Continuation.</header>

The ministers of the grace of God spoke through the Holy Spirit concerning repentance, and the Master of all things Himself spoke with an oath concerning repentance: "For as I live," says the Lord, "I do not desire the death of the sinner, but rather his repentance"; adding also a gracious decree: "Repent, O house of Israel, from your iniquity." Say to the sons of my people: "Even if your sins reach from the earth to heaven, and even if they be redder than scarlet and blacker than sackcloth, and you turn to me with all your heart and say 'Father,' I will listen to you as to a holy people." And in another place He speaks thus: "Wash and be clean, put away the wickednesses from your souls from before my eyes; cease from your wickednesses, learn to do good, seek judgment, rescue the wronged, give judgment for the orphan, and do justice for the widow; and come, let us reason together," He says. "And even if your sins be as crimson, I will make them white as snow; and if they be as scarlet, I will make them white as wool. And if you are willing and listen to me, you shall eat the good things of the earth; but if you are not willing and do not listen to me, a sword shall devour you; for the mouth of the Lord has spoken these things." Desiring, therefore, that all His beloved should partake of repentance, He established it by His almighty will.

# I. CLEMENT TO THE CORINTHIANS VII. VIII.

## VII. An Exhortation to Repentance.

These things, dearly beloved, we write not only to admonish you of your duty, but also to remind ourselves; for we are struggling in the same arena, and the same contest is set before us. Therefore, let us leave behind empty and vain cares, and let us come to the glorious and venerable rule <note>original: "lineam [metam]"; referring to the finish line or goal in a race</note> of our holy calling. Let us see what is beautiful, what is pleasant, and what is acceptable in the sight of our Maker. Let us look intently at the blood of Christ and consider how precious it is to God the Father <note>original: "[πατρὶ]" (patri)</note>, which, poured out for our salvation, offered the grace of repentance to the whole world. Let us look back at all the ages of the world and learn that in every generation the Lord has granted a place for repentance to those willing to turn to Him. Noah was a herald of repentance, and those who obeyed him were saved. Jonah preached destruction to the Ninevites; but they, performing repentance for their sins, appeased God with prayers and obtained salvation, even though they were strangers to God.

## VIII. Continuation.

The ministers of divine grace, inspired by the Holy Spirit, spoke of repentance. The Lord of all things Himself also spoke of repentance with an oath: "As I live," says the Lord, "I do not desire the death of the sinner, but rather his repentance"; adding also that excellent saying: "Repent, O house of Israel, of your iniquity. Say to the sons of my people: though your sins reach from earth to heaven, though they be redder than scarlet and blacker than sackcloth, if you turn to me with your whole heart and say, 'Father,' I will listen to you as to a holy people <note>original: "λαῷ ἁγίῳ" (laō hagiō)</note>." And in another place He says: "Wash and be clean, take away the evil from your souls, from before my eyes; cease from your wickednesses, learn to do good, seek what is right, deliver the oppressed, judge for the orphan, and justify the widow; and come and let us reason together <note>original: "[δι]ελεχθῶμεν" (dielechthōmen)</note>, says the Lord. And if your sins be as crimson, I will make them white as snow; if they be as scarlet, I will make them white as wool. And if you are willing and listen to me, you shall eat the good things of the earth; but if you are unwilling and do not listen to me, the sword shall devour you; for the mouth of the Lord has spoken these things." Desiring, therefore, that all His beloved should become partakers of repentance, He confirmed this decree by His almighty will.

<header>I. CLEMENT TO THE CORINTHIANS IX. X.</header>

<header>IX. Examples of the Saints, who through faith and obedience etc. obtained the grace of God. Enoch and Noah.</header>

Therefore let us be obedient to His magnificent and glorious will, and becoming suppliants of His mercy and kindness, let us fall down before Him and return to His compassions, forsaking vain labor <note>original: ματαιοπονίαν; some scholars suggest "vain talk" based on other early Christian letters</note>, and strife, and the jealousy which leads to death. Let us fix our gaze <note>original: Ἀτενίσωμεν</note> upon those who have perfectly served His magnificent glory. Let us take Enoch, who, being found righteous in obedience, was translated, and his death was not found. Noah, being found faithful, through his service preached regeneration <note>original: παλιγγενεσίαν; a "new birth" or "renewal" for the world</note> to the world, and through him the Master saved the living creatures that entered in harmony into the ark.

<header>X. Continuation. Abraham.</header>

Abraham, who was called "the Friend," was found faithful in that he became obedient to the words of God. He, through obedience, went out from his country, and from his kindred, and from his father’s house, so that by leaving behind a little country, and weak kindred, and a small house, he might inherit the promises of God. For He says to him: "Depart from your land, and from your kindred, and from your father’s house, to the land which I shall show you; and I will make you into a great nation, and I will bless you, and I will magnify your name, and you shall be blessed; and I will bless those who bless you, and I will curse those who curse you, and in you shall all the tribes of the earth be blessed." And again, when he was separated from Lot, God said to him: "Look up with your eyes, and see from the place where you now are, toward the north and the south-west <note>original: λίβα; the wind from Libya, meaning the south-west</note> and the east and the sea; for all the land which you see, I will give it to you and to your offspring forever. And I will make your offspring as the sand of the earth; if anyone is able to count the sand of the earth, then your offspring also shall be counted." And again He says: "God led Abraham out, and said to him: Look up toward the heaven and count the stars, if you are able to count them; so shall your offspring be. And Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness." Because of his faith and hospitality <note>original: φιλοξενίαν</note> a son was given to him in his old age, and through obedience he offered him as a sacrifice to God upon one of the mountains which He showed him.

<header>I. CLEMENT TO THE CORINTHIANS XI. XII.</header>

<header>XI. Continuation. Lot. The punishment of dissension.</header>

Because of his <term>hospitality</term> <note>original: "philoxenian"</note> and piety, Lot was saved out of Sodom, when all the surrounding region was judged by fire and brimstone. The Master <note>A common early Christian title for God or Christ</note> made it clearly known that He does not forsake those who hope in Him, but those who turn aside to other ways He appoints to punishment and torment. For when his wife went out with him, being of a different mind and not in <term>harmony</term> <note>original: "homonoia," a key theme in Clement's letter</note>, she was made a sign to this end, so that she became a pillar of salt unto this day, to be known to all that the <term>double-minded</term> <note>original: "dipsychoi," meaning those who waver in faith</note> and those who doubt concerning the power of God are for a judgment and a warning to all generations.

<header>XII. The rewards of faith and hospitality. Rahab.</header>

Because of faith and hospitality, Rahab the harlot was saved. For when spies were sent by Joshua the son of Nun to Jericho, the king of the land knew that they had come to spy out their country, and he sent men to seize them, so that having been seized they might be put to death. The hospitable Rahab, therefore, having received them, hid them in the upper room under the <term>flax-stalks</term> <note>original: "linokalamen"</note>. And when the men from the king stood before her and said: "The spies of our land came unto thee; bring them out, for the king so commands," she answered: "The two men whom you seek did enter in unto me, but they departed quickly and are on their way," while she did not show the men to them. And she said to the spies: "I know surely that the Lord your God is delivering this city to you; for the fear and dread of you has fallen upon those who inhabit it. When, therefore, it happens that you take it, save me and my father's house." And they said to her: "It shall be as you have spoken to us. When, therefore, you perceive that we are coming, you shall gather all your kinsfolk under your roof, and they shall be saved; for as many as are found outside the house shall perish." And they further gave her a sign, that she should hang from her house a scarlet thread, making it manifest that through the blood of the Lord there shall be redemption for all who believe and hope in God. You see, beloved, that not only faith but <term>prophecy</term> was found in this woman.

<header>XI. Continuation. Lot. The punishment of dissension.</header>

Because of his <term>hospitality</term> <note>Latin: hospitalitatem</note> and <term>piety</term> <note>Latin: pietatem</note>, Lot escaped safely out of Sodom, while the entire surrounding region was punished with fire and sulfur. The Lord thereby made it manifest that He does not forsake those who hope in Him, but on the contrary, He punishes those who turn away from His commands with sufferings and torments. For his wife, who went out together with him, because she disagreed with him and did not persist in <term>concord</term> <note>harmony or agreement</note>, was therefore set as a sign, and was made into a <term>pillar of salt</term> <note>Latin: salis statua</note> unto this very day; so that it might be known to all that those who are double-minded and who waver concerning the power of God are set forth as a judgment and a sign for all generations.

For when <term>spies</term> <note>Latin: speculatoribus</note> were sent to the city of Jericho by Joshua the son of Nun, the king of the land learned that they had come to scout their region, and he sent out men to seize them, so that once captured they might be put to death. # I. CLEMENT TO THE CORINTHIANS XIII. XIV. XV.

## XIII. An exhortation to humility.

Let us therefore be humble-minded, brothers, laying aside all arrogance and conceit and foolishness and anger; and let us do what is written (for the Holy Spirit says: *Let not the wise man boast in his wisdom, nor the strong man in his strength, nor the rich man in his riches; but let him who boasts boast in the Lord, to seek Him out, and to do judgment and righteousness* <note>original: "δικαιοσύνην"</note>)¹) especially remembering the words of the Lord Jesus, which He spoke while teaching gentleness and patience. For He spoke thus: *Be merciful, that you may obtain mercy; forgive, that it may be forgiven to you; as you do, so shall it be done to you; as you give, so shall it be given to you; as you judge, so shall you be judged; as you show kindness, so shall kindness be shown to you; with what measure you measure, it shall be measured to you.* By this commandment and these precepts let us strengthen ourselves to walk in obedience to His holy words, being humble-minded. For the holy Word says: *Upon whom shall I look, but upon him who is gentle and quiet and who trembles at my oracles?*

## XIV. We must obey God rather than the authors of sedition.

It is right and holy, therefore, brothers, that we should be obedient to God rather than follow those who in arrogance and disorder <note>original: "ἀκαταστασίᾳ"</note> are leaders of a detestable jealousy. For we shall undergo no ordinary harm, but rather great danger, if we recklessly surrender ourselves to the wills of men who launch out into strife and sedition to estrange us from what is good. Let us be kind to one another according to the compassion and sweetness of Him who made us. For it is written: *The kind shall be inhabitants of the land, and the innocent shall be left upon it; but those who act lawlessly shall be destroyed from it.* And again it says: *I saw the ungodly lifted high and exalted like the cedars of Lebanon; and I passed by, and behold, he was not, and I sought his place, and I did not find it. Guard innocence and behold uprightness, for there is a remnant for the peaceful man.*

## XV. We must cling to those who cultivate peace, not those who pretend to cultivate it.

Therefore let us unite ourselves with those who keep peace with godliness, and not with those who wish for peace with hypocrisy. For it says somewhere: *This people...*

<header>I. CLEMENT TO THE CORINTHIANS XIII. XIV. XV.</header>

<header>XIII. An exhortation to humility.</header>

Therefore, let us be humble in mind, brothers, laying aside all arrogance, pride, foolishness, and anger; and let us do what is written (for the Holy Spirit says: "Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, nor let the mighty man glory in his might, nor let the rich man glory in his riches; but let him who glories glory in the Lord, in seeking Him, and in doing judgment and justice" <note>original: "ius et iustitiam"</note>) especially remembering the words of the Lord Jesus, which He spoke while teaching fairness and long-suffering. For He spoke thus: "Be merciful, that you may obtain mercy; forgive, that it may be forgiven to you; as you do, so shall it be done to you; as you give, so shall it be given to you; as you judge, so shall you be judged; as you are kind, so shall you experience kindness; with the measure you use, it shall be measured to you." By this precept and these commands let us strengthen ourselves, so that we may always walk in obedience to His holy words with all humility. For the holy word says: "Upon whom shall I look, if not upon him who is humble and quiet and who trembles at my words?"

<header>XIV. We must obey God rather than the authors of sedition.</header>

It is therefore right and holy, brothers, that we should be obedient to God rather than follow those who, in pride and turbulence, are the leaders and authors of detestable rivalry. For we shall undergo no small harm, but rather great danger, if we rashly surrender ourselves to the wills of men who aim for strife and sedition <note>original: "seditiones collineant"</note> <margin>The word is neutral. Gallicciolli translates: "those who pull toward discord," noting: they aim = they target = they have in view.</margin> so as to alienate us from what is right and good. Let us be kind toward them, according to the mercy and sweetness of our Creator. For it is written: "The kind shall be inhabitants of the land, and the innocent shall be left upon it; but the wicked shall be exterminated from it." And again He says: "I saw the impious highly exalted and lifted up like the cedars of Lebanon; and I passed by, and behold, he was not; and I sought his place, and did not find it. Guard innocence, and behold equity, for there are remnants for the peaceful man." <margin>By "remnants" <note>Greek: ἐγκατάλειμμα</note> Euthymius understands memory; which is preserved in two ways, either through offspring or through good works. But the most ingenious Ferrandus paraphrases the passage thus: "There will be a time when a fitting reward is repaid to the innocent man." Both follow the mind of the Psalmist.</margin>

<header>XV. We must cling to those who cultivate peace, not those who pretend to cultivate it.</header>

Let us therefore cling to those who cultivate peace with godliness, and not to those who desire peace with hypocrisy. <margin>Davis prefers "those who are struck"; Le Clerc conjectures "those who advise."</margin> For He says in a certain place: "This people <margin>Isaiah 29:13; Mark 7:6; Matthew 15:8.</margin>

<column-break/>

### XVII. The Saints, especially Abraham, Job, and Moses, as examples of humility.

Let us also become imitators of those who wandered about in goatskins and sheepskins, preaching the coming of Christ; we mean Elijah and Elisha, and also Ezekiel, the prophets; and besides these, those who have been well-attested. Abraham was greatly attested, and was called the "friend of God," and he says, looking intently at the glory of God in humility: "But I am earth and ashes." And furthermore, concerning Job it is thus written: "Job was righteous and blameless, true, god-fearing, keeping himself from all evil." But he, accusing himself, said: "No one is clean from filth, even if his life be but for one day." Moses was called "faithful in all his house," and through his service God judged Egypt through their plagues and torments; but even he, though greatly glorified, did not use boastful words, but said, when an oracle was given to him from the bush: "Who am I, that you send me? I am feeble-voiced and slow-tongued." And again he says: "I am but smoke from a pot."

### XVIII. David as an example of humility.

And what shall we say of David, who was well-attested? To whom God said: "I have found a man after my own heart, David the son of Jesse, in eternal mercy I have anointed him." But he himself says to God: "Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy, and according to the multitude of your compassions blot out my transgression. Wash me yet more from my iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin..."

# I. CLEMENT TO THE CORINTHIANS. XVIII. XIX. XX.

For I acknowledge my transgression, and my sin is ever before me. Against You only have I sinned, and done this evil in Your sight; that You may be justified in Your words, and overcome when You are judged. For behold, I was conceived in transgressions, and in sins did my mother conceive me. For behold, You have loved truth. The uncertain and hidden things of Your wisdom You have made known to me. You shall sprinkle me with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed; You shall wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow. You shall make me hear joy and gladness; the bones which have been humbled shall rejoice. Turn Your face away from my sins, and[1] blot out all my transgressions. Create in me a clean heart[2], O God, and renew a right spirit³ within my inward parts. Cast me not away from Your presence, [and] take [not] Your Holy [Spirit from] me. Restore to me the joy of [Your salvation, and] uphold me with a [guiding] spirit. [I will teach] the [transgressors] Your ways, and the [ungodly] shall return to You. [Deliver me from blood-guiltiness, O God, the God of [my salvation. My tongue shall rejoice] in [Your righteousness. O Lord, You shall open] my mouth, and my lips [shall declare] Your praise. For if [You had desired sacrifice, I would have given it; You will not be pleased with] burnt offerings. The sacrifice to God is a broken spirit; a broken and humbled heart God will not despise.⁴ <note>original: "ἐξουθενώσει" — This entire section is a direct quotation of Psalm 51 (Psalm 50 in the Septuagint numbering), used by Clement to illustrate the humility of King David.</note>

## XIX. Imitating these examples, let us seek peace.

The humility¹ and the submissiveness² through obedience of so many and such great men who have thus been attested, has made not only us, but also the generations before us better—even those who received³ His oracles⁴ in fear and truth. Having therefore participated⁶ in many great and glorious deeds, let us run back to the goal of peace delivered to us from the beginning, and let us look steadfastly to the Father and Creator of the whole world, and let us cleave to His magnificent and surpassing gifts of peace and His benefits.⁷ Let us behold Him in our mind, and let us look with the eyes of our soul into His long-suffering will. Let us consider how free from anger⁸ He is toward all His creation.

## XX. The harmony of the world and the order of nature demonstrate that peace and concord are loved by God; from which many benefits flow to us.

The heavens, moving by His management, are subject to Him in peace. Day and night accomplish the course assigned by Him, in no way hindering one another. The sun and the moon, and the choirs of stars, according to His appointment, roll on in harmony without any deviation through the limits assigned to them. The fruitful earth, according to His will, brings forth in its proper seasons an abundance of food for men and beasts and all the living creatures that are upon it, [never] failing...

The humility, therefore, and the subjection through obedience of such and so many men who have obtained so celebrated a report <note>original: "elogium"</note>, has made not only us, but also the generations before us better—those, namely, who received his oracles <note>original: "eloquia"</note> in fear and truth. <margin>5) He seems to imitate the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews 12:1.</margin> Since, then, we have become sharers in many great and illustrious deeds <note>original: "gestorum"</note>, let us run back to the goal of peace delivered to us from the beginning, <margin>6) We are sharers of "deeds" <note>original: "πράξεων"</note> because Holy Scripture hands down the memory of them to us. — Davis.</margin> and let us look steadfastly unto the Father and Creator of the whole world, and let us cleave firmly to his magnificent and surpassing gifts of peace and his benefits. <margin>7) Let us hold a peace as firm as that which is held in the nature of things. — H.</margin> Let us contemplate him with our thought, and with the eyes of the mind let us look upon his long-suffering will. <margin>8) By establishing the harmony of the world (ch. 20), God shows himself merciful toward every creature. — H.</margin> Let us see how free from wrath he shows himself toward all his creation.

### XX. *That peace and concord are loved by God is demonstrated by the harmony of the world and the order of nature; whence many benefits flow to us.*

## XXII. These exhortations are strengthened by Christian faith, which proclaims the misery of sinners.

## XXIII. Be humble. Believe that Christ is coming.

The merciful in all things and beneficent Father has compassion <note>original: "splangchna," literally 'bowels' or 'inner organs,' the seat of deep emotion</note> upon those who fear Him, and kindly and lovingly bestows His favors upon those who approach Him with a sincere mind. O foolish ones! Compare yourselves to a tree; take a vine. First it sheds its leaves, then a shoot comes, then a leaf, then a flower, and after these a sour grape, then the ripened cluster. You see that in a short time the fruit of the tree reaches maturity. In truth, quickly and suddenly shall His will be perfected, the Scripture also bearing witness: "For He shall come quickly, and shall not delay; and suddenly the Lord shall come to His temple, even the Holy One whom you expect."
