# II. CLEMENT TO THE CORINTHIANS V. VI. VII.

...to depart from this world. For the Lord says: "You shall be as lambs in the midst of wolves." <note>original: "ἔσεσθε ὡς ἀρνία ἐν μέσῳ λύκων." This is a variation of Matthew 10:16 or Luke 10:3.</note> But Peter answered and said to Him: "What if the wolves should tear the lambs?" Jesus said to Peter: "The lambs should not fear the wolves after they have died; and you, do not fear those who kill you and can do nothing more to you; but fear Him who, after you have died, has power over soul and body to cast them into the Gehenna <note>Gehenna: a term for a place of fiery judgment.</note> of fire." And know, brothers, that our stay in this world in this flesh is small and short-lived, but the promise of Christ is great and wonderful, even the rest of the coming kingdom and eternal life. What then must we do to obtain these things, except to walk in holiness and righteousness, and to regard these worldly things as foreign to us, and not to desire them? For in desiring to acquire these things, we fall away from the righteous path.

### VI.

->The present age and the future one are two enemies. Spurning the former, let us love the latter. Otherwise, there is no hope of salvation.<-

And the Lord says: "No servant can serve two masters." <note>original: "οὐδεὶς οἰκέτης δύναται δυσὶ κυρίοις δουλεύειν." See Luke 16:13.</note> If we wish to serve both God and Mammon <note>Mammon: a term for wealth or property, often personified as a false god.</note>, it is unprofitable for us. "For what is the benefit if someone gains the whole world, but forfeits his soul?" Now this age and the one to come are two enemies. This one speaks of adultery, corruption, avarice, and deceit; but that one renounces these things. We cannot, therefore, be friends of both; but we must renounce this one and make use of that one. Let us consider that it is better to hate the things here, because they are small, short-lived, and corruptible; and to love those things, the good and incorruptible. For by doing the will of Christ, we shall find rest; but if not, nothing shall rescue us from eternal punishment if we disobey His commandments. And the Scripture also says in Ezekiel: "Even if Noah, Job, and Daniel were to arise, they would not rescue their children in the captivity." If even such righteous men cannot rescue their children by their own righteousness, with what confidence shall we enter the palace of God, if we do not keep our baptism pure and undefiled? Or who shall be our advocate if we are not found having holy and righteous works?

->We must struggle so that we may be crowned.<-

Let us then compete so that we may all be crowned. Therefore, let us set ourselves on the straight path, the incorruptible contest, and many...

# II. CLEMENT TO THE CORINTHIANS V. VI. VII.

...for the Lord says: "You shall be as lambs in the midst of wolves." But Peter answered and said to Him: "What if the wolves should tear the lambs?" Jesus said to Peter: "The lambs should not fear the wolves after they have died; and as for you, do not fear those who kill you and after that can do nothing more to you; but fear Him who, after you have died, has power over soul and body to cast them into the Gehenna <note>Gehenna: a valley outside Jerusalem used as a metaphor for a place of fiery judgment.</note> of fire." And know, brothers, that the pilgrimage of this flesh in this world is brief and lasts but a little time; but the promise of Christ is great and wonderful, even the rest of the coming kingdom and eternal life. What then can we do to attain these things, except by living holily and justly, and by regarding these worldly things as foreign to us, and not desiring them? For while we desire to acquire these things, we fall away from the righteous path.

### VI.

->The present age and the future are two enemies. Spurning the former, let us love the latter. Otherwise, there is no hope of salvation.<-

And the Lord says: "No servant can serve two masters." <note>original: "nullus servus potest duobus dominis servire." See Luke 16:13.</note> If we wish to serve both God and Mammon <note>Mammon: an Aramaic term for wealth or property, used here as a personification of worldly greed.</note>, it is disadvantageous for us. "For what is the profit, if one should gain the whole world, but suffer the loss of his soul?" <note>original: "Nam quae utilitas, si quis universum mundum lucretur, animam autem detrimento afficiat?" See Matthew 16:26.</note> Furthermore, this age and the future are two enemies. This one preaches adultery, corruption, avarice, and deceit; the other renounces these things. We cannot, therefore, be friends of both; it is necessary that we say farewell to this one and make use of that one. Let us consider it better to hate the things that are here, because they are small and of short duration and subject to decay; and to love those things there, as they are good and incorruptible. For if we do the will of Christ, we shall find rest; but if not, nothing shall rescue us from eternal punishment, if we neglect His commandments. For the Scripture says in Ezekiel: "If Noah and Job and Daniel should rise up, they shall not deliver their children who are in captivity." <note>original: "si Noe et Iob et Daniel resurgant, non eruent liberos suos..." See Ezekiel 14:14, 20.</note> Now if such righteous men cannot deliver their own children by their own righteousness, with what confidence shall we enter into the palace of God, unless we have kept our baptism pure and undefiled? Or who shall be our advocate, if we are not found possessing pious and righteous works?

# II. CLEMENT TO THE CORINTHIANS VII. VIII. IX.

...let us set sail for it and compete, so that we may also be crowned. And if we cannot all be crowned, let us at least come close to the crown. We must know that he who competes in the corruptible contest <note>The author uses the imagery of Greek athletic games, where the "corruptible" prize was a wreath of leaves that would soon wither.</note>, if he is found cheating, is whipped, removed, and thrown out of the stadium. What do you think? What will he suffer who cheats in the contest of incorruptibility? For regarding those who have not kept the seal <note>original: "sphragida." This is a common early Christian term for baptism, viewed as a "seal" of ownership by God.</note>, He says: "Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched, and they shall be a spectacle to all flesh." <note>A quotation from Isaiah 66:24, often used in the early church to describe the consequences of turning away from the faith.</note>

### VIII. *While we are in this world, let us perform penance and keep the flesh pure.*

Therefore, while we are on earth, let us repent; for we are clay in the hand of the Craftsman <note>original: "technitou." Refers to God as the master artisan or potter.</note>. Just as the potter, if he makes a vessel and it is distorted or broken in his hands, molds it again; but if he has already cast it into the furnace of fire, he can no longer help it; so we also, while we are in this world, let us repent from our whole heart for the evil things we have done in the flesh, so that we may be saved by the Lord while we still have time for repentance. For after we have departed from the world, we can no longer confess or repent there. Therefore, brothers, by doing the will of the Father, and keeping the flesh holy, and guarding the commandments of the Lord, we shall receive eternal life. For the Lord says in the Gospel: "If you have not kept that which is small, who will give you that which is great? For I say to you, that he who is faithful in a very little thing is also faithful in much." <note>See Luke 16:10-12.</note> This, then, is what He means: "Keep the flesh pure and the seal unspotted, so that you may receive eternal life."

### IX. *In the flesh we shall be judged; therefore let us prepare ourselves in time.*

And let none of you say that this flesh is not judged, nor does it rise again. Know this: in what state were you saved? In what state did you recover your sight, if not while you were in this flesh? We must therefore guard the flesh as a temple of God. For just as you were called in the flesh, so you shall also come in the flesh. If Christ the Lord, who saved us, being first spirit <note>original: "pneuma." In this context, it refers to Christ's divine, pre-existent nature before the Incarnation.</note>, became flesh and thus called us; so also we shall receive our reward in this flesh. Let us love one another, then, so that we may all come into the kingdom of God. While we have time to be healed, let us give ourselves to God the Healer, giving Him a recompense. What kind? Repentance from a sincere heart. For He is the foreknower of all things, and knows what is in our heart.

### TO THE EPHESIANS, FROM IGNATIUS.^2

Ignatius, who is also called Theophorus <note>original: Θεοφόρος (Theophoros); literally meaning "God-bearer."</note>, to the church at Ephesus in Asia—a church worthy of all beatitude, blessed in greatness through the fullness <note>original: πληρώματι (plērōmati); a term often used in early Christianity to describe the "abundance" or "totality" of God's divine power.</note> of God the Father, predestined before the ages to be forever for an enduring and unchangeable glory, united and chosen in true passion by the will of the Father and of Jesus Christ our God: abundant greetings in Jesus Christ and in blameless grace.

---

1) You owe this title to the Laurentian Medicean Codex, which indeed has "The First Epistle of Saint Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans" noted on the front; "To the Smyrnaeans, by Saint Ignatius the Bishop" is the inscription in the Casanatensian Codex. In both manuscripts, the title precedes the Epistle to the Smyrnaeans. There are three things which the Epistles of Ignatius—if you except the one sent to the Romans—chiefly regard. For this reason, they declare war against the "Sabbatizers" <note>original: τοῖς σαββατίζουσι (tois sabbatizousi); those who insisted on following Jewish Sabbath laws.</note>, that is, those who bring Jewish customs into the Gospel of Christ; they recommend episcopal monarchy <note>The rule of a single bishop over a local church.</note>, because salvation lies uniquely in harmony and union with the leaders of the church; and for that same reason, they argue that all those who attempt to introduce heresies into Christ's flock must be rejected.

2) I provide this title according to the Laurentian Codex and the transcript of Holstenius, where it is written "Ignatius to the Ephesians." In the margin is the number 3. The name "IGNATIUS" is missing in the Armenian version and in the printed books. When Ignatius was being led as a prisoner from Antioch to Rome, he put into Smyrna, where Polycarp was bishop. The Ephesians sent their bishop Onesimus to him there, along with the deacon Burrhus, and Crocus, Euplus, and Fronto, to greet him. From this, Igna-

<column-break/>

tius took the opportunity to celebrate their charity (chapters 1, 21, 2). He then warns them that they should all remain united in the discipline of the church, obeying the bishop and the presbytery <note>The council of elders or priests.</note> (chapters 3–6), and that they should beware of foolish and wicked doctrines (chapters 7–10). There follows an admonitory part of the Epistle, which dwells more fully on the investigation of individual matters relating to that subject (chapters 11–20). The Preface and the first chapter of this Epistle, with a few exceptions of little importance, were translated by the Syrian <note>The scholar William Cureton, who published a shorter Syriac version of Ignatius.</note>. From his work and the Armenian version (by Petermann), I have noted the readings that seemed to be of greater weight.

3) Compare Wernsdorf, *Regarding Ignatius the Theophorus*, in his memorial for C. Timothy Seidelius, Helmstadt 1758. Düsterdieck, in *On the Authenticity of the Epistles of Ignatius* (Gottingen 1843, p. 89), thinks the word "Theophorus" was added to all the Ignatian epistles by someone else. # SAINT IGNATIUS

## EPISTLES.

---

### TO THE EPHESIANS.

Ignatius, who is also called Theophorus <note>original: "Theophorus" (Θεοφόρος), meaning "God-bearer."</note>, to the church at Ephesus in Asia—rightly called blessed, being blessed in the greatness of God the Father with fullness <note>original: "plenitudine" (the Latin equivalent of the Greek *pleroma*), referring to the totality of divine power.</note>; predestined before the ages to be always united and elected for an enduring and unchangeable glory through a true passion, by the will of the Father and of Jesus Christ our God: abundant greetings in Jesus Christ and in perfect grace.

### TO THE EPHESIANS.

* Ignatius, who is also called Theophorus, to the church which is rightly most blessed, being at Ephesus in Asia; blessed in the greatness of God the Father with fullness, predestined before the ages so that it might always exist in lasting, unchangeable glory, united and chosen in true passion, by the will of God the Father and of Jesus Christ our God: abundant greetings in Jesus Christ and in irreproachable grace. <note>This second version is a variant translation provided by the scholar Lucas Holstenius.</note>

---

<columns>2</columns>

The comparison to "Saul, who is also called Paul" (Acts 13:9) is somewhat awkward, both because of the "alliteration" (as they call it) which was hardly achieved by chance, and because of the allegory inherent in the proper meaning of each name. Nevertheless, no one will deny that Ignatius was one of the "God-bearing men" <note>original: ἐκ τῶν θεοφόρων ἀνδρῶν</note>. Others, though far inferior to him, have earned that epithet from others. Compare the *Published and Unpublished Works of Epiphanius, Monk and Presbyter*, edited by A. Dressel, page 45: "It seemed good also to me, in my longing and searching here and there, to investigate and select from the accounts of eyewitnesses and God-bearing men <note>original: θεοφόρων ἀνδρῶν</note> the facts concerning these things—from Clement of Rome, Evagrius of Sicily, and Epiphanius of Cyprus."

4) Compare Ephesians 1:19 and 1 Corinthians 2:5.
5) The "Enlarger" <note>The "Interpolator," an ancient editor who expanded the original letters of Ignatius.</note> of the common <note>vulg.</note> text adds "and in the fullness."

<column-break/>

The Syriac and the old Latin translator omit this. We have excluded the particle following Codices C and L, as well as our more recent, longer recensions B, F, O, R, V, and the Armenian version; this was done without injury to the connection of the thoughts. Compare Ephesians 3:19.
6) Compare Ephesians 1:4 and 3:11.
7) The word "to be" <note>original: εἶναι</note>, which was omitted by Vossius, is restored from Codices C and L; it is also read in the Interpolator's version and in the other translations.
8) Compare Ephesians 4:3 and following.
9) The words "of Asia" were transposed by the Armenian translator; the Syriac version does not read them.
10) *From the 4th edition:* "In joy": this is to be restored based on the Interpolator and the Syriac and Armenian versions.

*) This second version of these epistles of Ignatius is owed to Holstenius. We have distinguished it everywhere by a prefixed star. Furthermore, see the Prolegomena <note>The introductory section of the book.</note>.

# THE LETTER OF IGNATIUS TO THE EPHESIANS. CHAPTERS I. II.

---

### I. *Praise of the Ephesians for the delegation sent to him. Praise of Onesimus.*

Having welcomed <note>original: "’Αποδεξάμενος"</note> in God your well-beloved name, which you have obtained by a righteous nature, according to faith and love in Jesus Christ our Savior. Being imitators of God, and having been rekindled <note>original: "ἀναζωπυρήσαντες"; often used of a fire being poked into life</note> by the blood of God, you have perfectly completed the work natural to you. For having heard that I was bound and coming from Syria for the sake of our common name and hope, and hoping by your prayer to succeed in fighting wild beasts at Rome, so that through martyrdom I might be able to be a disciple of Him who offered Himself for us as an offering and sacrifice to God—when, therefore, I received your large number in the name of God in the person of Onesimus, a man of inexpressible love and your bishop in the flesh; whom I pray you love according to Jesus Christ, and that you all be like him. For blessed is He who has granted you, being worthy, to possess such a bishop.

### II. *Praise of the remaining delegates. Exhortation to obedience toward the bishop and the presbytery.*

Regarding my fellow-servant Burrhus, your deacon who is blessed in all things according to God, I pray that he might remain for the honor of yourselves and the bishop. And Crocus also, who is worthy of God and of you, whom I received as a pattern of the love you have shown, has refreshed me in every way—

---

<columns>2</columns>

**11)** The words "Having welcomed... our Savior" serve as a transition from the introduction to the Letter itself and are to be joined with the greeting "sends greetings" <note>original: "χαίρειν... λέγει"</note>. Compare below to *Smyrnaeans* chapter 1. See also the word "Glorifying" <note>original: "Δοξάζων"</note> and the reading of the Ottobonian Codex "having been able" <note>original: "δεδυνημένος"</note> instead of "I have been able" <note>original: "δεδύνημαι"</note> at the top of chapter 1 of the Homily of 1 Clement to the Romans, edited by A. Dressel.

**12)** That is, "your name" means "you." For this manner of speaking, see Galatians 6:1. That Latin usage of "name" <note>original: "nomen"</note> meaning "all Romans" is also well known in Aulus Gellius’s *Attic Nights* I, 2. The sense is: In the person of Onesimus your bishop (see just below in chapter 2), I have received you Ephesians yourself as if present. From the interpolator <note>a later editor who added to the text</note> and the Syriac and Armenian versions, the word "your" <note>original: "ὑμῶν"</note> should be restored. Fourth edition of Hefele.

**13)** Specifically "you." Compare 2 Timothy 1:6. But it is better to understand it in an intransitive sense, as in Clement of Rome’s *1 Corinthians* 27: "Let his faith therefore be rekindled in us," and the Septuagint <note>Greek Old Testament</note> at Genesis 45:27.

**14)** That is, the soul-saving passion and death of Christ. At the end of the sentence, the word "you completed" <note>original: "ἀπηρτίσατε"</note> was taken by Vossius from the Interpolator; in manuscript C it was changed to "you met" <note>original: "ἀπαντήσατε"</note>; manuscript L has "you completed" <note>original: "ἀπαρτίσατε"</note>. Graziani translates: "you have perfectly completed a work natural to you." I would say the adverb "perfectly" <note>original: "τελείως"</note> (which the Syriac seems to have read as "quickly" <note>original: "ταχέως"</note>) means the same thing

<column-break/>

as "toward the end." Perhaps then the passage should be read and punctuated: "Being imitators of God, having rekindled the natural work by the blood of God, you have perfectly met [the requirement]."

**15)** Here the concluding thought "you hastened to see" <note>original: "ἰδεῖν ἐσπουδάσατε"</note> from the old Translator and the Syriac must be inserted. (Hefele inserted it into the text in his 4th edition). Perhaps it should be written: "For having heard that I (following the Syriac) was bound from Syria for the sake of the common name and hope, and hoping by your prayer... to be a sacrifice, you hastened to see me."

**16)** The Syriac version reads "God," omitting the following words: "who offered Himself for us as an offering and sacrifice to God."

**17)** The true force of the conjunction "since" <note>original: "ἐπεὶ"</note> escapes those who think it serves no purpose other than to increase the meaning of the particle "therefore" <note>original: "οὖν"</note>. For the introductory clause which it begins does not lack a concluding thought; indeed, it begins with the words "It is therefore fitting" in the following chapter. Furthermore, "great number" <note>original: "πολυπληθίαν"</note> in manuscript C is the only correct reading; manuscript L has "fullness" <note>original: "πολυπληρίαν"</note>, as Jacobson asserts somewhat inaccurately. For from that same manuscript, Holstenius previously—and after me also Th. Heysius—transcribed "great number."

**18)** The Interpolator, together with the Syriac and Armenian versions, does not read the words "in the flesh." Compare 1 Peter 2:25.

# THE LETTER OF IGNATIUS TO THE EPHESIANS. I. II.

---

### I. *Praise of the Ephesians for the delegation sent to him. Praise of Onesimus.*

I have welcomed in God your name, which is greatly beloved and which you have acquired by an upright nature according to faith and love in Jesus Christ our Savior. Since you are imitators of God, and have been restored to life <note>original: "ad vitam revocati"</note> through the blood of God, you have perfectly completed the work of brotherhood. For after you heard that I was bound and coming from Syria for the sake of our common name and hope, you hurried to see me, as I hope through your prayers to succeed in fighting against the wild beasts at Rome, so that through martyrdom I may be able to become a disciple of Him who offered Himself for us as an offering and a sacrifice to God. Therefore, I received your whole multitude in the name of God in the person of Onesimus—a man of indescribable love and your bishop in the flesh—whom I pray you love according to Jesus Christ, and I wish for you all to be like him. For blessed is He who, by His grace, has deemed you worthy to possess such a bishop.

* I. I have welcomed your most desired name in God, which you possess by a righteous nature according to faith and love in Jesus Christ our Savior. Since you are imitators of God, stirring up the work natural to you <note>original: "cognatum opus"; referring to the shared labor of the Christian community</note> by the blood of Christ, you have rendered it perfect and complete. For when you heard that I was being led from Syria as a prisoner for the sake of our common name and hope—hoping that by your prayers I would attain the chance to fight the beasts at Rome—I might then, through martyrdom, succeed in being a disciple of Him who offered Himself for us as an offering and a sacrifice to God. Since, therefore, I have received your great number in the name of God in the person of Onesimus, a man of inexpressible love and your bishop according to the flesh, I pray that you love him according to Jesus Christ and that you all be like him. For blessed is He who, according to your merit, has granted you to have such a bishop.

### II. *Praise of the remaining delegates. Exhortation to obedience toward the bishop and the presbytery.*

Regarding my fellow-servant Burrhus, your deacon according to God and blessed in all things, I pray that he may always remain an honor to you and the bishop. And Crocus, who is worthy of both God and you, and whom I received as a pattern of your love, has refreshed me in every way—just as the Father of Jesus Christ may also refresh him—

* II. Concerning Burrhus, our fellow-servant and your deacon according to God, who is blessed in all things, I pray that he may remain for your honor and that of the bishop. Crocus also, worthy of God and of you, whom I received as a pattern of your love, has refreshed me in every way; just as may the Father of Jesus Christ refresh him—

Chapter II. 1) In the Syriac version <term>Syriac version: An ancient translation of the letters often shorter than the Greek or Latin versions</term>, these words and those following are missing up until the middle of the third chapter. To Hefele, it seems that the pious monk who prepared the Syriac version omitted everything that he thought was less consistent with or necessary for his own ascetic practice. However, it seems that he 

<column-break/>

diligently collected the hortatory sections <note>original: "paraeneticos"; passages containing moral advice</note> of the Ignatian Epistles and all the exhortations for leading a good life. Petermann thinks these sections fell out by chance, as they still exist in the Armenian version. I would hardly believe it.

2) Written poorly as <note>original Greek: "Βόῤῥου" (Borrhos)</note> in the Pseudo-Ignatius <term>Pseudo-Ignatius: Later additions or forged letters attributed to Ignatius</term>; and poorly in the old version as *Borro*. Burrhus is a common enough Roman name; however, it is not *Birrus*, *Byrrus*, or *Borrus*. —*Vossius* <note>Isaac Vossius (1618–1689) was a Dutch scholar who published the first edition of the shorter, more authentic Greek text of Ignatius.</note>

3) *πᾶσιν* (pasin) in manuscripts C and L; *πᾶσι* (pasi) in the Vossius edition.

# THE LETTER OF IGNATIUS TO THE EPHESIANS. II. III. IV.

...refreshed <note>original: "παυσεν," literally "rested" or "gave relief"</note> me, just as the Father of Jesus Christ may also refresh him, together with Onesimus, Burrus, Euplus, and Fronto; through these men I have seen all of you in the spirit of love. May I always have joy in you, if indeed I am worthy. It is therefore fitting, in every way, to glorify Jesus Christ, who has glorified you; so that in a single obedience you may be made perfect in the same mind and in the same judgment, and that you all may say the same thing about the same subject, so that being subject <note>original: "ὑποτασσόμενοι"</note> to the bishop and the presbytery <note>The council of elders or priests</note> you may be sanctified in all things.

->III. Without any pride—led by love—I exhort you toward unity.<-

I do not give you orders as if I were someone great. For even though I am bound in the Name <note>original: "ἐν τῷ ὀνόματι," referring to the name of Christ</note>, I have not yet been made perfect in Jesus Christ. For now I am only beginning to be a disciple, and I speak to you as my fellow-students <note>original: "συνδιδασκαλίταις"</note>. For I had need to be anointed <note>original: "ὑπαλειφθῆναι"; a term used for athletes being prepared for a contest</note> by you with faith, admonition, endurance, and patience. But since love does not allow me to be silent concerning you, I have therefore taken the initiative to exhort you, so that you may run together in harmony with the mind of God. For Jesus Christ, our inseparable life, is the mind of the Father, just as the bishops, who are appointed throughout the ends of the earth, are in the mind of Jesus Christ.

->IV. Imitate the unity of the presbytery with the bishop.<-

Wherefore it is fitting for you to run together in harmony with the mind of the bishop, which is exactly what you are doing. For your presbytery, which is worthy of its name and worthy of God...

<columns>2</columns>

4) A Pauline expression; see 1 Corinthians 16:18 and 20. *Jacobson.*
5) Thus in the Latin and the ancient version. *Voss, Cotton, and Smith* read "will refresh" <note>original: "ἀναψύξει"</note> following the Interpolated version and supported by the Armenian. The future tense is preferable if it is seen as a prophecy. Compare 2 Timothy 1:16 and Acts 3:19.
6) "Fronto" is spelled with an omicron in the manuscripts, though here corrected to an omega.
7) Ignatius frequently uses this Apostolic phrase, which seems to be taken from St. Paul's Epistle to Philemon. *Jacobson.*
8) Jacobson and those who followed him omit the "is" <note>original: "ἐστι"</note>, despite the evidence of the manuscripts.
9) The words "in the same mind and in the same judgment, and that you all may say the same thing about the same subject" were omitted by the ancient translator and the Armenian version; some think they were wrongly inserted from 1 Corinthians 1:10. However, they exist in both manuscripts. I do not see why Ignatius, with these words fixed in his memory, could not have used them for a similar purpose. He frequently uses entire sentences from the New Testament mixed with his own.
10) The manuscripts and earlier editors read "commanding" <note>original: "ἐπιτασσόμενοι"</note>, but the Interpolated version and others read "being subject" <note>original: "ὑποτασσόμενοι"</note>. Our author joins this verb with both the genitive and dative cases. Compare chapter 5 below and the Letter to the Trallians, chapter 2.

<column-break/>

**Chapter III.** 1) From the third chapter, the Syriac version translates only a single sentence: "But since love does not allow me to be silent concerning you, I have therefore taken the initiative to exhort you, so that you may run together in harmony with the mind of God," and it connects this poorly with the end of the first chapter. This sentence fits much more aptly with the words immediately preceding it ("you are my teachers"). *Hefele.*
2) "The Name" <note>original: "τὸ ὄνομα"</note> used on its own can be found below in chapter 7 and in the Letter to the Philadelphians, chapter 10. *Jacobson.* It seems to me the words "of Jesus Christ" were suppressed because they were to be expressed in a different grammatical case immediately after.
3) Graziani translates: "and I speak to you as to my colleagues in the teaching office." Ignatius says the Ephesians are teachers just as he is, and since he had just affirmed he was a beginner in his training, he rightly desires to be confirmed in faith by the Ephesians as teachers.
4) That is: *to be anointed, to be encouraged, to be instructed, or to be prepared for a contest.* *Pearson.*
5) Jacobson believes Ignatius is looking back to the Epistle to Philemon, verses 8 and 9.
6) "Our [life]" <note>original: "ἡμῶν"</note> is the reading of Voss and the ancient version, supported by the Armenian and the Letter to the Trallians, chapter 1. The manuscripts read "your." Compare John 15:5 and Colossians 3:4.

...of Christ, together with Onesimus and Burrhus and Euplus and Fronto, through whom I have seen you all in the spirit of love. May I enjoy your company forever, if I am worthy. It is therefore fitting for you in every way to glorify Jesus Christ, who has glorified you, so that you may be made perfect in a single obedience, with the same mind and the same judgment, and that you all may say the same thing about the same subject, so that being subject to the bishop and the <term>presbytery</term> <note>The "presbytery" refers to the council of elders or priests who advised the bishop.</note> you may be sanctified in all things.

[The Father] of Jesus Christ, together with Onesimus, Burrhus, Euplus, and Fronto, through whom I have seen you all in love: so may I enjoy you forever, if I deserve it. It is therefore appropriate in all ways to glorify Jesus Christ, who glorifies you, so that you may be perfect in one obedience, with the same mind and the same judgment, and that you all may speak the same concerning the same things, so that being subject to the Bishop and the Presbytery you may be sanctified through all things.

### III. Without any pride—led by love—I exhort you to unity.

I do not give you orders as if I were someone of importance. For although I am a prisoner for the name of Christ, I am not yet perfect in Jesus Christ. For now I am only beginning to be a disciple, and I speak to you as my fellow-teachers <note>Latin: "condoctores"</note>. For I needed to be strengthened by you in faith, admonition, patience, and composure. But since love does not allow me to be silent concerning you, I have therefore taken the initiative to admonish you, so that you may be united in the mind of God. For even Jesus Christ, our inseparable life, is the mind of the Father, just as the bishops, established throughout the reaches of the earth, are in the mind of Jesus Christ.

\* III. I do not give you orders as if I were someone great; for although I am a prisoner for this name, I am not yet perfect in Jesus Christ. For now I begin to be a disciple, and I speak to you as my fellow-disciples <note>Latin: "condiscipulos"</note>. For I ought to have been trained by you in faith, admonition, patience, and long-suffering: but since love does not permit me to be silent about you, I have therefore stepped forward to warn you, that you may run together with the will of God. For even Jesus Christ, your life, is the will of the Father: just as the Bishops, established in their respective places, are in the will of Jesus Christ.

### IV. Imitate the unity of the presbytery with the bishop.

Wherefore it is fitting for you to run together in harmony with the mind of the bishop, which is exactly what you are doing. For your memorable council of elders <note>Latin: "presbyterium"</note>, being worthy of God, is so harmoniously fitted together...

\* IV. Wherefore it also becomes you to agree with the mind of the Bishop, just as you do: for that memorable college of your Presbyters, worthy of God...

# THE EPISTLE OF IGNATIUS TO THE EPHESIANS. IV. V. VI.

124

...worthy [of the name of the presbytery], is so joined to the bishop as strings are to a lyre. <note>original: χορδαὶ κιθάρᾳ</note> Because of this, Jesus Christ is sung within your harmony and symphonic love. And you, each and every one, should become a choir, so that being harmonious in concord and taking up the melody of God <note>original: χρῶμα Θεοῦ</note> in unity, you may sing with one voice through Jesus Christ to the Father, so that He may both hear you and recognize, through your good deeds, that you are members of His Son. It is useful, therefore, for you to remain in blameless unity, so that you may always partake of God.

---

->V. *The praise and benefit of this unity.*<-

For if I, in a short time, had such fellowship with your bishop—which was not merely human but spiritual—how much more do I call you blessed, who are united <note>original: ἐνκεκραμένους</note> to him as the church is to Jesus Christ, and as Jesus Christ is to the Father, so that all things may be harmonious in unity. Let no one be deceived: if anyone is not within the sanctuary, <note>Literally "inside the altar-place," referring to the community gathered around the bishop.</note> he is deprived of the bread of God. For if the prayer of one or two has such power, how much more that of the bishop and the whole church? He, therefore, who does not come together in the assembly is already arrogant and has judged himself. For it is written: "God resists the proud." <note>A reference to Proverbs 3:34, also cited in James 4:6 and 1 Peter 5:5.</note> Let us be careful, then, not to resist the bishop, so that we may be submissive to God.

---

->VI. *You should look upon the bishop as Christ himself. Onesimus praises you in this matter.*<-

And the more anyone sees a bishop keeping silence, the more let him revere him. For everyone whom the master of the house sends for his own stewardship <note>original: οἰκονομίαν</note>...

2) The same metaphor is also used in the *Epistle to the Philadelphians*, chapter 1, when speaking about their Bishop. [Archbishop] Ussher notes that the symbol of a lyre with tuned strings was a frequent and popular one among early Christians, especially on gemstones. Compare Clement of Alexandria, *The Instructor* <note>Latin: Paedagogus</note> III, 11: *“And let our seals be a dove, or a fish, or a ship running before the wind, or a musical lyre, which Polycrates used; or a ship's anchor, which Seleucus had engraved on his signet ring,” etc.*

3) Vossius restored the reading “you sing” <note>ᾄδετε</note> and “you partake” <note>μετέχετε</note> based on certain manuscripts. The conjunction “so that” <note>ἵνα</note> occurs with the indicative mood in the New Testament as well, such as in 1 Corinthians 4:6 and Galatians 4:17. See Winer's *Grammar*, 4th edition, p. 266.

4) Following the lead of Salvinius, I have written “he may recognize” <note>ἐπιγινώσκῃ</note> according to the old Latin Translation and the Armenian version, the former of which read: *“and may recognize Him, through whom you do well.”* In both [Greek] Codices, you find “recognizing” <note>ἐπιγινώσκων</note>. I suspect the adverb “well” <note>εὖ</note> may be a redundancy.

4) I had conjectured "to him" <note>αὐτῷ</note>, which I now see Petermann has restored from the Armenian; Codices C and L read "thus" <note>οὕτως</note>. A later editor changed this to "those hanging upon him."

5) [The article] "the" <note>ὁ</note> was added by Cotelerius and others following Vossius, but Codex C has "as" <note>ὡς</note>. # THE LETTER OF IGNATIUS TO THE EPHESIANS. IV. V. VI.

125

...to the bishop, as strings are to a lyre. <note>original: "chordae citharae"</note> Because of this, Jesus Christ is sung within your harmony and concordant love. But you also, each and every one, should become a choir, so that being harmonious in concord and receiving the melody of God in unity, you may sing with one voice through Jesus Christ to the Father; so that He may both hear you and recognize, by the good things you do, that you are members of His Son. It is useful, therefore, for you to remain in unblemished unity, so that you may always partake of God.

...is so joined and harmonized with the bishop as strings are to the lyre itself. For this reason, Jesus Christ is sung within your harmony and concordant love; and you, each and every one, constitute a single choir together, so that with the common harmony of your souls, receiving the melody <note>original: "chroma," a musical term for the color or character of a scale</note> of Christ in unity, you may sing with one voice through Jesus Christ to the Father. Therefore, it is useful for you to be in unblemished union, so that you may everywhere be partakers of God.

### V. *The praise and benefit of this unity.*

For if I, in a short span of time, formed such an association with your bishop—which was not merely human, but spiritual—how much more blessed do I judge you to be, who are joined to him as the church is to Jesus Christ, and as Jesus Christ is to the Father, so that all things may agree in unity. Let no one be deceived: unless one is within the sanctuary, <note>original: "intra altare," referring to the gathering place of the faithful around the altar</note> he is deprived of the bread of God. For if the prayer of one or two has such power, how much more that of the bishop and the whole church? He, therefore, who does not come to the assembly is already puffed up with pride, and has separated and judged himself. For it is written: "God resists the proud." <note>Proverbs 3:34</note> Let us strive, therefore, not to resist the bishop, so that we may be submissive to God.

* V. For if I, in a short span of time, joined in such fellowship with your Bishop—which was not merely human, but spiritual—I judge you more blessed, who are so mixed with him from among many, just as the Church is with Jesus Christ, and as Jesus Christ is with the Father, so that all things may agree in unity. Let no one be deceived; unless one is within the sanctuary, he is deprived of the bread of God. For if the prayer of one and another has such power, how much more that of the Bishop and the whole Church. He, therefore, who does not come together into one, is already looking down on others and has segregated himself. For it is written: God resists the proud. Let us strive, therefore, not to resist the Bishop, so that we may be subjects of God.

### IX. *You did not lend your ears to false teachers, you who are temples of God.*

I have learned, however, that some have passed through from there <note>original: "illic." Likely referring to travelers from other regions carrying heretical ideas.</note> who hold a distorted doctrine. You did not permit them to sow seeds among you, and you stopped your ears so as not to receive the things scattered by them. You are like stones of the Father’s temple, prepared for the building of God the Father, being lifted up to the heights by the hoist <note>original: "machinam." Ignatius uses a vivid construction metaphor here, imagining the Cross as a crane or siege engine lifting the believers like heavy stones into the heavenly structure.</note> of Jesus Christ, which is the Cross, using the Holy Spirit as a rope. Your faith is your upward pull, and love is the way that leads up to God. You are, therefore, all fellow-travelers: God-bearers and temple-bearers, Christ-bearers, and bearers of holy things <note>original: "Deiferi et Templiferi, Christiferi, Sanctiferi." These titles emphasize the early Christian belief that the believer's body is a literal dwelling place for the divine.</note>, adorned in every way with the commands of Jesus Christ. Because of you I exult, for I have been found worthy—through these words I write—to converse with you and to share your joy; because, concerning the other life <note>original: "ratione alterius vitae." Referring to the spiritual or eternal life as opposed to worldly existence.</note>, you love nothing except God alone.

* IX. I have learned, however, that some have turned aside there in passing, who hold a distorted doctrine. Do not allow them to sow those things among you at all, but stop your ears so that they do not receive what is being scattered. For you are stones of the Father’s temple, prepared for the building of God the Father, lifted up on high by the hoist of Jesus Christ, which is the Cross, using the Holy Spirit as a small rope. It is your faith that raises you up, and love is the path leading upward to God. You are, therefore, all God-bearers and temple-bearers, Christ-bearers and bearers of holy things, adorned in every way with the commands of Jesus Christ. And I rejoice that through these things I write, I have been permitted to speak with you and to share in your joy, because in the remaining life you love nothing except God alone.

### X. *Pray for others, be gentle, humble, etc.*

But also pray without ceasing for other people. For there is hope of repentance for them, that they may reach God. Therefore, allow them to be taught by you, at least by your works. Be gentle in response to their anger, humble in response to their boastful words; meet their blasphemies with your prayers, remain firm in faith against their errors, and be mild-mannered against their savage ways. Do not seek to imitate them in return—

* X. And you pray without ceasing for other men. For there is hope of repentance in them, that they may reach God. I ask that you allow them to become your disciples, even through your works. In the face of their anger, you be mild; in the face of their boasting, you be humble. Against their blasphemies, you offer prayers; against their errors, you be stable in faith; against their cruelty, you be gentle, and do not seek to imitate them in return.

...let us be found [to belong to Him] by our gentleness. Let us strive to be imitators of the Lord, even if someone is more wronged, or deprived, or set aside <note>original: "ἀθετηθῇ." This refers to being rejected or treated as of no account.</note>, so that no weed of the devil <note>Ignatius frequently uses the metaphor of "heresy" or "sin" as a weed planted by the devil among the good wheat of the church.</note> might be found among you; but in all purity and self-control, remain in Jesus Christ, both bodily and spiritually.

XI. *The times are final; let us fear the Lord; pray for me.*

These are the last times. Finally, let us be ashamed and let us fear the long-suffering of God, so that it does not become a judgment against us. Apart from Him, let nothing seem fitting to you. In Him I carry around these bonds <note>Ignatius was writing these letters while in chains, being transported to Rome for execution.</note>, which I call "spiritual pearls"; in these, may it be granted to me to rise again through your prayer, in which I hope always to be a participant. I desire this so that I may be found in the lot <note>The "lot" or "portion" refers to one's spiritual inheritance or station among the saints.</note> of the Christians of Ephesus, who have always been of one mind with the apostles through the power of Jesus Christ.

4) Uhlhorn: In *The Relationship of the Shorter Greek Recension of the Ignatian Epistles to the Syriac Translation* (page 40), he wishes to read: "not striving to imitate them in return, let us be found their brothers. But in gentleness, let us be imitators of [the Lord]."

5) The first edition reads: "who is more wronged, who is deprived, who is set aside, so that etc." Markland thought another reading should be substituted for this overly weak one, and set it apart in parentheses: "to be, (who has been more wronged? who has been deprived? who has been set aside?) so that etc." Pearson restored the passage this way: "by whom someone is more wronged etc." as a question. Hefele, following Markland's footsteps: "to be (who having been more wronged, who having been deprived, who having been set aside?) so that." This phrase in no way refers to Christ (for it would be entirely disconnected in the flow of thought and would smell of a later addition), but is to be referred solely to the imitators of Christ. Manuscripts C and L show: "to be; who is more wronged; who is deprived; who is set aside." I retain this reading and with a slight change write: "to be, even if someone is more wronged and deprived and set aside, so that." Nothing is more common in both manuscripts than the exchange of the diphthong "ei" and "ē." Compare 1 Corinthians 6:7. The words "so that... they will not be seen" at the end of chapter 14 are not translated by the Syriac version.

6) The same metaphor is used below in the *Letter to the Philadelphians* (chapter 3) and *To the Trallians* (chapter 6).

<column-break/>

7) Together with both manuscripts, I have restored "remain" [as a command] which was changed without cause by Jacobson into "that you may remain." The phrase beginning with "but in..." depends on the preceding "so that" only if forced.

8) The scribe of Manuscript C wishes the final words of the chapter to be understood as referring to the Eucharist.

Chapter XI. 1) No punctuation in Manuscripts C and L. Following the later expanded version, some punctuate after "finally." But the speaking habit of the Apostle Paul (1 Corinthians 7:29) suggests that the punctuation mark be placed *before* it.

2) I have distinguished with a larger punctuation mark after "two" according to Manuscripts C and L, from which Tischendorf copied for me: "let us love; one of the two; only," as it is in C. This escaped the notice of Vossius and Jacobson. Other editors more correctly placed a comma or a period after "two." Gallandi notes: In the *Damascene Parallel* fragments of Rupefucaldinus, there is a fragment that presents this passage thus: "let us love in the present life, only let us be found in Christ Jesus."

3) The word "as" should be supplied. Thus the infinitive "to be found" has something to depend on.

4) Vossius silently corrected the reading "to the" found in Manuscripts C and L. Perhaps "to this" should be written, with a period placed after "fitting." Compare Polycarp *To the Philippians* (chapter 1).

5) Thus Vossius with the later expanded version and the old Latin translator; Manuscripts C and L and Holstenius's copy read "in one." Perhaps it should be written "in one lot."

Chapter XII. 1) Manuscripts C and L read "having received mercy," whereas printed books before Jacobson, following Vossius, read "having been pitied."

### XI. *These are now the final times; let us fear the Lord; pray for me.*

The times are final; therefore, devoting ourselves to repentance, let us fear the long-suffering of God, lest it turn into judgment for us. For let us either fear the coming wrath or love the grace that is present—one of the two. Only let us be found in Christ Jesus for the living of the true life. Apart from Him, let nothing seem fitting to you, in whom I carry about these chains, these spiritual pearls <note>original: "spiritales margaritas." Ignatius poetically describes his prison shackles as precious gems, as they are the marks of his service to Christ.</note>, in which may it be my lot to rise again through your prayer, in which I hope always to be a participant, so that I may be found in the lot of the Ephesian Christians, who have always consented with the Apostles in the power of Jesus Christ.

*X. Moreover, the times are final; let us revere and fear the long-suffering of God, lest it become a judgment for us. For we shall either fear the future wrath or love the present grace. Only one of the two, so that we may be found in Jesus Christ for the obtaining of the true life. Apart from Him, let nothing befit you. In Him I carry about my chains, these spiritual pearls. In which may it be my lot to rise again by your prayers, in which let it be permitted to me to be always a participant, so that I may be found in the lot of the Ephesian Christians: who even now have always offered their assent to the Apostles in the power of Jesus Christ.

### XIII. *Meet more frequently for the worship of God.*

Seek, therefore, to meet together more frequently for the thanksgiving <note>original: "eucharistia." While this later became the specific name for the Sacrament, here it carries the broader sense of communal gratitude and worship.</note> of God and for His glory. For when you meet frequently in the same place, the powers of Satan are cast down, and the destruction he causes is dissolved by the harmony of your faith. Nothing is better than peace, by which all war—of both heavenly and earthly beings—is abolished.

### XIV. *Hold fast to faith and love, and show yourselves to be Christians by your works.*

None of these things are hidden from you, if you possess faith and love perfectly toward Jesus Christ, which are the beginning and the end of life. Faith is the beginning, and love is the end. These two, when they exist in unity, are of God; all other things follow toward moral excellence <note>original: "kalokagathia," a Greek concept of nobility and goodness combined.</note>. No one who professes faith commits sin, nor does anyone who possesses love hate. The tree is made manifest by its fruit; so those who profess to be Christians shall be seen by what they do. For the work [of a Christian] is not a matter of a current profession, but is found in the power of faith, if one perseveres until the end.

### XV. *Let us profess the Lord not only by speaking, but also by remaining silent.*

It is better to be silent and to be [a Christian], than to speak and not be one. It is good to teach, if the one speaking also acts. There is one teacher, who spoke and [it was done]...

...came to be; and even those things which he did in silence are worthy of the Father. He who truly possesses the word of Jesus is also able to hear his silence, so that he may be perfect, so that he may act through what he speaks, and be known through his silence. ## XVI. *Those who corrupt the faith with false doctrines shall go into eternal fire.*

Do not be led astray, my brothers. Those who corrupt families <note>original: "oikophthoroi" - literally "house-destroyers," referring to those who ruin households through adultery or moral corruption</note> shall not inherit the kingdom of God. If, then, those who acted according to the flesh in these things died, how much more if someone should corrupt the faith of God through evil teaching, for which Jesus Christ was crucified? Such a person, having become defiled, will go into the unquenchable fire, and likewise the one who listens to him.

## XVII. *Beware of the false doctrines of heretics.*

For this reason, the Lord received the ointment upon his head, so that he might breathe incorruption into the Church. Do not be anointed with the foul stench of the teaching of the ruler of this world <note>A common early Christian reference to the devil or the spiritual forces opposing God</note>; let him not lead you away as captives from the life set before you. And why are we not all wise, having received the knowledge of God, which is Jesus Christ? Why do we perish foolishly, being ignorant of the gift which the Lord has truly sent?

## XVIII. *The glory of the cross. The birth and baptism of Christ.*

Where is the wise man?

### XIX. Three mysteries to be proclaimed.

And the virginity of Mary and her giving birth were hidden from the ruler of this world <note>A reference to the devil.</note>, as was the death of the Lord; three mysteries to be loudly proclaimed <note>original: "mysteria clamoris."</note>, which were performed in the silence of God. How then was he manifested to the ages? A star shone in heaven, surpassing all the stars in brilliance, and its light was unspeakable, and its novelty struck everyone with wonder. All the remaining stars, together with the sun and moon, formed a choir for this star; but it spread its light over all. And there was a disturbance, wondering from where this novelty, so unlike them, had come. Consequently, all magic was dissolved, and every bond of malice was abolished; ignorance was destroyed, and the ancient kingdom was ruined, when God was manifested in human form for the newness of eternal life. What had been prepared by God from the beginning now took its start. From that point, all things were moved, because he was planning the abolition of death.

# ->IGNATIUS TO THE MAGNESIANS.<-¹

Ignatius, who is also called Theophoros <note>The name "Theophoros" literally means "God-bearer."</note>, to the church blessed in the grace of God the Father, in Jesus Christ our savior, in whom I salute the church which is in Magnesia near the Maeander <note>A river in Asia Minor, famous for its winding path.</note>, and I wish you most abundant joy in God the Father and in Jesus Christ.

## 1. *The reason for the letter and pious prayers.*

Having known the great orderliness of your love according to God, I rejoiced and chose <note>original: "προειλόμην"</note> to speak to you in the faith of Jesus Christ. For having been deemed worthy of a most God-befitting name <note>likely referring to "Theophoros" or "prisoner of Christ"</note>, in these chains which I carry about, I sing the praises of the churches, in which I pray for a union of the flesh and spirit of Jesus Christ—who is our life forever—and of faith and love, to which nothing is preferred; and what is more important, of Jesus and the Father. In Him, if we endure all the outrages of the ruler of this age <note>A common early Christian reference to the devil or the spirit of the world.</note> and escape them, we shall attain unto God.

## II. *I rejoice in your delegates.*

1) Jacobson added "IGNATIUS" based on the Latin manuscript (L); the Curetonian (C) also acknowledges the name, though it was neglected by Vossius and other editors. Yet it is necessary at the head of any Epistle so inscribed, as it would not have been sent here or there without the sender's name. The Syriac translator did not translate this Epistle. However, one should consult Cureton (pp. 29. 47.) concerning passages from it quoted here and there by Syriac writers. A complete Armenian version exists. — Following the example of the Ephesians, the Christian citizens of Magnesia, located near the Maeander in Ionia, sent to Smyrna a delegation consisting of Damas the bishop, the presbyters Bassus and Apollonius, and Sotion the deacon, to visit and console Ignatius (chapters 2 and 15). For this reason, their charity is praised as known through the bishop, whose youth he warns no one to despise (chapters 1. 3–7). They must carefully flee those who observe the Mosaic law along with the gospel of Christ (chapters 8–11). The exhortatory part of the Epistle follows (chapters 12–15). Here, excellent proofs of the writer’s humility are put forward; but the Magnesians also, although they are "Christ-bearers" and "cry out for God" <note>original: "χριστοφόροι et θεοῦ gemant"</note> (chapter 14), should beware lest they be puffed up with arrogance, but rather should strive for humility

Ignatius, also known as Theophorus <note>The name "Theophorus" means "God-bearer" in Greek.</note>, to the church blessed by the grace of God the Father in Jesus Christ our savior; in his name I greet the church which is in Magnesia near the Maeander <note>A river in Asia Minor famous for its winding course, from which we get the word "meander."</note>, and I wish you the fullest health and salvation in God the Father and in Jesus Christ.

<header>EPISTLE OF IGNATIUS TO THE MAGNESIANS. II. III. IV. V.</header>

...of my fellow-servant, the <term>deacon</term> <note>A 'diakonos' or minister who assists the elders.</note> Sotion, whose company I hope to enjoy; for he is subject to the bishop as to the grace of God, and to the <term>presbytery</term> <note>The council of elders or priests within the local church.</note> as to the law of Jesus Christ.

### III. Honor your youthful bishop.

And it is also fitting for you not to take advantage of the bishop’s age, but according to the power of God the Father, to pay him all reverence. Just as I have known the holy presbyters also to do—they have not looked upon his seemingly youthful state <note>original: "νεωτερικὴν τάξιν" (neoteriken taxin), literally "youthful order" or "rank."</note>, but as men wise in God, they defer to him. Yet it is not really to him they defer, but to the Father of Jesus Christ, the Bishop of all. For the honor, then, of Him who willed us <note>original: "θελήσαντος ἡμᾶς" (thelesantos hemas), referring to God's will and love.</note>, it is fitting to obey without any hypocrisy. For it is not that a man deceives this bishop who is seen, but rather he attempts to cheat the One who is invisible. In such a case, the matter is not with flesh <note>Meaning, not with a mere human being.</note>, but with God, who knows the hidden things.

### IV. Some act wrongly without the bishop.

It is right, therefore, not only to be called Christians, but also to be so in reality. For there are some who call a man "bishop," yet do everything without him. Such people do not appear to me to be of good conscience, because they do not gather together validly according to the commandment.

### V. Death is set before such people, because they do not have love, the "mark" of Christians, and do not die to their own desires.

Since then all things have an end, and two choices are set before us together—death and life—and each person is about to go to his own place... <note>A phrase used in the New Testament (Acts 1:25) to describe a person's final destiny.</note>

### III. *Honor your youthful bishop.*

But it also becomes you not to treat the bishop’s age with too much familiarity, but, out of respect for the power of God the Father, to pay him all reverence. This is just as I have known the holy <term>presbyters</term> to do; they do not take advantage of his manifest youthful condition, but as men wise in God, they yield to him—or rather, not to him, but to the Father of Jesus Christ, the bishop of all. Therefore, for the honor of Him who desired him, it is right for us to obey without any hypocrisy; for a man does not merely deceive this visible bishop, but attempts to cheat the One who is invisible. Such a deed is not a matter concerning flesh <note>Meaning, a matter of human relations.</note>, but concerns God, who knows the hidden things.

* III. It is not fitting for you to take advantage of the age of the Bishop, but according to the power of God the Father, to show him all reverence. I know that the holy Presbyters also do this, not taking advantage because his rank appears somewhat new <note>original: "recentior ille ordo," likely referring to the bishop's youth or recent appointment.</note>, but as men wise in God, they submit to him; yet not so much to him as to the Father of Jesus Christ, the Bishop of everyone. Therefore, for the honor of Him who so willed it, it is right for us to obey without any pretense, since one does not just deceive this visible Bishop, but cheats the invisible one. The reason for such a matter does not look to the flesh, but to God, who knows secrets.

---

### IV. *Some act wrongly without the bishop.*

It is right, therefore, not only to be called Christians, but also to be so; just as some people speak of a bishop by name, but do everything without him. Such people do not seem to me to be endowed with a good conscience, because they do not gather together firmly according to the commandment.

* IV. It is proper, then, that we should not only be called Christians, but truly be so. For just as some use the name of the Bishop, but do everything without him, such people do not seem to me to be endowed with a good conscience at all, because they do not gather with solid firmness according to the commandment.

---

### V. *Death is set before such people, because they do not have the mark of Christians, which is love, and do not die to their desires.*

Since things are coming to an end, these two also are set before us at once: death and life; and each person is going to go to his own place. Just as

* V. Since, therefore, things have an end, these two things are also imminent: death and life; and each person is about to depart to his own place.

### VIII. Beware of the false doctrines of those who follow Jewish customs.

Do not be led astray by strange doctrines <note>original: "ἑτεροδοξίαις," the root of the word "heterodoxy."</note> nor by old fables, which are useless. For if we continue to live according to the Jewish Law until now, we admit that we have not received grace. For the most divine prophets lived according to Christ Jesus. This is why they were persecuted; they were inspired by His grace so that those who were disobedient might be fully convinced that there is one God, who manifested Himself through Jesus Christ His Son, who is His eternal Word <note>original: "Logos."</note>, not proceeding from Silence <note>original: "Sige." This term was a technical one in Gnostic theology, referring to a divine "Silence" from which the Word emerged. Ignatius uses it here to argue that Christ, as the Word, has always existed with God.</note>, and who in all things was well-pleasing to the One who sent Him.

### X. Do not follow Jewish customs. <note>original Latin: "Nolite iudaizare."</note>

Let us not, therefore, be insensible to His kindness. <term>Kindness</term> <note>original: "chrēstotētos." 6) *By whom* — Manuscripts C and L read "from whom." See Matthew 27:52.
Chapter X. 1) *Kindness* — Found in manuscripts C and L. This seems to reference Saint Paul’s Epistle to the Romans, chapter 2, verse 4.
2) *Should He imitate* — Various manuscripts offer different spellings of "imitate" (*mimēsētai*, *mimēsetai*). Compare with Psalm 130:3.
3) In Manuscript C, the words "For whoever is called by another name more than this" are repeated in the margin. The scholar Graziani translates this as: "Since anyone who is called by another name, outside of this, is not of God."
4) *Discard* — Manuscripts C and L use "Discard" (*Hyperthesthe*); other versions use "Put away" (*Apothesthe*). Compare with 1 Corinthians 5:7.
5) The author pursues the metaphor,

<column-break/>

as is his custom; for a foul odor comes from rot, as noted by the scholar Pearson. The manuscript shows "impulse" (*hormēs*), but I have admitted Vossius’s certain correction "scent" (*osmēs*) into the text, following Ussher, Pearson, and Smith. Compare the Epistle to the Ephesians, chapter 17: "the stench of [false] teaching." Vossius also suggests "you will be convicted" (*elenchthēsesthe*) as an emendation, but the Medicean Codex actually contains this reading. Manuscript C also reads "you will be convicted by your impulse."
6) *To speak* — Manuscripts C and L read "to speak" (*lalein*), not "to call" (*kalein*) as was published in the Cotelerius edition.
7) I have written "but" (*all’*) following manuscripts C and L.
8) The scholar Bunsen thought this should be "to whom" (*hō*).
9) Compare John 10:16. I might conjecture "resounded together" (*synēchthē*) in an internal sense. Compare Sophocles, *Oedipus at Colonus*, 1500.
Chapter XI. 1) This means: "not that I have known some of you to follow Jewish customs."
2) *Be on guard* — Found in manuscripts C and L.
3) *To be fully convinced* — Noted by the scholar Heysius in manuscripts C and L.

...living a new life, in which also our life rose up through Him and His death; which some deny: through whom we received the mystery of believing, and therefore we endure, that we may be found to be disciples of Jesus Christ, our only master: how shall we be able to live without Him, whose disciples even the Prophets were in spirit, as they expected Him as master? And so He whom they rightly expected, being present, raised them from the dead.

### X. Do not follow Jewish customs. <note>original: "Nolite iudaizare." This refers to the practice of "Judaizing"—Christians continuing to observe the Mosaic Law as a requirement for salvation.</note>

Far be it from us, then, not to be moved by His kindness. For if He were to imitate us according to what we do, we would already be lost. Therefore, having become His disciples, let us learn to live according to Christianity. <note>original: "Christianismus." This is one of the earliest historical uses of the term "Christianity" as a distinct system of life and belief compared to "Judaism."</note> For whoever is called by any name besides this is not of God. Cast away, therefore, the evil leaven, which is old and sour, and be transformed into the new leaven, which is Jesus Christ. Be salted in Him, so that none of you may be corrupted, since you will be convicted by your scent. <note>Ignatius uses the metaphor of salt as a preservative against the "rot" of false teaching and the "scent" of one's life as a witness to their true faith.</note> It is absurd to speak the name of Jesus Christ and to follow Jewish customs. For Christianity did not believe in Judaism, but Judaism in Christianity, so that every tongue believing in God might be gathered together.

<column-break/>

* X. Therefore, let us not with a dull mind neglect His kindness. For if He should punish us by our own example according to what we do, we would no longer survive. Wherefore, having become His disciples, let us learn to live by the Christian rite. For whoever is called by any name other than this, he is not of God. Cast away therefore this evil leaven, obsolete and sour, and be transformed into the new leaven, which is Jesus Christ. Be sprinkled with salt in Him, lest anyone rot among you, because the force of your fervor will prove you. It is absurd to call upon Jesus Christ and yet follow Jewish customs. For Christianity did not believe in Judaism, but Judaism in Christianity: just as every tongue believing in God has been joined together.

### XI. I write these things not to rebuke you, but to forewarn you.

I write these things, my beloved, not because I have known that any of you are so minded, but, as one who is lesser than you, I desire you to be on your guard, so that you do not fall into the hooks of empty doctrine. Instead, be fully certain of the birth, the passion, and the resurrection, which happened during the time of the governorship <note>The text likely refers to Pontius Pilate, a common historical marker in early creeds to ground Jesus’s life in history rather than myth.</note>

Chapter XV. 1) These were not Ephesians who lived in Smyrna for the sake of business, but those who had come from Ephesus with Bishop Onesimus to greet Ignatius.
2) Thus Vossius follows the "interpolated" text, in whose version the word is *divided*, as shown in manuscripts C and L. Compare the Letter to the Ephesians ch. 3 and the Letter to the Trallians ch. 1.

1) This is the title as given in manuscripts C and L. — Driven by a love equal to that of other cities, the brothers living in Tralles sent Bishop Polybius to Smyrna (ch. 1. 12.) to congratulate Ignatius on his chains. Having learned of the natural sincerity of the Trallians' minds and their faith from the bishop himself, Ignatius celebrates them with praise; he exhorts them, as is his custom, toward obedience to the bishop, the elders, and the deacons, as well as toward mutual love and unity (ch. 2. 3.). He states that he has need of humility (ch. 4.); although he could hand down heavenly precepts, he affirms he is but a disciple (ch. 5.). He warns: guard yourselves against erroneous doctrines, especially from the <term>Docetists</term><note>Early heretics who believed Christ's physical body and suffering were only an illusion.</note>, by cultivating gentleness, faith, and charity (ch. 6–11.). I greet you together with the delegates of the churches present in Smyrna; remain in faith and love, and be mindful of me and the church of Syria in your prayers (ch. 12. 13.).

### II. *Be subject to the bishop, the presbyters, and the deacons.*

For when¹ you are subject to the bishop² as to Jesus Christ, you appear to me to be living not according to human standards,³ but according to Jesus Christ, who died for our sake,⁴ so that by believing in his death, you might escape dying. It is therefore necessary, just as you do, to do nothing without the bishop; but be subject⁵ also to the <term>presbytery</term><note>The council of elders or priests within a local church.</note>, as to the apostles of Jesus Christ, our hope, in whom we shall be found living.⁶ It is also necessary⁷ that the deacons, being ministers of the <term>mystery</term>⁸<note>original: *mysteriou*. In this context, it refers to the sacred truths or the Sacraments of the faith.</note> of Jesus Christ, please everyone in every way. For they are not deacons of food and drink, but servants of the church of God. It is therefore necessary for them to guard against accusations⁹ as they would against fire.

### III. *Honor the deacons, the bishop, and the presbyters.*

Similarly, let everyone respect the deacons as the commandment of Jesus Christ, and the bishop as Jesus Christ, who is the Son of the Father,¹ and the presbyters as the council of God and as the bond² of the apostles. Without these, a group is not called a church. Regarding these matters, I am persuaded that you are so disposed. For I have received the pattern of your love, and I have it with me³ in the person of your bishop, whose very demeanor—

For he says that there ought not to be anyone whom the deacons do not please in all ways. For they are not ministers of meats and drinks, but ministers of the mysteries of God, or the Sacraments." He says, therefore, that deacons ought to be immune from all sin; and as becomes them, they should avoid crimes like fire: while others ought to treat such men with due reverence. I wonder, however, at Antiochus, who cites these words of Ignatius in Sermon 124, but changed them so that what is said here of deacons is attributed to presbyters—unless the passage in his work is incomplete or some words have fallen out. The Armenian seems to have read "fellow-initiates" <note>original: *symmystas*</note>.
9) Codex L reads "guard yourselves" <note>original: *phylassesthe*</note>; Codex C reads the same as above.

Ignatius argues that a church cannot exist without these three offices, which represent the authority of Christ and the Apostles.</summary>

->II. *Be subject to the bishop, the presbyters, and the deacons.*<-

<columns>
These people even mix Jesus Christ with their own poisons, speaking things that are unworthy of belief; they are like those who give a deadly drug mixed with honey-wine, <note>original: "vino mulso". ### VII. Guard yourselves against heretics.

Guard yourselves, therefore, against such people. This will happen if you are neither puffed up with pride nor torn away from God, Jesus Christ, and the bishop, and the commands of the Apostles. He who is within the sanctuary <term>sanctuary: literally "the place of the altar" (altare); used here to symbolize the fellowship and assembly of the church.</term> is pure; [but he who is outside is not pure]; that is, he who does anything without the bishop, the council of elders, and the deacons, is not pure in his conscience.

He who is within the sanctuary is pure; that is, he who does anything without the Bishop, the Council of Elders, and the Deacon, this man is by no means pure in his conscience.

### VIII. Be armed against the devil's snares with gentleness, faith, and love.

I do not write these things because I have discovered any such problem among you; rather, I wish to forearm you, as my most beloved children, because I foresee the snares of the devil. Therefore, putting on gentleness, renew yourselves in faith—which is the flesh of the Lord—and in love—which is the blood of Jesus Christ. <note>Ignatius often uses "flesh" and "blood" to describe the spiritual realities of faith and love, mirroring the language of the Eucharist.</note> Let none of you hold a grudge against his neighbor. Give no occasions to the Gentiles, so that because of a few foolish individuals, the multitude joined in God may not be slandered. <meta>This page continues Ignatius’s polemic against false teachers. Following his warning in Chapter VIII to remain rooted in faith and love, he now provides the specific "test" of orthodoxy: a firm belief in the physical reality of Christ’s birth, life, death, and resurrection, directed specifically against the Docetists who claimed Jesus only "seemed" to be human.</meta>

<page-num>160</page-num>
->### IGNATIUS’S LETTER TO THE TRALLIANS. IX. X. XI.<-

### IX. Do not listen to those who speak without Christ. The History of Christ.

Be deaf, therefore, when anyone speaks to you apart from Jesus Christ, who was of the family of David, and of Mary; who was **truly** born, both ate and drank, was **truly** persecuted under Pontius Pilate, was **truly** crucified and died, while those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth looked on. He was also **truly** raised from the dead, his Father raising him up; in the same way, his Father will also raise us up who believe in him through Christ Jesus, apart from whom we do not have the true life.

### X. If Christ did not truly suffer, I bear these chains in vain.

But if, as some who are atheists—that is, unbelievers—claim, he suffered only in appearance <note>Ignatius uses the Greek word *dokein* ("to seem"), from which the "Docetist" heresy takes its name. These thinkers believed Christ was a pure spirit who only appeared to have a body.</note> (they themselves being only an appearance!), why then am I in bonds? Why do I pray to fight with wild beasts? If his suffering was a sham, then I die for nothing. Am I then speaking falsely about the Lord?

### XI. Flee the deadly plantings of the Docetists.

Flee, therefore, from these wicked offshoots, which produce death-bearing fruit; if anyone tastes it, they die immediately. For these are not the Father’s planting. <note>This echoes Matthew 15:13: "Every plant which my heavenly Father has not planted will be uprooted."</note> For if they were, they would appear as branches of the Cross, and their fruit would be incorruptible; through the Cross, by his suffering, he calls you who are his members. A head cannot be born without members, since God promises a union, which is himself.

---

<columns>2</columns>

2) "And" was added by Jacobson from 'L', now confirmed by 'C'.

3) Smith conjectured this reading based on the ancient translator; 'C' and 'L' read: "according to the likeness; who also [raises] us who believe." Vossius has "as" instead of "who" with the same word order. I agree with Markland that the words "his Father in Christ Jesus" should be removed, and following Petermann, the pronoun changed to read: "who also in the same likeness will raise us who believe in him, apart from whom we do not have the true life." Compare 1 Corinthians 15:49. Bunsen thought it should be written: "who also... will thus raise [his Father] in Christ."

4) Compare John 3:36; 5:40; 14:6; 20:31.

**Chapter X.** 1) Thus 'C' and 'L'; Hefele reads *Ara* as a question, taking the preceding part as an inquiry. — Vossius emends with a slight change

<column-break/>

(the word *oun*). But the reading of the Medicean Codex, which the ancient translator follows, seems correct to retain; especially if the words are taken as a question: *Is it not so, that if Christ (as they blaspheme) suffered only in appearance, I myself, by dying, would be portraying the Lord Christ with this grand lie?* — Smith. The Interpolator <note>A later writer who expanded Ignatius's letters in the 4th century.</note> writes: "I die then in vain; do I then also lie against the Cross of the Lord?" Aldrich, followed by Hornemann, prefers the question mark at "I die": "Surely I do not invent a lie about the Lord." Ruchat translates: *It is then uselessly that I die. I lie then in favor of the Lord.* Wocher: *So do I die in vain? So do I even speak falsely of the Lord?* Chevallier, following Wake: *Then do I die in vain. Verily I lie not against the Lord.* Ignatius here imitates the Apostle Paul discussing the resurrection of Christ.

<meta>This page continues Ignatius’s forceful defense of the physical reality of Jesus’s life and death. Having previously warned the Trallians to stay united with their bishop, he now addresses the specific "Docetist" heresy—the belief that Christ’s body was an illusion—by emphasizing that Christ was "truly" born, "truly" suffered, and "truly" rose again.</meta>
