->THE LETTER OF IGNATIUS TO THE SMYRNAEANS. X. XI.<-

### X. *You have kindly received my companions; your reward will not fail.*

You did well in receiving Philo and Rheus Agathopus <note>original: "Ῥέον Ἀγαθόπουν"</note> as servants of Christ God, for they followed me for the sake of the Word of God. They also give thanks to the Lord on your behalf, because you refreshed them in every way. Nothing you have done for them will be lost to you. My spirit is a sacrifice for you <note>original: "Ἀντίψυχον ὑμῶν," meaning a ransom or a substitute for your souls</note>, as are my chains, which you did not despise nor were you ashamed of. Neither will the perfect faith, Jesus Christ, be ashamed of you.

### XI. *Send an envoy to the people of Antioch for the sake of the peace restored there.*

Your prayer has reached the church in Antioch of Syria. From there, bound in these most godly chains, I greet everyone. I am not worthy to be from there, being the very last of them; yet by the will [of God] I was deemed worthy—not by my own conscience <note>meaning his own merit or awareness of worthiness</note>, but by the grace of God. I pray that this grace may be given to me in perfection, so that through your prayer I may attain to God. Therefore, so that your work may be perfect both on earth and in heaven, it is fitting for your church, for the honor of God, to appoint a "God-envoy" <note>original: "θεοπρεσβύτην," a sacred ambassador</note> to go as far as Syria to rejoice with them, because they are now at peace, have regained their proper stature, and have had their own corporate body <note>original: "σωματεῖον," referring to the restoration of their communal organization</note> restored to them. It seemed to me, therefore, a worthy thing to send one of your people with a letter, so that he might join in glorifying the [peace]...

# THE LETTER OF IGNATIUS TO THE SMYRNAEANS. X. XI.

### X. *You have kindly received my companions; your reward will not fail.*

You have kindly received my companions; your reward will not fail you.

In receiving Philo and Rheus Agathopus, who followed me for the sake of God, as ministers <note>original: "ministros," referring to those who serve the church</note> of Christ God, you have done well. They also give thanks to the Lord on your behalf, because you refreshed them in every way. None of these things will be lost to you. In return, may my spirit and my chains—which you did not despise and of which you were not ashamed—be a refreshment for you. Nor will the perfect faith, Jesus Christ, be ashamed of you.

* X. You did well in receiving Philo, Rheus, and Agathopus as my companions in the word of God, just as you would receive ministers of Christ God. They also give thanks to the Lord for you, because you revived them in every possible way. Nothing of your benefit to them will perish; for I, in turn, am ready to offer my spirit and my chains for your soul <note>original: "pro anima vestra," suggesting a spiritual sacrifice or dedication</note>, which you did not look down upon, nor did you blush because of them. Therefore, our perfect faith, Jesus Christ, will not be ashamed of you either.

### XI. ->*Send an envoy to the people of Antioch for the sake of the peace restored there.*<-

Your prayer has reached the church which is in Antioch of Syria; from there, bound in chains most pleasing to God, I greet everyone. I am not worthy to hold that office of bishop, being the very least among them; yet the will [of God] has deemed me worthy, not according to my own conscience <note>meaning his own sense of merit</note>, but by the grace of God. I pray that this grace may be given to me in perfection, so that through your prayer I may attain to God. So that your work may now be made complete before God and men, it is fitting for the honor of God that your church elect a sacred envoy <note>original: "sacrum legatum," a representative of the church</note> who, when he arrives in Syria, may congratulate them that they have achieved peace, and have regained their greatness, and that their corporate body <note>original: "corpus," referring to the organized structure of the local church</note> has been restored to them. Therefore, it seemed a worthy thing to me that you should send someone of your own with a letter, who might join them in glorifying the tranquility which, according to God’s will—

* XI. Your prayer has reached the Church of Antioch in Syria, from which I, bound in most God-worthy chains, greet everyone. I am not worthy to be counted among their number, being the very last of them; yet by [God’s] will I was held worthy—not from my own conscience, but by the grace of God. I pray that this grace may be granted to me in perfection, so that through your prayer I may reach God. Therefore, so that your work may be perfect both on earth and in heaven, it is fitting for the honor of God that your Church elect a sacred envoy to travel to Syria to rejoice with them that they have obtained peace, regained their greatness, and that their little body <note>original: "corpusculum," a diminutive or endearing term for the congregation</note> has been restored to them. Therefore, it seemed to me a worthwhile task that you send one of your own with a letter, so that he may glorify God together with them for the tranquility—

# THE LETTER OF IGNATIUS TO THE SMYRNAEANS. XI. XII. XIII.

...calm, and that through your prayer I have already reached a safe harbor. Since you are perfect, have perfect thoughts; for to those who desire to do good, God is ready to provide.

## XII. Greetings.

The love of the brothers in Troas greets you, from where I also write to you by the hand of Burrhus, whom you sent with me along with the Ephesians, your brothers; he has refreshed me in every way. I wish that everyone would imitate him, for he is a model <term>exemplar: a pattern or standard of behavior</term> of God’s service. Grace will reward him in all things. I greet your bishop, who is worthy of God, and your most venerable council of elders <note>original: "presbyterion"</note>, and my fellow-servants <note>original: "sundoulous"</note> the deacons, and each of you individually and all together, in the name of Jesus Christ, and in His flesh and blood, in His passion and resurrection, both physical and spiritual, in the unity of God and of you. Grace, mercy, peace, and patience be with you always.

## XIII. Greetings.

I greet the households of my brothers, along with their wives and children, and the virgins who are called widows <note>In the early church, the "Order of Widows" was a recognized group of women dedicated to prayer and service; Ignatius here notes that even some who had never married—virgins—were counted in this group</note>. Farewell to you in the power of the Spirit. Philo, who is with me, greets you. I greet the household of Tavia, and I pray that she may be established in faith and love, both physical and spiritual. I greet Alce, a name very dear to me, and the incomparable Daphnus, and Eutecnus, and all of you by name. Farewell in the grace of God.

# THE EPISTLE OF IGNATIUS TO POLYCARP. I.
<columns>2</columns>

## **IGNATIUS TO POLYCARP.**¹

Ignatius, who is also called Theophorus <note>The name means "God-bearer" or "one carried by God."</note>, to Polycarp, bishop of the church of the Smyrnaeans,² or rather, who is himself overseen <note>original: "episkopēmenō"</note>³ by God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ: abundant greetings.

### I. Praise and exhortation.

Appreciating your godly mind,⁴ which is founded as if upon an unshakeable rock, I give exceeding glory to God,⁵ having been deemed worthy of seeing your blameless face,⁶ in which may I have joy⁷ in God. I exhort you by the grace with which you are clothed,⁹ to press forward¹⁰ in your course, and to exhort all people so that they may be saved. Maintain¹¹ your position with all care, both physical and spiritual. Give thought to unity, for nothing is better than that. Bear with all people, as the Lord also bears with you. Suffer all in love, just as you already do. Devote yourself to unceasing prayers.¹² Ask for more understanding than you already have. Be watchful, possessing a spirit that does not sleep.¹⁴ Speak to each person individually according to the help¹⁵ of God. Bear the infirmities of all, like a perfect athlete. Where there is more¹⁶ labor, there is much gain.

---

1) This title is from the CL and the copy <note>original: "apographum"</note> of Holstenius. — Ignatius had to depart suddenly from Troas to Neapolis in Macedonia (chapter 8). Before proceeding there, he wrote this Letter to Polycarp, the bishop of the Smyrnaeans, which from beginning to end is a pastoral exhortation. Indeed, he discusses at length those things which are becoming to and adorn a bishop and his flock.
There are some who call this Letter into doubt, moved chiefly by the fact that Ignatius, after writing to the Smyrnaeans, also wrote to their bishop separately. However, Eusebius stands in opposition to this view, who in his *Church History* (III, 36) brings forward testimony from Polycarp’s own Letter to the Philippians: "You and Ignatius wrote to me," etc. Jerome, Chrysostom, Antiochus, John of Damascus, and other ancient writers also stand in opposition, as they clearly left record that the bishop of Antioch sent a Letter to Polycarp. In our own age, those doubts were mostly refuted by Huther (in Illgen’s *Journal for Historical Theology*, Vol. XI, p. 62 ff.) and Düsterdieck, *On the Authenticity of the Ignatian Epistles*, etc., p. 42 ff. A Syriac version of the Letter exists in two manuscripts, the first of which is said to have been written in the sixth century, the other in the eighth. Cureton published it from the older one, illustrating the text with various readings brought from the more recent one. The version of both Syriac manuscripts extends to the end of the sixth chapter, corresponding almost exactly to the Greek text. Only two sen-

<column-break/>

tences taken from the remaining part are added there.
2) "To Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna" in the Syriac; "To Polycarp, bishop of the church of the city of Smyrna" in the Armenian.
3) A beautiful correction <note>original: "epanorthosis"</note> and plainly Apostolic. Galatians 4:9. Pearson. Vairlenius, in order to render this wordplay <note>original: "paronomasiam"</note> as much as possible, gave in his version: "to the overseer, or rather him who is overseen by God." Ignatius uses such wordplay in *To the Trallians* chapters 5, 10; *To the Romans* 8; *To the Smyrnaeans* chapters 2, 5, 10; *To Polycarp* chapter 3; from which the Sacred Writers did not shrink, e.g., Paul in Philemon 11, 20. *Iac.* With both manuscripts I have restored "overseen" <note>original: "episkopēmenō"</note>, which Vossius already expressed. Jacobson changed that reading to "having been overseen" <note>original: "epeskopēmenō"</note> on the authority, as he writes, of Cotelerius. But neither the first edition of Cotelerius, nor the second or third by Le Clerc, shows anything other than "or rather overseen."
4) Gallicciolli translates: "Approving of your divine sentiments." This refers to that phrase in *To the Romans* chapter 7: "my mind which is toward God."
5) "I give exceeding glory [to God]" in the Syriac and Armenian. Already Holstenius: "I extol God with the highest praises."
6) While I was a captive at Smyrna.
7) A manner of speaking familiar to Ignatius. Compare *Letter to the Ephesians* chapter 2; *To the Magnesians* chapters 2 and 12; *To the Romans* chapter 5.
8) Smith, against the authority of both manuscripts and the Interpolator, adds "of God" from the old interpretation. Neither the Syriac nor the Armenian support this word.

->THE EPISTLE OF IGNATIUS TO POLYCARP. I.<-

### TO POLYCARP.

Ignatius, who is also called Theophorus <note>The name means "God-bearer."</note>, to Polycarp, bishop of the church of the Smyrnaeans, who himself rather has for his bishop God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ: abundant greetings.

### * THE EPISTLE OF IGNATIUS TO POLYCARP.

* Ignatius, who is also called Theophorus, to Polycarp, Bishop of the Church of Smyrna, or rather [who is] under the Oversight of God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ: abundant greetings.

### I. Praise and exhortation.

Approving your godly mind, as if it were founded upon an unshakeable rock, I lift up my voice in the highest praise, because I have been deemed worthy of seeing your holy face; may I always be able to enjoy it in God. I beseech you by the grace with which you are clothed, that you may press forward in your course, and exhort everyone so that they may be saved. Defend your position with every care, both physical and spiritual. Give thought to unity, for nothing is better than that. Bear with all people, as the Lord also bears with you. Suffer all in love, just as you already do. Devote yourself to unceasing prayers. Ask for more wisdom than you already have. Be watchful, possessing a spirit that does not sleep. Speak to each person individually as God helps you. Bear the sicknesses of all, like a perfect athlete. Where there is more labor, there is much gain.

* I. Approving your mind which is established in God, as if upon an unshakeable rock, I lift up my voice in the highest praise to God, because I have merited to see your blameless face, in which I hope to find joy in God. I beseech you by the grace with which you are clothed, that you may advance your course, and exhort everyone so that they may be saved. Claim and protect your position with all diligence, both bodily and spiritual. Give thought to unity, for nothing is better than that. Carry everyone, just as the Lord carries you; endure all in love, just as you already do. Devote yourself to prayers without ceasing. Ask for a greater understanding than you have. Be watchful, having a spirit that does not sleep. Speak to each person according to the help of God. Bear the infirmities of all, like a perfect athlete. Where there is more labor, there is more profit.

9) He imitates St. Paul, who often uses the word <term>ἐνδύω</term> <note>original: "endyō" — to clothe or put on</note> and <term>ἐνδύομαι</term> <note>original: "endyomai" — to be clothed</note> in this sense, for example in Ephesians 6:14 and Colossians 3:12. *Pearson.*

10) Compare the phrases <term>πληροῦν τὸν δρόμον</term> <note>original: "plēroun ton dromon" — to fulfill the course</note> in Acts 13:25 and <term>τελειοῦν τὸν δρόμον</term> <note>original: "teleioun ton dromon" — to finish the course</note> in Acts 20:24 and 2 Timothy 4:7. *Pearson.* In the C manuscript, it reads <term>προσθῆναι</term> <note>original: "prosthēnai" — to add to or increase</note>.

->THE EPISTLE OF IGNATIUS TO POLYCARP. II. III. IV.<-

## II. Continuation of exhortations.

If you love good disciples <insert>only</insert>, it is no credit to you; rather, subdue the more troublesome ones with gentleness. Not every wound is healed by the same plaster. Soothe the <term>paroxysms</term> <note>original: παροξυσμοὺς; refers to violent fits or sharp attacks of a disease</note> with <term>embrocations</term> <note>original: ἐμβροχαῖς; medicinal lotions or poultices</note>. Be wise as a serpent in all things, and harmless as a dove. For this reason you are both fleshly and spiritual, that you may treat kindly those things which appear before your face; but as for the invisible things, pray that they may be revealed to you, so that you may lack nothing and abound in every spiritual gift. The season requires you—as pilots require winds and as a storm-tossed man requires a harbor—in order to reach God. Be sober as God’s athlete; the prize is incorruptibility and eternal life, concerning which you are already convinced. In all things, I am your <term>substitute</term> <note>original: ἀντίψυχον; literally "one who gives his life for another," a term of deep affection and commitment</note>, I and my bonds, which you have loved.

## III. Continuation.

Let those who seem to be trustworthy but teach strange doctrines not dismay you. Stand firm like an anvil when it is struck. It is the mark of a great athlete to be bruised and yet to conquer. Especially for God’s sake, we must endure all things, so that He may also endure us. Become more diligent than you already are. Mark the seasons. Look for Him who is above time—the Timeless, the Invisible, who became visible for our sake; the Intangible, the Impassible <note>one who cannot suffer or be affected by external force</note>, who for our sake became passible, who in every way endured for our sake.

## IV. Continuation.

Let widows not be neglected. After the Lord, you be their guardian. Let nothing be done without your approval, nor do anything without God’s <insert>approval</insert>; which indeed you do not do; be steadfast. Let gatherings be held more <term>frequently</term>...

*Chapter II.* 1) If you love [only] — Syriac version according to Cureton.
2) "Grace to you" was the reading in manuscript C.
3) Compare Acts 24:5.
4) Cureton thinks that the Syriac translator (whom the Armenian follows) either read the word "paroxysm," or a completely different word, or poorly understood the passage.
5) "In lotions" in manuscripts C and L.
6) Compare Matthew 10:16.
7) I have provided "as the [dove]" following C and L; Vossius and other editors printed "as if." The Syriac and Armenian versions of this sentence are longer.
8) That is: the secret faults of certain people (Junius). Or: the secret mysteries of God; or: those things which will happen in the future (Smith).
9) The Syriac version reads "ship" instead of "winds."
10) "For your soul" (or "in your place") in Syriac; "May my person be in the place of your person" in Armenian. Compare the Epistle to the Ephesians chapter 21, and to the Smyrnaeans chapter 10.
*Chapter III.* 1) "To be something" instead of "to be trustworthy" in the Syriac and Armenian. Compare Galatians 6:3 and Ignatius's Epistle to the Tarsians chapter 9.

<column-break/>

2) Compare 1 Timothy 1:3 and 6:3.
3) "Athlete" in Syriac; "strong man" in Armenian.
4) The words "Become more diligent" etc. until the end of the chapter are also found in Syriac in the writings of Severus, the Patriarch of Antioch. Compare Cureton’s work.
5) Thus C and the copy of Holstenius read it as two words ("above time"); Peter del Furia transcribed it for me from L as a single word, contrary to Jacobson, and that is how it appears in the first printed edition. Or write it as "over-seasoned," which in another sense means "too mature."
*Chapter IV.* 1) "Through" in Syriac; the words "After the Lord" are omitted in the Armenian.
2) [approval], which is missing in C and L, was inserted by Vossius from the Interpolated (longer) version; it is also present in the Syriac and Armenian versions, and in a homily on the "One Legislator of Both Testaments" attributed to Saint Chrysostom.

4) Pearson understands "more frequently" (or "more densely") as referring to crowded and full meetings, rather than just the frequency of the gatherings. Compare the Epistle to the Ephesians chapter 13.

->THE EPISTLE OF IGNATIUS TO POLYCARP. II. III. IV.<-

### II. *Continuation of exhortations.*

If you love good disciples, you deserve no credit for it; rather, subdue the more <term>troublesome</term> <note>original: "pestilentiores," literally "more pestilent" or "infectious"</note> ones with gentleness. Not every wound is healed by the same bandage. Calm feverish attacks with <term>lotions</term> <note>original: "superfusionibus," refers to the medicinal pouring of liquids over the body</note>. Be wise as a serpent in all things, and simple as a dove. For this reason you are both physical and spiritual, so that you may handle those things which appear before you peacefully; but as for invisible things, ask that they be revealed to you, so that you may lack nothing and abound in every gift. The time demands you—as a pilot requires winds and as one tossed by a storm requires a harbor—so that you may reach God with those under your care. Be sober as an athlete of God; the prize set before you is immortality and eternal life, of which you are already convinced. In all things, I—along with my bonds which you have loved—am your <term>refreshment</term> <note>original: "recreeris," used here in the sense of a devoted substitute or one who provides mutual support</note>.

* II. If you love good disciples, no thanks are owed to you. Rather, compel the worse ones to obedience through gentleness. Not every wound is healed by the same bandage. Calm the worsening attacks with lotions. Be wise in all things like a serpent, and simple as a dove. Therefore, you are carnal and spiritual, so that you may treat those things which appear to your eye kindly and softly. But ask for those things which are not seen, so that they may be manifested to you, lest you lack anything and may abound in every grace. This time demands you, just as pilots demand the winds and those harassed by a storm demand a harbor, so that you may reach God. Be sober, like an athlete of God. The prize set before you is incorruption and eternal life, of which you are also entirely persuaded. I will gladly spend myself for you—both my soul and these bonds which you have loved.

### III. *Continuation.*

Let those who seem to be worthy of trust, yet teach strange doctrines, not terrify you. Stand firm like an anvil that is struck. It is the mark of a great athlete to be beaten and yet to conquer. We must especially endure all things for God’s sake, so that He may also endure us. Become more diligent than you are. Consider the times. Look for Him who is beyond time—the timeless, the invisible, yet made visible for us; the untouchable, the <term>impassible</term> <note>original: "impatibilem," meaning incapable of suffering or being affected by external force</note>, yet for us made capable of suffering, who in every way endured for our sake.

* III. Let those who seem to deserve trust, yet teach foreign things, not terrify you. Stand firm, even as an anvil that is struck. It is the mark of a great athlete to be beaten and to conquer. Above all, however, all things must be endured by us for God’s sake, so that He may also endure us. Show yourself more industrious and diligent than you are: learn the opportunities of the time: look for Him who is above time, lacking time, invisible and for us made visible, untouchable, impassible, and for us made capable of suffering, and exercising every manner of patience for our sake.

### IV. *Continuation.*

Let not widows be neglected. After the Lord, you be their guardian. Let nothing be done without your will, nor should you do anything without God's will; which indeed you do not do, since you are constant. Let gatherings be held more frequently. Seek out all by name.

* IV. Let not widows be neglected. After the Lord, you be their guardian. Let nothing be done without your judgment, nor should you do anything without God, just as you do nothing, being constant and well-composed. Let more frequent gatherings be celebrated.

### VII. Send an envoy to the people of Antioch because peace has been restored.

Since the church at Antioch in Syria is at peace—as has been made known to me—through your prayer, I also have become more encouraged, resting in God’s care; provided that through suffering I may attain to God, so that I may be found a disciple at your resurrection. It is fitting, Polycarp, most blessed of God, to convene a most God-pleasing council and to appoint someone whom you hold very dear and who is tireless, who can be called "God’s runner." Authorize this man to go to Syria to glorify your tireless love to the glory of Christ. A Christian has no authority over himself, but gives his time to God. 3) "Strive together" — written as <note>original: "synathlete"</note> in some manuscripts.
4) From this and following passages, certain learned men have tried to show that this epistle is not by Ignatius, or at least not this part, because so many Latin words occur in it. For, they ask, was Ignatius so ignorant of the Greek language that he did not know what the Greek terms were for *deposit*, *receive*, or *deserter*? This judgment has, I believe, deceived these most learned men. For all these words are taken from Roman military service and law; they were no less known to the Greeks than to the Romans—indeed, they were even more familiar than the native terms. Who does not know that all military vocabulary obtained a foothold even among the Greeks? Anyone who is ignorant of this has never read the <term>Tacticians</term> <note>Greek and Roman writers on military strategy</note>; from whom one may learn that not only offices, parts of the army, and drills, but even military laws were written and read out in Latin. The same logic applies to Greco-Roman law, where innumerable terms were transferred into Greece along with the Empire. The books of the ancient jurists do not allow us to be ignorant of this. It is therefore not surprising if those words—*opsonion* for military pay, *desertor*, *deposita*, and *accepta*—were better known to the common people than those used by the ancient Greeks. In the Acts of the Smyrnaean Church regarding Polycarp, you find the term <term>konphektor</term> <note>original: "confector" — an executioner or finisher</note>, and six hundred others of that kind elsewhere, even in the books of the New Testament. I wonder, however,

<column-break/>

what came into the mind of the ancient translator, that he substituted "idle" for *deserter*. For who does not know that in the military, deserters are called <note>original: "leipotaktountas"</note>? A later age called not only them, but also rebels and traitors by that name. *Vossius.*
5) Very elegantly, "deserter" and "remain" are placed in opposition; and "deposits" is skillfully joined, to which the word "accepted dues" corresponds. *Cotelerius.* Vossius wonders what came into the mind of the ancient translator to substitute "idle" for deserter. A manuscript code still shows the word <note>original: "argos"</note>—meaning idle—written in the margin in this way; and the ancient translator transferred this marginal explanation of the unusual word "deserter" into the text. *Jacobson.* In the text of Codex C is "deserter," to which the word "idle" corresponds, written in the margin by another hand with the mark ·/·.
6) Ignatius uses the word "remain" in this way because deserters used to throw away their weapons. *Pearson.*
7) Variant spelling for "deposits" in some manuscripts.
8) This appears in the interpolated versions; others suggest "you may receive."

...you are prepared for good works belonging to God. Knowing, then, your earnestness for the truth, I have exhorted you through this brief letter.

### VIII. *Let other churches also send envoys or letters to Antioch.*

->Greetings.<-

Since¹ I was not able to write to all the churches because of my sudden sailing from Troas to Neapolis, as the <term>will</term> <note>original: "thelēma" — This could refer to God’s will or the orders of the Roman guards</note>³ commands; you shall write to the churches ahead, as one possessing the mind of God, so that they might do the same—those who are able sending messengers on foot, and others sending letters through those you send. In this way, you all may be glorified⁴ by an eternal work, as one who is worthy. I greet everyone by name, and also the wife of the <term>Governor</term> <note>original: "Epitropos" — likely a Roman official or a high-ranking household steward</note> with her whole household and children. I greet Attalus, my beloved. I greet the one who will be honored to journey to Syria. Grace will be with him always, and with Polycarp who sends him. I pray that you may always be well⁵ in our God, Jesus Christ,⁶ in whom may you remain⁷ in the unity of God and in <term>oversight</term> <note>original: "episkopē" — referring to the office of the bishop or divine supervision</note>.⁸ I greet Alce, a name very dear to me. Farewell in the Lord.

Chapter VIII. 1) The <term>Syriac version</term> <note>original: "Syrus"</note> recites one sentence from the eighth chapter in such a way as if he had read: *I greet the one honored to go to Antioch in my place, just as I commanded you.* These final words, *in my place, just as I commanded you*, are not recognized by the Armenian version and seem to be an addition by another hand.

2) "Was able" <note>original: "ēdunēthē"</note> in Codex C.

3) That is, the command of the emperor, or of the soldiers who were leading Ignatius, or the will of God. "Will" <note>original: "Thelēma"</note> is used in an absolute sense in the Epistle to the Smyrnaeans, chapter 11, by Jacobson.

<column-break/>

4) *That you may be glorified* (singular) in the old Latin interpretation. But I would rather read *that you all may be glorified* (plural) *by an eternal work, as one who is worthy.*

8) Read "of the bishop," as the Augustanus and Leicestrensis codices (of the <term>interpolated</term> <note>Later versions of Ignatius's letters that were expanded by scribes</note> epistle) have it, according to Smith. To me indeed, the reading "oversight" (episcopacy) seems to have been introduced at a later age, not without purpose, in place of the former reading.

<header>MARTYRDOM OF ST. IGNATIUS. I. II. </header>

# THE MARTYRDOM OF THE HOLY HIEROMARTYR IGNATIUS THE GOD-BEARER.

### I. *Ignatius’s pastoral care and his desire for martyrdom.*

Recently<gloss>1</gloss> after Trajan had succeeded to the Roman government, Ignatius, the disciple of the apostle John,<gloss>2</gloss> was a man<gloss>3</gloss> in all respects apostolic. He governed the church of the Antiochians with great care,<gloss>4</gloss> having with difficulty guided them through the past storms of many persecutions under Domitian. Like a good pilot, by the helm of prayer and fasting, and by the constancy of his teaching and spiritual vigor,<gloss>6</gloss> he held out against the opposing surge, fearing lest he might lose any of the faint-hearted or more simple-minded. Therefore, he rejoiced at the stability of the church when the persecution ceased for a little while. However, he was troubled within himself that he had not yet attained to a true love for Christ, nor to the perfect rank of a disciple. For he reflected that the confession made through martyrdom would bring him into a closer relationship with the Lord. Wherefore, remaining with the church for a few more years, and like a divine lamp<gloss>7</gloss> enlightening the mind of everyone through the explanation of the [divine]<gloss>8</gloss> scriptures, he at last obtained the objects of his prayer.

### II. *Ignatius is condemned by Trajan.*

For after these things, in the ninth year<gloss>1</gloss> of Trajan’s reign, the Emperor was emboldened by his victory over the Scythians and Dacians<gloss>2</gloss> and many other nations. Thinking that the <term>godly community</term> <note>original: "theosebes systema" — a reference to the organized Christian church</note> of the Christians was the only thing still lacking for his total subjugation of all, he threatened a persecution unless they chose to enter into the worship of demons<gloss>3</gloss> along with all the other nations. He compelled everyone living godly lives either to sacrifice or to die. At that time, therefore, the noble soldier of Christ, fearing for the church of the Antiochians, was voluntarily<gloss>5</gloss> led to Trajan, who was staying at that time in Antioch, as he was hastening toward Armenia and the Parthians. When he stood face to face with Trajan—

Chapter I. 1) It is known that Trajan succeeded the Emperor Nerva in 98 AD. Whether Ignatius suffered martyrdom in 107 AD according to Ussher and Burton, or in 112 AD according to others, or in 115 AD as it seems to Greswell, or in 116 AD according to the opinions of Pearson and Clericus, the word "Recently" cannot be understood as referring to a newly made Emperor, but must be taken as referring to the early part of his reign.

2) Regarding the discipleship of St. Ignatius under the care and instruction of St. John the Apostle, ecclesiastical writers remain deeply silent; most of whom, being occupied with narrating the Martyrdoms of the Saints, neglected to commit to writing for posterity the memory of their parents, homeland, and birth, or the entire record of their preceding lives, their education, and other circumstances. In the meantime, based on the reliability of these Acts, it seems established—

<header>MARTYRDOM OF ST. IGNATIUS. I. II.</header>

# THE MARTYRDOM OF THE HOLY PRIEST-MARTYR IGNATIUS THE GOD-BEARER.

## I. *Ignatius’s pastoral care and his desire for martyrdom.*

When Trajan had not long ago succeeded to the Roman Empire, Ignatius—the disciple of the Apostle John—was a man in all respects apostolic in character. He governed the church of the people of Antioch with the greatest care. He had narrowly survived the old storms of the many persecutions under Domitian; for, like a good pilot at the helm of prayer and fasting, and by the constancy of his teaching and his tireless spiritual struggle, he resisted the opposing tempest. He did this out of fear that he might lose any of those who were more fearful or simple-minded. Therefore, he certainly rejoiced in the tranquility of the church when the persecution ceased for a short time; however, he was troubled in his soul that he had not yet attained a true love for Christ, nor the perfect rank of a disciple. For he reflected in his mind that through the confession made by martyrdom, he would become more like Christ. Thus, having remained in the church for a few more years, and like a divine lamp illuminating the understanding of everyone through the interpretation of the [divine] scriptures, he at last achieved the object of his prayers.

## II. *Ignatius is condemned by Trajan.*

For after these things, in the ninth year<gloss>1</gloss> of his reign, Trajan was emboldened by the victory he had won over the Scythians, the Dacians,<gloss>2</gloss> and many other nations. He considered that the godly assembly of Christians was the only thing still lacking for the total subjection of all to his power. He threatened them with persecution unless they embraced the worship of demons along with all the other nations, and he began forcing all those living religiously either to offer sacrifices or to die. It was then that the noble soldier of Christ, fearing for the church of Antioch, was voluntarily led before Trajan. At that time, the Emperor was staying in Antioch, though he was hastening to march against Armenia and the Parthians. When he stood in the presence—

6) <note>original: "spirituali"</note> Regarding the "spiritual" labor. The latter emendation is to be preferred; for both of the old Latin translators have: "spiritual." Le Clerc prefers the reading "with a vigorous spirit," meaning firm and constant; Smith prefers "spiritual labor." Jacobus Syrus seems to have read it as "of continuous fasting and the teaching of spiritual labors," or, if the punctuation of Ribai is ignored, "of spiritual labor" or "spirit." The Armenian version reads "with teaching and spiritual labor" or "labor of the spirit."

Chapter II. 1) Ussher and Smith change the reading "fourth" found in the old Cottonian translator to "ninth." Grabe suspects that in the Greek text it was written as the nineteenth year.

<column-break/>

2) The first war against the Dacians was waged during Trajan's fourth consulship and was finished then. But here the text refers to the second war, in which King Decebalus took his own life after being defeated, and Roman colonies were sent into Dacia. For this reason, Trajan was named "Dacicus" <note>Conqueror of Dacia</note>, as is read on his triumphal column which still stands in Rome.

5) Ignatius voluntarily brought himself to Trajan so that he might appease him by an explanation of Christian doctrine, or, if he could not appease him, that he might draw all the Emperor's anger upon himself and thus free the church of Antioch from fear. — Le Clerc.

Then, like a distinguished ram leading a fine flock, he was seized by the brutal cruelty of the soldiers to be carried away to Rome as food for bloodthirsty beasts.

### III. Ignatius sails to Smyrna.

With great eagerness and joy, therefore, out of his desire for suffering, he went down from Antioch to Seleucia <note>The seaport of Antioch.</note>, and from there he began his voyage. After much labor, he reached the city of the Smyrneans. Stepping down from the ship with great joy, he hastened to see the holy Polycarp, the bishop of Smyrna, his fellow-hearer; for they had both long ago been disciples of the holy Apostle John. Having been brought to him, and having shared spiritual gifts with him, and boasting in his bonds, he urged Polycarp to struggle along with him in his purpose. He made this request especially to the whole church in common (for the cities and churches of Asia welcomed the saint through their bishops, priests, and deacons, all of them hurrying to him, hoping to receive some share of a spiritual gift).

### III. Ignatius Sails to Smyrna.

Therefore, with great eagerness and joy, and a longing to suffer, he went down from Antioch to Seleucia <note>The port city of Antioch</note>, and from there he took ship. After much labor, when he had arrived at the city of Smyrna, he disembarked with great joy and hastened to see the holy Polycarp <note>Bishop of Smyrna and a famous martyr in his own right</note>, the bishop of the Smyrneans, who was his former fellow-disciple. 5) A Pauline phrase. Compare Romans 1:11.

### IV. *Ignatius writes to the churches, especially the Roman church.*

And he said these things and bore witness in this way, extending his love for Christ to such a degree that—since he was about to lay hold of heaven through his "good confession" <note>A "good confession" refers to a public declaration of faith, often in the face of death, modeled after Christ's own testimony before Pontius Pilate.</note> and the earnest prayers of those supporting his struggle—he wished to repay the churches that had met him through their leaders. He did this by sending letters of thanks to them, which dripped with spiritual grace through prayer and exhortation. Therefore, seeing that everyone was kindly disposed toward him, and fearing that the affection of the brotherhood might cut short his eagerness for the Lord—now that a "good door" of martyrdom had opened for him—he wrote the following to the Church of the Romans:

->*The Epistle of St. Ignatius to the Romans is read here. See above page 164 etc.*<-

### V. *Ignatius is led from Smyrna to Rome.*

Having thus instructed <note>Specifically, he was "setting right" the minds of the Roman Christians who wanted to save him. See note 1 below.</note> those brothers in Rome against their will through his letter, he set sail from Smyrna. For "Christophoros" <term>Christophoros: A title meaning "Christ-bearer," similar to Ignatius’s other name, Theophorus. It signifies a person who carries the presence of Christ within them.</term> was being hurried along by the soldiers to arrive in time for the ambitious displays <note>original: "φιλοτιμίας." This refers to the lavish public games and spectacles sponsored by the Emperor.</note> in great Rome, so that he might be delivered to wild beasts in the sight of the Roman people and thus obtain the crown of his struggle. He then reached Troas. From there he was brought down to Neapolis and passed through Philippi in Macedonia, and across Epirus near Epidamnus. Finding a ship in the coastal regions, he sailed across the Adriatic Sea, and from there entered the Tyrrhenian Sea. As they passed various islands and cities, and as Puteoli was pointed out to the saint, he was eager to disembark, wishing to walk in the footsteps of the Apostle Paul <note>Puteoli is the modern Pozzuoli, where St. Paul stayed for seven days on his own journey to Rome (Acts 28:13-14).</note>. However, a violent wind arose and would not allow it, as the ship was being driven forward from the stern. So, after blessing the love of the brothers in that place, he sailed on. Thus, using favorable winds for one day and night, we <note>The use of "we" suggests the narrator was an eyewitness traveling with Ignatius.</note> were carried along against our will, grieving over the coming separation of this righteous man from us. But for him, things were turning out according to his prayer, as he was eager to depart from the world more quickly to reach the Lord whom he loved. Having sailed into the Roman harbors just as the impure spectacles were nearing their end, the soldiers were annoyed by the delay, but the bishop joyfully obeyed those hurrying him on.

Chapter IV. 1) *about to* — This is the reading in the manuscript; Jacobson, following Toup, wishes to restore the phrase "to be about to."
2) Grabe proposes *thanksgiving*; Toup suggests *gracious*.
3) Almost the same meaning as the phrase *to be refreshed* in Ignatius’s Letter to the Magnesians, chapter 14.
4) He feared, of course, that the Roman Church, moved by love for him, might use friends at the court of Trajan—who was otherwise not an unmerciful Prince—to obtain a pardon for him; if that had happened, he would lose a remarkable opportunity to prove his constancy to God and men. *Clericus.* <note>Jean Le Clerc (1657–1736), a famous theologian and scholar.</note>

Chapter V. 1) *That is*, to settle the minds of those feeling otherwise, and to lead them to approve of that which he himself desired. *Clericus.*

### IV. Ignatius writes to the churches, especially the Roman church.

And he spoke and bore witness in this manner, extending his love for Christ to such an extent that he was soon to lay hold of heaven through his noble confession <note>original: "confessionem" — a public declaration of faith in the face of death.</note> and the dedication of those who prayed together to God for his final struggle. He wished to return the favor to the churches that had met him through their leaders, giving thanks in letters sent to them, from which spiritual grace flowed along with his wishes and exhortations. When he saw that everyone was kindly disposed toward him, he feared that the love of the brothers might hinder his desire to go to God, just as the beautiful door of martyrdom was standing open for him. The things he wrote to the Church of the Romans are set down below.

->*The Epistle of Saint Ignatius to the Romans is read here. See above, page 164 etc.*<-

### V. Ignatius is led from Smyrna to Rome.

After he had settled the minds of the resisting Roman brothers through his letter as he desired, he set sail from Smyrna. For Christophorus <term>Christophorus: A title meaning "Christ-bearer," similar to Ignatius’s other name, Theophorus. It signifies a person who carries Christ within their heart.</term> was being pressed by the soldiers to hurry to the public games in Great Rome, so that he might receive the crown of the struggle by being handed over to wild beasts before the eyes of the Roman people. He then reached Troas. From there he was led to Neapolis and passed through Philippi, across Macedonia, and to that part of Epirus situated near Epidamnus. Finding a ship at the coast, he sailed across the Adriatic Sea; from there he entered the Tyrrhenian Sea, passing by islands and cities. When Puteoli was shown to the holy man, he wished to disembark, wanting to walk in the footsteps of the Apostle Paul <note>Puteoli is modern Pozzuoli, where St. Paul stayed for a week on his way to Rome (Acts 28:13).</note>. However, a violent wind blew in and prevented it, pushing the ship from the stern. He spoke of the blessed love of the brothers in that place and so sailed past. Thus, for one day and night, we were carried along by favorable winds—we, indeed, were unwilling, grieving because of our coming separation from that just man. But for him, things were happening as he wished, as he was hurrying to depart from the world. Therefore, when the ship arrived at the Roman ports [at Ostia] and the end of the unholy spectacle was near, the soldiers were frustrated by the delay, but the bishop joyfully obeyed those urging him on.

### VI. *Ignatius is devoured by wild beasts in Rome.*

From there they were pushed out from the place called Portus<gloss>1</gloss> (for the reports concerning the holy martyr had already spread abroad). We met<gloss>2</gloss> with the brothers who were filled with both fear and joy: they rejoiced that they were deemed worthy of an encounter with the "God-bearer" <note>original: "Theophorus" — Ignatius's chosen title</note>, but they were afraid because such a man was being led to his death<gloss>3</gloss>. To some, he even gave the command to remain silent—those who were fervent and saying they should restrain the crowds so they would not seek to destroy the righteous man. Ignatius, immediately knowing this in his spirit and greeting them all, asked of them a true love. He spoke at greater length than he had in his letter<gloss>4</gloss> and persuaded them not to envy him as he hastened toward the Lord. Thus, with all the brothers kneeling, he besought the Son of God on behalf of the churches, for the cessation of the persecution, and for the love of the brothers for one another. Then, he was led with haste into the amphitheater. There, he was immediately cast in according to the former<gloss>5</gloss> command of Caesar, just as the public games <term>original: "philotimion" — literally "expressions of honor," referring to the lavish gladiatorial shows and beast hunts funded by officials to gain public favor</term> were about to end. For it was a prominent festival<gloss>6</gloss>, as they believed, called the "Thirteenth"<gloss>7</gloss> in the Roman tongue, on which the people used to gather in great earnest. Thus he was thrown to the fierce beasts near the temple<gloss>8</gloss>, so that the desire of the holy martyr Ignatius might be fulfilled immediately, according to what is written: "The desire of the righteous is acceptable"<note>Proverbs 10:24</note>. This was so that he would not be a burden to any of the brothers through the collection of his remains, just as he had previously expressed in his letter his desire for his own perfection <note>meaning his "completion" or "martyrdom"</note>. For only the harder parts of his holy remains were left over, which were carried back to Antioch and placed in linen<gloss>10</gloss>, left to the holy church as an priceless treasure by the grace that was in the martyr.<gloss>11</gloss>

### VII. *The dead Ignatius appears to those who sleep.*

These things took place thirteen days before the Kalends of January<gloss>1</gloss>, that is, the twentieth of December, in the consulship of Sura and Senecio for the second time.<gloss>2</gloss> We, having been eyewitnesses of these things, spent the entire night at home in tears; and with many kneelings and prayers, we besought the Lord to give assurance<gloss>3</gloss> to us in our weakness regarding the events that had occurred...

Chapter VI. 1) Understand "Portus" as the harbor built by Emperor Claudius, later enlarged by Trajan and granted the status of a city. Now nothing remains of that famous city but a half-ruined palace from the Middle Ages in the marshes, to which the name of the suburban Bishopric of Porto is attached.
2) Thus restored by Jacob with the Paris manuscript, from which Ruinart had published "with him indeed." Smith noted that the ancient interpreter had already read it this way.

<column-break/>

because Trajan had pronounced the sentence some months earlier. —Le Clerc.
6) Namely a "festival." On that day and those following they celebrated the *Sigillaria* <note>A Roman festival following the Saturnalia, where small figurines were given as gifts</note>; concerning which see Lipsius, *Saturnalia* 1, 4. ("The Saturnalia itself consisted of five days; but the Sigillaria, which followed, took two.") —Le Clerc. ### VI. *Ignatius is devoured by wild beasts in Rome.*

From there they departed from the place called Portus (for by now the fame of the holy martyr had spread abroad). We met with the brothers who were filled with both fear and joy: they rejoiced because God had deemed them worthy of an encounter with the "God-bearer" <note>original: "Theophorus" — Ignatius’s chosen title, meaning one who carries God within</note>, but they were afraid because such a great man was being led to his death. He even warned some to remain quiet—those who were acting fervently and saying they would calm the people so the crowd would not seek the death of the righteous man. Ignatius, immediately knowing this in his spirit and greeting them all, asked of them a true love. He spoke at greater length than he had in his letter, and he persuaded them not to envy him as he hastened toward the Lord. Then, after all the brothers had knelt, he himself prayed to the Son of God on behalf of the churches, for the cessation of the persecution, and for the mutual love of the brothers for one another. 

He was then led immediately into the amphitheater and cast in, according to the command of Caesar given long before. The public games <term>original: "spectaculorum" — likely referring to the lavish hunts and executions held during festivals</term> were nearing their end (for it was a solemn day, as they believed, called the "Thirteenth" in the Roman tongue <note>original: "tertius decimus" — referring to the 13th day before the Kalends of January, or December 20th</note>, on which the people used to gather in great numbers). Thus, he was thrown to the cruel beasts near the temple, so that the desire of the holy martyr Ignatius might be fulfilled immediately, just as it is written: "The desire of the righteous is granted" <gloss>Proverbs 10:24</gloss>. This happened so that he would not be a burden to any of the brothers in the collection of his remains, just as he had previously wished in his letter for his own completion to occur. Only the harder parts of his holy remains were left; these were carried back to Antioch and placed in linen <gloss>original: "linteo"</gloss> as an invaluable treasure, left to the holy church through the grace of the martyr.

### VII. The dead Ignatius appears to those who sleep.

These things took place on the 13th day before the Kalends of January <note>December 20th</note>, when Sura and Senecio were consuls among the Romans for the second time. We ourselves were eyewitnesses of these things; and having spent the whole night in tears, and having prayed to the Lord with knees bent and much petition, that He might strengthen us who are weak—

7) Namely, before the Kalends of January, as appears from chapter 7: "These things happened on the 13th day before the Kalends of January." On that day, the *Sigillaria* <note>a festival where small figurines were given as gifts</note> was celebrated for two days, added to the *Saturnalia*. *H.*
8) The Amphitheater was sacred either to Jupiter Latiaris, or to the Stygian Jupiter and Diana, which is why it is not surprising that a temple is mentioned here. *Clericus.* The ancient translator does not read "near the temple," but has instead "by the impious," perhaps reading *para ton anosion* or *anomon* in the Greek. *Smith.*
9) *Proverbs* 10:24.
10) The ancient version says: "and placed in a box" <note>original: "capsa"</note>; therefore Dr. Nolte thinks that instead of "linen" <note>Greek: "lino"</note>, one should read "basket" <note>Greek: "lichno"</note>. *H. edition IV.*
11) See Eusebius, *Church History* IV, 15. Compare Chrysostom’s sermon on St. Ignatius, chapter 5.

Chapter VII. 1) The Greeks celebrate the feast of Ignatius on the 20th day of the month of December, the day on which the *Acts* testify he suffered; however, the Latins celebrate it on the first day of February. Is this perhaps due to some translation <note>the formal movement of holy relics from one place to another</note> of his remains? For it is established that there were several such transfers. *Ruinart.*
2) That is, when both were consuls together for the second time. They were first consuls together in the year of Christ 102 (specifically Senecio for the 3rd time and Sura for the 2nd). They served together in this office for the second time in the year of Christ 107 (Senecio for the 4th time and Sura for the 3rd). See Pagi, *Critique* on the years 102 and 107. *H.*
3) That is, to make us more certain whether the martyrdom of Ignatius was acceptable to God. *Clericus.*

...and the riddles of the *Queen of the Ethiopians* <note>Traditionally identified as the Queen of Sheba.</note>, which came in a torrent like the currents of the Nile, he [Solomon] solved in such a way that the woman, wise as she was, was moved beyond herself with astonishment.

IV. And Josiah, the beloved of God, while still barely able to speak articulate words, rebuked those possessed by the evil spirit, showing that they were liars and deceivers of the people. He revealed the deception of demons and exposed the gods who do not truly exist. Even though he was just a child, he executed those who served as their priests, overturned their altars, and defiled their sacrificial places with the remains of the dead. He destroyed their shrines, cut down their sacred groves,¹ smashed their pillars, and dug up the graves of the ungodly so that not even a trace of the wicked might remain. Such a zealot for true religion was he, and a punisher of the ungodly, even while his tongue was still stammering.² And David, the prophet and king alike, the "root of the Savior according to the flesh" <note>This refers to the Christian belief that Jesus Christ was a physical descendant of King David.</note>, was anointed as king by Samuel while he was still a youth. <column-break/>

...to the Queen of the Ethiopians, whose riddles flowed with a force like the flooding Nile, he provided such solutions that she, though wise herself, was struck with awe.

IV. Josiah, moreover, a lover of God, while still speaking almost without distinct articulation, proved that those held by an evil spirit were speakers of lies and seducers of the people. He reveals the trickery of demons, demonstrates that those they worship are not truly gods, and—being but a boy—kills those consecrated to them. He overturns their shrines, pollutes their altars with dead remains, destroys temples, cuts down the woods, shatters columns, and digs up the sepulchers of the impious so that no sign of the wicked remains any longer. Thus he was a zealot for religion and a punisher of the impious, even with a stammering tongue. David, too, at once Prophet and King, the root of the Savior according to the flesh, is anointed as king by Samuel while a boy. For he says in a certain place: "When I was small among my brothers and the younger in the house of my father."

*IV. Truly that Josiah, most beloved of God, when his voice was scarcely yet articulate, argued against those possessed by a malignant spirit as being liars and seducers of the people. He uncovers the imposture of demons, exposes the fictitious gods, and, still a child, kills their priests. III. I have gladly fulfilled the things commanded by you through your letter; doubting in nothing those things which you yourself have judged to be good. For I recognized that you have given your testimony to these two men by the judgment of God, and not by carnal favor. # THE LETTER OF IGNATIUS TO MARIA OF CASSOBOLA. IV. V.

THE EPISTLE OF IGNATIUS TO THE TRALLIANS. I. II. III.

### THE EPISTLE OF THE SAME AUTHOR TO THE TRALLIANS.^1

->Ignatius, who is also called Theophoros, <note>original: "Theophoros"; This title means "God-bearer," signifying someone who carries Christ within their heart.</note> to the holy church beloved by God the Father and Jesus Christ, which is in Tralles,^2 <note>Tralles was an ancient city in Lydia, Asia Minor, located in modern-day Turkey.</note> chosen and worthy of God, possessing peace in flesh and spirit through Jesus Christ, our hope, in His passion upon the cross and through His death and resurrection; which church I also salute in its fullness, in the apostolic character, and wish very many greetings.<-

I. I have learned that you possess a mind that is blameless and unhesitating in patient endurance,^4 not merely for outward use, but as a permanent possession,^5 as Polybius your <term>bishop</term> <note>From the Greek *episkopos*, meaning "overseer." In the early church, the bishop was the primary leader and guardian of a local community.</note> has shown, who by the will of God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ His Son, and with the cooperation of the Spirit, came to me in Smyrna. And he so greatly rejoiced with me in my bonds in Christ Jesus, that I beheld your entire multitude in him. Having therefore received your godly goodwill through him, I felt encouraged, finding you to be imitators of Jesus Christ the Savior.

II. Be subject to the bishop as to the Lord;^1 for he watches over your souls as one who must give an account to God. Therefore, you appear to me to be living not according to the way of men, but according to Jesus Christ, who died for us, so that by believing in His death you might become partakers of His resurrection through baptism.^2 It is therefore necessary that, whatever things^3 you do, you do nothing without the bishop. But be subject^4 also to the <term>presbytery</term>, <note>From the Greek *presbyterion*, the council of elders who advised the bishop.</note> as to the apostles of Jesus Christ, our hope, in whom we shall be found if we live our lives in Him. It is also necessary that the <term>deacons</term>, <note>From the Greek *diakonos*, meaning "servants" or "ministers."</note> being ministers of the mysteries of Christ Jesus, should please everyone in every way;^5 for they are not deacons of food^6 and drink, but servants of the Church of God. Therefore, they must guard against accusations^7 as they would against a blazing fire. Let them be such men.

III. And you, for your part, respect them as you would Jesus Christ, whose guardians of the place they are;^1 just as the bishop is a type of the Father of all, and the presbyters are as the council of God and the assembly of the apo— <note>The text breaks off here mid-word; it likely intended to say "apostles."</note>

<columns>2</columns>

The Epistle to the Trallians survives without its beginning <note>original: "acephala"; literally "headless," a scholarly term for a manuscript missing its opening.</note> in Manuscripts F, O, and U. A small note in O advises: "The second letter to the Trallians: — the beginning of the letter to the Trallians is missing, and of the first, the whole is missing." With other things having been prefixed, on the fifth page our Epistle begins thus, just as it does in F: "as the gentleness in them, in which the ruler is destroyed" (chapter 4). In a similar way, Codex V, in whose margin a more recent hand wrote: "From here begins the second letter, or rather the text; however, the beginning is missing. The part above is not by Ignatius. The scribe erred, confusing and mixing them both."

# THE EPISTLE OF IGNATIUS TO THE TRALLIANS. I. II. III.

## THE EPISTLE OF THE SAME AUTHOR TO THE TRALLIANS. WRITTEN FROM SMYRNA.¹

Ignatius, who is also called Theophorus, <note>original: "Theophorus"; meaning "God-bearer."</note> to the holy church beloved by God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, which is in Tralles, chosen and worthy of God, having been brought into peace in flesh and Spirit by Jesus Christ, our hope, in His passion through the cross and death and resurrection; which church I also salute in the fullness of the apostolic character, and wish very many greetings in God.²

I. I have learned that you possess a mind that is blameless and unhesitating in patient endurance, not merely for outward use, but as a permanent possession, according to what Polybius³ your <term>Bishop</term> <note>From "episkopos," meaning overseer; the primary leader of the local church.</note> has shown me, who by the will of God the Father and Jesus Christ His Son, and with the cooperation of the Spirit, came to me in Smyrna. And he so greatly rejoiced with me in my bonds in Christ Jesus, that I beheld your entire multitude in him. Having therefore received your godly benevolence⁴ through him, I recognized your goodwill, finding you to be imitators of Jesus Christ our Savior.

II. Be subject to the Bishop as to the Lord. For he watches over your souls as one who must give an account to God.¹ Because of this, you appear to me to be living not according to the way of men, but according to Jesus Christ,² who died for us, so that by believing in His death you might be made partakers of His resurrection through the sharing of baptism. It is necessary, therefore, that you do nothing without the Bishop. But be also subject to the <term>Presbyters</term>, <note>From "presbyteros," meaning elders; a council of leaders who advised the bishop.</note> as to the Apostles of Jesus Christ, our hope, in whom if we continue to live, we shall be found in Him. It is also necessary that the <term>Deacons</term>, <note>From "diakonos," meaning servants or ministers; they assisted with the practical and liturgical needs of the community.</note> who are in the ministry³ of Jesus Christ, should please everyone in every way. For they are not ministers of food and drink, but ministers of the Church of God. It is therefore necessary to observe their precepts⁴ as one would a burning fire. Let them truly be such.

III. Moreover, reverence them as the Lord¹ Jesus Christ, for they are the guardians of His place: just as the Bishop is the model of the Father of all; the Presbyters, however, are as the council² of God and the assembly³ of the Apostles...

# IGNATIUS’S EPISTLE TO THE TRALLIANS. III. IV. V. VI.

...the apostles of Christ. Without these, a chosen church does not exist,² nor a gathering of saints,³ nor an assembly of the holy; but I am persuaded that you are also so disposed. For I received the pattern of your love⁴ and have it with me in the person of your bishop, whose very demeanor is a great lesson, and whose gentleness is power—a power which⁵ I believe even the godless respect. Out of love for you, I spare you, though I might write more sharply, lest I should seem to some to be overbearing⁶ or demanding. I am indeed bound for the sake of Christ, but I am not yet worthy of Christ; but if I am perfected, I shall perhaps become so.

IV. I do not issue commands as if I were an apostle,¹ but I measure myself, lest I should perish in my boasting. For it is good to boast in the Lord. Even if I am strong in the things of God, I must fear all the more, and not give heed to those who vainly puff me up; for those who praise me scourge me.² But I do not know if I am worthy; for the zeal of the enemy is not apparent to many, but it wages war against me.³ I have need, therefore, of gentleness, by which the prince of this age, the devil, is destroyed.

V. For could I not have written to you more mystical things?¹ But I fear lest I should cause harm to you who are infants; and forgive me,² lest,³ being unable to grasp the intensity of it, you might be choked. For even I, though I am bound, am not for that reason able to understand heavenly things: the <term>angelic orders</term>⁴ <note>Ranks or hierarchies of angels.</note>, the variations of angels and armies,⁵ the differences between powers and lordships, the distinctions between thrones and authorities, the greatness of the ages,⁶ the excellence of the <term>Cherubim and Seraphim</term>,⁷ the loftiness of the Spirit, the kingdom of the Lord, and above all, the incomparable nature of Almighty God.⁸ Knowing these things, I am not yet altogether perfected, nor am I a disciple such as Paul and Peter;⁹ for many things are lacking to me,¹⁰ so that I may not be separated from God.

VI. I exhort you, therefore—not I, but the love of Jesus Christ—that you all speak the same thing,¹ and that there be no schisms among you; but that you be joined together in the same mind and in the same judgment. For there are some vain talkers and deceivers, not Christians, but <term>Christ-mongers</term> <note>original: "χριστέμποροι"; those who make a trade of or profit from the name of Christ.</note>, who carry about the name of Christ in deceit, and hawk the word of the Gospel, mixing the poison of error with the sweet address, just as those who mix <term>hemlock</term>⁵ with <term>honey-wine</term> <note>Hemlock is a highly poisonous plant; honey-wine (oinomel) was a common sweet beverage.</note>, so that he who drinks, being deceived by the sweet quality of the taste, unguardly meets with death.

<header>IGNATIUS’S EPISTLE TO THE TRALLIANS. III. IV. V. VI.</header>

...of Christ. For without these, an elect church <note>original: "ecclesia electa"</note> does not exist, nor a gathering of saints, nor a holy congregation. For I am confident that you also stand in this way. I have received the examples of your charity, and I hold them with me in the person of your Bishop; for his very training is a great teaching. Indeed, his gentleness is his power, which I believe even those who are without God respect. But because I love you, I spare you from writing more frequently, lest I should appear to some to be overbearing or tedious. I am indeed bound for the sake of Christ, but I am not yet worthy of Christ. If, however, I reach my end <note>Ignatius is writing while being transported to Rome for his execution; "consummating" or "reaching the end" refers to his expected martyrdom.</note>, perhaps I shall be.

IV. I do not issue commands as if I were an Apostle, but I measure myself, lest I should perish in my boasting. For it is good to boast in the Lord. And even if I am saved before God, I ought to fear all the more, and not pay attention to those who would puff me up. For those who praise me actually scourge me. I choose to suffer, but I do not know if I am worthy. For the jealousy of the enemy <note>Referring to the Devil or spiritual adversary.</note> is not seen by many, but it wages war against me. I must, therefore, be gentle, so that the prince of this world, the Devil, may be undone.

V. Could I not have written to you of more secret things? But I fear lest I might inflict injury upon you, since you are still infants. Forgive me, for you are not able to bear the weight of these bonds, just as I am bound. And I am indeed able to understand heavenly things: the ranks <note>original: "ordines"</note> of Angels and Archangels, the various orders of the celestial armies, the differences between Virtues and Dominions, the distances between Thrones <note>original: "Sedium"</note> and Powers, the splendors of the Eternal ones, the excellencies of the Cherubim and Seraphim, the sublimity of the Spirit, the kingdom of the Lord, and above all these, the incomparability of Almighty God. Even though I know these things, I am not yet entirely perfect, nor can I be a disciple such as Paul or Peter. For much remains for me, lest I be forsaken by God.

VI. I ask you, therefore—not I, but the love of Jesus Christ—that you all speak the same thing, and that there be no <term>schisms</term> <note>From the Greek "schismata," meaning divisions or tears in the unity of the group.</note> among you; but be perfect in the same mind and in the same knowledge. For there are certain idle talkers and deceivers of the mind, not Christians, but those who "merchandise" Christ <note>Those who exploit the faith for profit or personal gain.</note>, carrying around the name of Christ as a deception, and trading on the word of the Gospel, mixing the poison of error with a sweet allure, just as one might mix a toxin with honey-wine <note>original: "oenomelli," a mixture of wine and honey used here as a metaphor for a "sweetened" but deadly false doctrine.</note>, so that whoever drinks that palatable drink, through its sweetness...

<meta>This page continues Ignatius’s warning against false teachers (heretics) who distort the nature of Christ. It concludes Chapter VI and provides the entirety of Chapter VII, emphasizing the importance of church hierarchy—bishops, presbyters, and deacons—as a defense against spiritual error.</meta>

<page-num>232</page-num>
<header>IGNATIUS’S EPISTLE TO THE TRALLIANS. VI. VII. </header>

...be pierced with death. One of the ancients advised: "Let no one be called good who mixes the good with the evil." For they speak of Christ, not so that they might preach Christ, but so that they might reject Christ; and they do not establish the law, but they do so to proclaim lawlessness. For they alienate Christ from the Father; they slander the law of Christ and His birth from a Virgin; being ashamed of the cross, they deny the passion <note>The "passion" refers to the suffering and death of Jesus.</note>, and they do not believe in the resurrection; they introduce an unknown God; they consider Christ to be unbegotten <note>A heresy claiming Christ was never born or had no beginning.</note>; and as for the Spirit, they do not even acknowledge that He exists. Some of them say that the Son is a mere man; and that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are the same person; and that the creation is the work of God, not through Christ, but through some other foreign power.

VII. Guard yourselves, therefore, against such people, so that you do not take a snare for your own souls. And keep your life blameless toward all men, so that you do not become a trap for the watchtower, and like a spread-out net. For he who does not heal himself in his own works is the brother of him who harms himself. If, then, you also put away puffing up, arrogance, vanity, and pride, it is possible for you to be inseparable from God. For He is near to those who fear Him; and "Upon whom," He says, "shall I look, but upon the humble and quiet man, and him who trembles at my words?" <note>A reference to Isaiah 66:2.</note> Respect also your bishop as Christ, according to what the blessed apostles commanded you. He who is within the sanctuary <note>Literally "within the altar-place."</note> is clean; therefore, he also obeys the bishop and the presbyters; but he who is outside is he who does anything without the bishop and the presbyters and the deacons; such a person is defiled in his conscience, and is worse than an unbeliever. For what is a bishop? Nothing else but one who holds power and authority above all, as much as it is possible for a man to hold, becoming an imitator of Christ the God according to his power. And what is a presbytery? <note>The council of elders or priests.</note> Nothing else but a sacred gathering, counselors and assessors of the bishop. And what are deacons? Nothing else but imitators of the angelic powers, performing for him a pure and blameless service—as the holy Stephen [did] for the blessed James...

<meta>This page concludes the sixth chapter and provides most of the seventh chapter of Ignatius’s letter to the Trallians. It focuses on identifying specific heresies—such as those denying Christ’s humanity or the distinction of the Trinity—and emphasizes that the only safety from such errors is found in humility and obedience to the established church hierarchy of bishops, presbyters, and deacons.</meta>

<page-num>233</page-num>
<header>IGNATIUS’S EPISTLE TO THE TRALLIANS. VI. VII.</header>

...more heedlessly be condemned to death. One of the ancients warned that no one should be called good who has mixed evil with good. For they name Christ, not to preach Christ, but to despise Christ; and they bring forward the law, not to establish the law, but to announce things contrary to the law. For they alienate Christ from the Father; they reject the law of Christ and His birth from a Virgin, being ashamed of the cross, denying the passion <note>The suffering and death of Jesus.</note>, and not believing in the resurrection. They profess an unknown God <note>A Gnostic concept of a deity removed from the material world.</note>; they consider Christ to be unbegotten <note>Existing without a beginning or birth.</note>, and they do not even acknowledge the existence of the Holy Spirit. Some of them say that the Son is a mere man; others say that He is the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit all at once; and they say that creation is not the work of God through Christ, but the work of some other foreign power.

VII. Beware, therefore, of such people, so that you do not take a snare for your own souls. Keep your life blameless before all men, so that you do not become a trap of scrutiny, like nets spread out. <note>A reference to Hosea 5:1.</note> For he who does not spare himself in his own works is the brother of him who pollutes himself. <note>A reference to Proverbs 18:9.</note> If you lay aside your natural pride, and your boastful and swollen arrogance, it will be possible for you to be inseparable from God. "For the Lord is near to those who fear Him"; and "Upon whom," He says, "shall I look, but upon the humble and quiet man, and him who trembles at my words?" <note>Citations from Psalm 85:9 and Isaiah 66:2.</note> Revere your Bishop as you would Christ, according to what the blessed Apostles commanded you. For he who is established within the sanctuary <note>Literally "within the altar," meaning those in full communion with the church.</note> is clean; for this reason, obey your Bishop and the Presbyters <note>The council of elders.</note>. But he who is outside the sanctuary is one who acts apart from the Bishop, the Presbyters, and the Deacons; such a person is polluted in his conscience and is worse than an unbeliever. For what is the Bishop, but one who holds all the leadership and power over all, as much as is fitting for a man to hold, having become an imitator of God in virtue? What is the Presbytery <note>The body of elders.</note>, but a holy assembly, the counselors and confessors of the Bishop? And what are the Deacons, but imitators of Christ, ministering to the Bishop as Christ did to the Father, and performing for him a clean and blameless service, just as Saint Stephen

<meta>This page continues the long version of Ignatius’s Epistle to the Trallians. It follows the previous discussion on church order and warns against those who deny the physical reality of Christ’s life and death. This section moves from the importance of the clergy to a defense of the Incarnation.</meta>

<page-num>234</page-num>

# IGNATIUS’S EPISTLE TO THE TRALLIANS. VII. VIII. IX.

...Lord, and Timothy and Linus to Paul, and Anacletus and Clement to Peter <note>Ignatius lists these figures as successors or assistants to the Apostles to emphasize the continuity of the Church’s leadership.</note>. He, therefore, who disobeys these would be altogether godless and impious, and a rejecter of Christ, and one who belittles His arrangement <note>original: *diataxin*; referring to the established order or "disposition" of the church.</note>.

VIII. I am writing these things to you, not because I have known such people among you; but may God never allow such a thing to come to my ears—He who did not spare His own Son for the sake of the holy church. But foreseeing the snares of the evil one, I secure you beforehand with instructions, as my beloved and faithful children in Christ. I am, as it were, pre-medicating you with preventatives against the plague-like disease of the disobedient—a disease which you avoid by the good pleasure of Christ our Lord. You, then, taking up gentleness, become imitators of the sufferings of Jesus Christ and of His love, with which He loved us, giving Himself as a ransom for us, so that by His blood He might cleanse us from old impiety, and provide life for us, when we were almost about to perish by the wickedness within us. Let none of you, then, have anything against his neighbor. For "Forgive," says our Lord, "and it will be forgiven you." Do not give opportunities to the Gentiles <note>In this context, "Gentiles" refers to non-Christians or pagans.</note>, so that the Word and the teaching may not be blasphemed because of a few foolish people. "For woe," says the Prophet, as if from the face of God, "to him through whom my name is blasphemed among the Gentiles."

IX. Therefore, stop your ears when anyone speaks to you apart from Jesus Christ, the Son of God, who was of the line of David, who was from Mary; who was truly born both of God and of a virgin, but not in the same way; for God and man are not the same. He truly took a body; for "the Word became flesh," and lived among us without sin. For "Who," He says, "among you convicts me of sin?" He truly ate and drank; He was crucified and died under Pontius Pilate. He was truly crucified and died, and not in appearance <note>original: *dokesei*; this is a direct attack on "Docetism," a heresy claiming Jesus only seemed to have a body and only seemed to suffer.</note>, while those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth were looking on. Those in heaven as the bodiless natures <note>Refers to the angels.</note>; those on earth, the Jews and Romans and the men present at that time when the Lord was crucified; and those under the earth, the multitude that rose with the Lord. For "Many bodies," it says, "of the saints who had fallen asleep were raised," when the tombs were opened. And He descended into Hades alone, but He ascended with a multitude; and He rent...

<summary>This page contains Ignatius’s urgent defense of the physical reality of Jesus’s birth, life, and death against Docetic heretics who claimed Christ only appeared to be human. He emphasizes that Christ’s suffering was real and witnessed by all realms of existence—heavenly, earthly, and subterranean.</summary>
